item.title: USDA, FBI breached by hackers amid spate of tech outages – reports
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Hackers breached the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the FBI, national media reported on Friday, amid deepening concerns over a spate of tech outages at key American institutions.

The breaches were first reported by NBC News and CNN respectively, and it remained unclear whether they were related and who was responsible.

Major outages in recent weeks have disrupted travel, communications and e-commerce for countless users across the US, even affecting a top-secret network at the National Security Agency.

Donald Trump has sought to calm the public, urging people to “relax”. Officials said the various outages were not linked to criminal activity.

The USDA told employees that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers was targeted in a cyber-attack, NBC reported on Friday, citing two former department officials.

The hackers may use the payments system as a back door to access more sensitive material, the former officials told NBC.

The USDA deals with “a bunch of scary biologic issues” and “if an adversary or a competitor were to have access to that same information … they could use our own research against us,” a former official was quoted as saying.

CNN said separately on Friday that the FBI was hacked for the second time since September.

The bureau was investigating an intrusion of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) by apparent hackers, CNN reported citing two people briefed on the probe.

The NCIC has a nationwide criminal information database linking federal, state and local law enforcement and is used to share information on warrants and background checks.

“Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety,” a former FBI official told CNN.

The former official expressed concerns that hackers “could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on”.

AFP has asked the FBI and the USDA for comment.

Ironically, the FBI director, Kash Patel, on Thursday appeared on the Fox News show hosted by Sean Hannity to tout measures his agency had implemented to thwart cyber-attacks.

Patel said the FBI and the US intelligence community would continue to “monitor those activities for nefarious actors” through an anti-cyber-attack initiative dubbed Operation Winter Shield.

“And when and if such an actor comes up, you can rest assured that this FBI is going to hunt them down,” Patel said.

The newly uncovered breaches at the FBI and the USDA were described as hacks, which are different from outages such as the ones that afflicted Microsoft Outlook and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) earlier in November.

In September, a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.

The Trump administration fired cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross on Thursday as criticism mounted over the string of major outages.

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-21 14:09 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/21/usda-fbi-outages-cyber-attack

item.title: Why Anthropic's blockbuster IPO couldn't escape the stock market correction
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

No one can say the Anthropic initial public offering wasn't a success for the company. Deal size and pricing were signs of what IPO experts say was insatiable demand for "ANT" shares. But what came within a day is something that investors better get used to: anxiety in the stock market about valuations being assigned to artificial intelligence revenue and business models that should keep Anthropic shares volatile in the period ahead.

The Anthropic IPO reinforces those fears rather than running counter to them, says Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital, which researches IPOs and manages the Renaissance IPO ETF (IPO).

"The volatility in the AI trade we've been seeing for the past few months stems from valuations and whether we are in a bubble, and that's been heightened and highlighted by the Anthropic IPO," Marquez said on "ETF Edge" on Friday.

And in the case of Anthropic, which finished trading Friday down 9%, the valuation anxiety becomes "so much more prevalent," she added, because it is a new stock.

It is not just any new stock, but one that has Wall Street adding downside risks to research notes likely never seen before, and which may be the greatest understatement (or most subtle equities research joke) in the history of earnings analysis. "Anthropic could develop AI systems which become fully autonomous and wipe out humanity which may lead to a serious decline in earnings," Seaport Research Partners analyst wrote Jay Goldberg wrote on Nov. 18.

"It was challenging company to value ... and it's very richly valued," Marquez said. "We're seeing something more reasonable and investors grappling now with where should this company actually be valued," she added.

The fact that Anthropic pulled off the deal in this market and was able to command the price it did was an achievement, according to Yuri Khodjamirian, chief investment officer at Tema ETFs, which offers multiple funds that invest in pre-IPO shares of companies and held Anthropic in its Tema Photonics & Optical ETF (LAZR) well before IPO day. "We have to remember they pulled off a very large IPO in the middle of a very severe market with the volatility in the tech sector specifically," Khodjamirian said on "ETF Edge."

"You always have to be a bit skeptical about 'oversubscribed' ... bankers put out all these numbers, but the reality is the IPO was successful and when you see the tech trade volatility ... welcome to the equities markets. This is what happens day-in and day-out," he said.

Khodjamirian says the investor demand for AI remains, but amid a reassessment of returns. And he says an equally hard task has now begun for Anthropic. Investors are unwinding positions in everything from tech stocks to gold and bitcoin, and repositioning for 2027 based on their new outlooks. "We are in a bit of vacuum," he said.

"From here on the market is trying trying to figure out what direction to go in," Khodjamirian said, whether that is based on Fed policy, geopolitics, the midterm elections results, or the AI trade. "In many cases, the chief investment officers I speak to, and the clients, say 'I'm just gonna take some risk off and wait and see until I get more info.' And with the Anthropic, the revenue picture and how the AI adoption curve progresses will be a vital stat to watch," he added.

Plenty of value has already been wiped out in tech, according to Khodjamirian, but investors need new signals to buy. That doesn't just go for Anthropic but for much of the market's tech leadership. "One of the things most difficult for investors to understand right now is some of the leadership in the market that has been taken by semiconductor companies," he said, adding that the peak was 22% of S&P 500 earnings. But these companies, like Nvidia and Micron, have a very different earnings profile from the rest of the market.

The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), which was down over 10% on Friday and around 15% for the week, was on pace for its worst week since September 2001, according to CNBC data on Friday afternoon. It also lost 15% in one week of March 2020. The tech sector of the S&P 500, tracked by the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK), turned in its worst weekly performance since the Covid crash.

Khodjamirian said while these stocks may look cheap on a P/E basis right now after the heavy selling, that requires faith in the earnings estimates, which he says will be more important as results are released for the next few years. "Right now it looks cheap, but will companies like Micron and Nvidia actually deliver?"

Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday, adding to its worst stretch of weekly performance since 2008. What's more, the single biggest trade in the options market on Friday was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF has a long way more to fall.

And the same caution about the outlook goes for Anthropic, he said. "That's why we need to watch Anthropic's annual recurring revenue number, because it is a key part of puzzle," he said.

Marquez said there is always hype in names like SpaceX and Anthropic when they go public, and it is hard to know whether the pricing of the deal is based on fundamentals, "but we just need more time and lots price discovery," she said. "It is not going to happen overnight," she added.

As an IPO researcher, she says this "discernment" is a healthy thing for the markets. There are few cases to look to as comps for Anthropic, other than SpaceX, and before that, way back to Facebook's IPO in 2012. And neither example is one of quick recovery. SpaceX shares remain well below their first-day closing price more than five months after its IPO. Facebook (now Meta), meanwhile, "did not do well for the first year after going public and we see where it is now. It's just the nature of these disruptive tech companies that come to market," Marquez said. "They lend themselves to more volatility and a longer period of price discovery for investors."…

Source: CNBC Top | Published: 2026-11-21 14:07 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/20/anthropic-ipo-ai-stock-market-selloff.html

item.title: Denmark to expel Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill US-Ukrainian rapper
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.

“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,” Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days.

“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he added.

Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.

Rasmussen also said that Denmark was considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians. “We have launched work at the European level to further tighten the rules governing access of Russian nationals to Europe,” he said. “We are now stepping up our efforts towards a halt to all non-essential visas.

“The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine. And we fully intend to continue supporting Ukraine.”

According to Reuters, Rasmussen sent a message on Friday evening to senior European diplomats proposing that the EU should halt tourist visas for Russian citizens and cease recognition of Russian non-biometric passports throughout the 29-nation Schengen free-travel zone.

“We must take concrete actions that project European strength and decisiveness,” the message said. “There is clear momentum to act decisively now, and we should seize this moment to replace our current patchwork of national measures with a truly unified EU-wide approach.”

The note also urged each EU member state to offer Russians more limited visas that do not allow travel to other countries in the Schengen zone, and to set tougher entry restrictions for serving and former Russian soldiers.

Police thwarted the alleged plot when they arrested three men with links to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Viktorovich Vasiliev, was due to perform at a concert on 25 September, which was then cancelled, officials said. Vasiliev holds US and Ukrainian nationality.

Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, the head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, said: “It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian intelligence services.”

According to prosecutors, the suspects were driving towards the concert venue north of Copenhagen with two loaded pistols and two knives when police arrested them at about 9.55pm, five minutes before the concert was due to begin. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening, police said.

One of the suspects had bought a ticket to the concert, according to the charges.

The suspects are charged under Section 108 of Denmark’s criminal code, which covers assisting a foreign intelligence service, as well as attempted murder. They denied wrongdoing in court, the broadcaster DR reported.

Kieffer-Kristensen said: “A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and risk-taking Russia.

“We believe that the case is important for understanding the threat that Denmark faces from Russia.”

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stood in full solidarity with Denmark and with all member states targeted by Russian hybrid attacks. She said the bloc would soon propose a “new European security strategy” to reinforce preparedness and deterrence.

The Russian embassy in Copenhagen said that Denmark’s accusations were not backed with proof.

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-21 14:03 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/20/denmark-russian-diplomat-us-ukrainian-rapper-attempted-killing

item.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles

LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.

With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.

Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.

"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.

Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren't presented as evidence during the trial.

Juror says Rinderknecht's own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict

Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.

"It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said. "After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he's guilty."

Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a "lack of information" presented to the jury about the technical review.

In the end, it was Rinderknecht's own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.

"Stating that he was up on the hill, didn't smell a fire, didn't see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night," Cameron said.

Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been 'mad at everything'

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did.

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.

They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

"He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"

These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.

They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.

Defense argues fire's origin is unproven

Haney cast doubt on the government's case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.

The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.

Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors' request to strike his testimony.

Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.

He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act."…

Source: NPR News | Published: 2026-11-21 13:58 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6049625/palisades-fire-conviction

item.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.

He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".

Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."

In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".

The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.

It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

Related topics

item.title: Riemann hypothesis: Has the world’s most famous maths problem been cracked?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Riemann hypothesis: Has the world’s most famous maths problem been cracked?

Mathematicians say the claimed proof, made with Claude, could be historic, but it may take weeks to understand it.

A mathematician from the tech giant Anthropic claims to have proven one of the world’s most famous – and most elusive – maths problems with the help of AI.

Levent Alpoge wrote on his website on Friday: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”

If his claim holds up, the proof he says he has would settle a question that has defeated mathematicians for 167 years. Independent experts are now trying to verify it, but so far no human has read through the entire argument.

Here is what we know.

What is the Riemann hypothesis?

First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is widely regarded as the most important open question in pure mathematics.

Prime numbers are whole numbers which can be divided only by one and themselves, such as 2, 3, 5 and 7. They appear to be scattered along the number line with no obvious pattern but the Riemann hypothesis proposes that their overall distribution actually follows a deep, hidden order – just one that humans have yet to identify.

“The Riemann hypothesis is the most famous and important unsolved problem in mathematics,” Abhishek Saha, professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.

“The patterns of the primes are encoded in a mathematical object called the Riemann zeta function, introduced by Bernhard Riemann in 1859.”

It is one of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1m award.

What has the Anthropic mathematician claimed?

Alpoge, a member of the company’s technical staff, made the announcement on Friday in a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said the proof he has found covers the generalised Riemann hypothesis, which extends the original conjecture to a broader family of mathematical functions.

He did not publish a conventional paper. Alpoge released the argument in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks reasoning step by step. He was open about how much of the work was Claude’s, writing that “Claude far outpaced me near the finish line”.

Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said nobody yet understands what the proof actually shows.

“At the minute, we don’t even know why the theorem is true,” he told Al Jazeera. “It’s 17 million lines of Lean code, and this might correspond to tens of thousands of pages of mathematics. We don’t even yet know how much of this mathematics is new ideas, how much of it is just sort of standard stuff the machine just had to develop.

“At the minute, the proof is just millions of lines of gobbledygook written in a strange programming language,” he said. “And right now, as we speak, there’s people all over the world who are translating parts of this programming language back into English.”

He expects answers to come fairly soon, however. “Experience shows you that you give the humans the Lean code, and within a week or two, they have a much better understanding of what’s actually going on in this code,” he said.

Why is the Riemann hypothesis so important?

“The implications of this hypothesis extend across large parts of mathematics, and hundreds of other mathematical results have been proved assuming this hypothesis is true,” Saha said. “A proof would settle a question that has occupied some of the greatest mathematical minds for over 160 years.”

Buzzard said the result also matters beyond pure mathematics, including for internet security.

“We know there are some algorithms that we run where they’re very quick, but we don’t actually know for sure if they work,” he said. “They seem to work, and we know that if the generalised Riemann hypothesis is true, then they do work.”

He said cryptographers had long worked on the assumption that the Riemann hypothesis is true. “In practice, people do tend to assume that the Riemann hypothesis is true because it’s a viable hypothesis to assume, because there’s so much evidence that it’s true,” he said. “But we can sleep slightly safer in our beds at night because it is true.”

Buzzard said the result stands out among recent AI breakthroughs in mathematics. He compared it with the Navier-Stokes problem, another Millennium Prize problem, which OpenAI said an unreleased AI model had solved in September. “That one doesn’t really have any applications at all,” he said, calling it “just of theoretical interest”. “Whereas the Riemann hypothesis has applications to neighbouring fields.

“It’s a very hard problem, but it’s definitely not the hardest problem in mathematics,” he said, pointing to even stronger versions such as the “extended Riemann hypothesis and the grand Riemann hypothesis”.

“The Riemann hypothesis is just, in some sense, at the foot of a mountain,” he said. “We’re beginning our trek up the mountain with this theorem.”

Why has it remained so elusive for so long?

“The problem is relatively simple to state, but extraordinarily difficult to prove,” Saha said. “Mathematicians have developed vast amounts of sophisticated theory in their attempts to solve it, but none of the techniques developed over the past 167 years has been sufficient. The direct methods have all been tried, and none of them come close to resolving it.

“Until very recently, most mathematicians, myself included, believed that a proof would require substantial new mathematical theories, perhaps developed over the next few decades.”

He said the claimed proof had overturned his expectations. “My own intuition was that we were still several years away from a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. This claimed proof, if correct, shatters my model of reality,” he said.…

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-21 12:49 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/riemann-hypothesis-has-the-worlds-most-famous-maths-problem-been-cracked?traffic_source=rss

item.title: An ancient failed rift is reawakening inside one of Africa's oldest landmasses
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

An ancient failed rift is reawakening inside one of Africa's oldest landmasses

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

In April 2017, a magnitude 6.5 earthquake shook southern Africa from an unlikely place: the middle of the Kalahari Craton in eastern Botswana. Cratons are the ancient cores of continents, and this one is built from blocks of crust up to 3.7 billion years old. Geologists have long considered such regions too cold, too thick and too rigid to tear apart.

Now, a new study led by researchers at the Botswana International University of Science and Technology (BIUST) and the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory shows that the craton is indeed being pulled apart. It also shows that the rift doing the pulling has tried this before. The findings are published in the journal Tectonics. The work challenges long-held assumptions about continental stability, revealing how ancient geological seams can reactivate to fracture even the oldest continental cores.

"The earthquake happened in the middle of the craton, a region where no one expected to have an active fault slipping, let alone an active plate boundary developing," says co-author Folarin Kolawole. He is a structural geologist at Lamont and an assistant professor in the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences within the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

The new rift lies at the far southern tip of the East African Rift System, where the African continent is slowly stretching apart. Rifts like these are the earliest stage of a divergent plate boundary, the kind that splits a continent and opens a new ocean if successful. For decades, scientists thought the southern end of this system lay in the Okavango Rift Zone of northern Botswana, first identified in the 1970s by Lamont geologist Christopher Scholz and colleagues. Studies of the 2017 earthquake revealed that it reaches nearly 200 miles (320 kilometers) farther, into the craton itself.

This is a surprise, considering how rifts usually go around cratons rather than through them. Around the world, continental rifts tend to follow mountain belts—the younger and weaker zones where ancient cratons once collided. Only a handful of rifts, such as the one that opened the Labrador Sea between Canada and Greenland, are known to have broken across a craton. "It's counterintuitive," Kolawole says. "It basically challenges age-old thinking."

"Whether rifts do propagate through cratons has been a really big question in geoscience," says the study's lead author, Boniface Kgosidintsi of BIUST.

To understand how the rift is breaking into the craton, the team focused on the Khurutshe Fault, which cuts a 50-mile-long (80-kilometer-long) scarp, or step, across the flat Kalahari landscape about 50 miles (80 kilometers) south of the 2017 earthquake. In places, the land on one side of the fault sits as much as 400 feet (120 meters) higher than the other.

The researchers dug trenches across the scarp alongside Botswana's A1 highway and examined deeper excavations dug for a government water pipeline. They imaged the rock below with electrical resistivity tomography, which Kolawole likens to a CAT scan of the fault. And they analyzed records from 20 groundwater boreholes drilled across the area.

All three lines of evidence told the same story. When a fault slips, the land on one side drops, and sediment piles up in the low spot, forming a wedge that thickens toward the fault. The team found that both the modern Kalahari Desert sands and much older rock layers from the Jurassic period form such wedges against the same fault. That means the fault was moving in the Jurassic, roughly 180 million years ago, and is moving again today.

The trenches the researchers dug revealed more details about the fault's past. Beneath reddish-brown, windblown Kalahari sand, the team hit hard, highly cemented Jurassic sandstone shot through with white veins of calcite, "a spider web network of whitish lines through the rocks," Kolawole says. The calcite was deposited by hot fluids, like those that build mineral terraces at Yellowstone's hot springs, rising through cracks opened by the fault. Some rock surfaces were polished and scored by slip along the fault.

The team concludes that the rift first opened during a period of continent-wide stretching in the Jurassic, then failed and went dormant until the East African Rift System began pulling on it again. Exactly when it reawakened isn't known, but the fault has offset the young Kalahari sands, which were laid down mostly within the last 2.6 million years. "We believe Khurutshe is one of the failed Mesozoic rifts within the craton and is reactivating," Kgosidintsi says. The rift is in its earliest stage of development, but it is not new.

Flaws in the armor

The researchers also found that faulting began before volcanic activity reached the area during the Jurassic, suggesting that magma alone did not weaken the craton enough to start the rift. Instead, the rift appears to have exploited existing weak spots. The active rifts in eastern Botswana follow an ancient seam where the Kalahari Craton's oldest pieces fused together billions of years ago.

"While cratons are regarded as strong old continental blocks, they do have inherent zones of weakness that can localize a new plate boundary," Kolawole says. And breaking one may take persistence: "Maybe you need to reactivate the rift multiple times. You need to try multiple times before it actually succeeds."…

item.title: Meet the science adviser behind Netflix's hit series 'Below'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, clear explanation

Meet the science adviser behind Netflix's hit series 'Below'

Live Science spoke with marine biologist Annie Mercier about her role as a science adviser for Netflix's show "Below."

In Netflix's new series "Below," an ancient, squid-like creature known as "Mudder" threatens a small coastal community in Newfoundland, Canada, arriving around the same time as a mysterious iceberg that starts causing dangerous hallucinations in the town's residents.

The series blends marine science, horror and environmental themes, harking back to Newfoundland's long-standing connections with giant squid (Architeuthis dux), with the first sightings going back to the 1870s.

Annie Mercier, a marine biologist in the Department of Ocean Sciences at Memorial University in Newfoundland and Labrador, was brought on as a science adviser in 2025 just before Netflix began shooting "Below." Mercier's research focuses on deep sea organisms, studying their behavior, interactions and how they respond to environmental stressors like climate change.

Mercier's lab at the Ocean Sciences Center was used as a filming location, and she met with actor Mackenzie Davis, who plays the research scientist Dr. Fonda Howander to guide the character. Live Science spoke with Mercier about how she helped bring Mudder — and the scientific endeavour to unravel its mystery — to life.

Annie Mercier is a professor in the Department of Ocean Sciences at Memorial University inNewfoundland and Labrador, Canada. She studies marine animals and their response to environmental conditions, conducting research on the behaviors and interactions of diverse invertebrate species from Arctic and deep-sea environments.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How did you end up getting involved with "Below" as a scientific adviser?

Annie Mercier: Early in 2025, when they were just about to start filming or were finalizing the scripts, I heard that Jesse Mckeown [the director] was looking for a scientific adviser, preferably someone here in Newfoundland. We heard about it through Memorial University's communications team. They mentioned that there would be something about an ancient cephalopod in the series.

I'm not an expert in cephalopods … But I do have a broad background in marine biology, and I'm here at the Ocean Sciences Centre. I sent back my reply, and they eventually contacted me to ask more about what I was doing and what I'd worked on in the past. My research is centered around strange creatures and trying to understand them through curiosity-driven research, so I guess that resonated with them.

Another factor was that I'd previously worked as a consultant on documentaries and television series. I'd done a little work with the BBC, helping explain video sequences, as well as fiction series back in Quebec. I also write popular articles and books for general audiences, so I'm familiar with navigating between science and fiction and with trying to convey something wonderful about science in language that general audiences can understand. I guess that played a role as well, and they eventually asked me to be the adviser.

KHC: What did the advising process look like?

AM: There were two phases. The main thing was that they wanted to share the scripts early on. That's when I was brought in.

Jesse told me they would send scripts at regular intervals, in sequence, starting with the first episode, then the second, and so forth. They would securely send me each script. We had some preliminary discussions to establish exactly what they wanted, because that was my question: How much detail or what kind of feedback were they looking for?

They told me that whatever came to mind, I should suggest it. Of course, I knew they couldn't take everything into account, but I think they wanted to know how far-fetched or how close to reality some of the things were. They asked me to focus mostly on the scientific aspects.

That included the squid, but also how they portrayed the scientific work and the character involved in it. They had climate change, icebergs, ocean currents and a number of other scientific elements in the story.

I went through every script and provided feedback on all sorts of things. Sometimes it was something as simple as the timing of an event. I pointed out things related to the migrations of marine animals and other details that I knew were a little different from reality.

I provided written feedback and sometimes links to additional information. I'd send it back, and occasionally there would be a follow-up meeting or a remote conversation about certain elements. It depended on the situation.

When they started filming, Jesse wanted to schedule a time for me to go behind the scenes and chat with the crew. It was difficult to coordinate because they were filming on three or more sets around Newfoundland, and I was working. Eventually, I managed to visit on a Saturday when they were filming at the Ocean Sciences Centre. I spent some time in the control room, met Mackenzie [Davis] and got to see what they were doing on-site.

KHC: How much feedback did you end up giving on Mudder, the giant, squid-like creature? What aspects did you think were accurate, and where did the show take creative liberties?

AM: Of course, when you're asked about giant squids and you know it's a fictional show, all sorts of things come to mind. I was hoping they wouldn't go the route of having the arms come out and a giant squid jump onto a boat, or something like "20,000 Leagues Under the Sea." You see those kinds of things in some of the drawings from the 1800s, too. So I had some fears about that.

But when I read the scripts, I could see they were trying to make it as close to reality as possible. Obviously, they had some freedom because it's portrayed as an ancient, social type of cephalopod — more like a squid but with some octopus-like behaviors as well.…

Source: Live Science | Published: 2026-11-21 14:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'

Senior Editor

Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We've always had trouble measuring them in the "megaelectronvolt" (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the "MeV gap." But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20–200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

The "gap" comes from a technological blind spot. Scientists have plenty of tools in the lower-energy spectra, such as the Chandra X-ray Observatory, that can capture radiation at the X-ray end of the electromagnetic spectrum. They also have a great number of tools at the high end of gamma-ray spectroscopy, including the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which is capable of finding higher-energy gamma rays.

But why are low-energy gamma rays so hard to catch? Gamma rays notoriously pass right through mirrors and every other attempt to reflect them. Telescopes like Fermi-LAT can be thought of more as particle detectors in orbit than traditional telescopes. They track what happens when a gamma-ray photon hits layers of tungsten and silicon inside their chassis.

At high energies—around 1 gigaelectronvolt (GeV)—the damage done to those layers is catastrophic enough to be able to trace a line back to a source. However, in the lower 20–200 MeV range, the photons scatter much more randomly, making it difficult to track where precisely they came from.

Fermi-LAT is only capable of tracking a single 20 MeV photon to a patch of the sky about 20 degrees wide—more than 40 times the size of the full moon. Combine that with a massive amount of background radiation caused by everything from the sun to distant galaxies, and it can be a real pain to pick out the direction of any one particular source.

However, Fermi-LAT has been operating now for almost two decades, and with that much data, there's some math that can help. The researchers combined 14 years' worth of collected data with some advanced statistical modeling techniques to pinpoint 450 distinct gamma-ray sources, cataloged in what they are calling the Second Catalog of Low-Energy Fermi-LAT Sources, or 2FLE. Cross-checking them with other radio, optical and X-ray data showed known counterparts for 377 of those objects.

The vast majority of those objects—325 of them—are far outside the Milky Way. Almost half of the entire group of objects consists of flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), a very extreme type of active galactic nucleus. FSRQs represent a type of "blazar"—a supermassive black hole that is pointing one of its twin jets of plasma directly at Earth. The 2FLE catalog confirms that FSRQ blazars pump out the majority of their energy in this 20–200 MeV spectral window.

Closer to home, the catalog includes 52 sources from inside the Milky Way. Most of them are pulsars—the spinning leftovers left behind when a supermassive star explodes into a supernova. But one intriguing outlier was gamma rays that appear to be coming from M2, a globular cluster, which would mark the first time it's ever been observed at gamma-ray energies.

Perhaps the most intriguing part of the paper, though, is the 73 sources that don't have a clear counterpart at other energies. Sixty of those appear to be brand-new gamma-ray discoveries. And while some of those signals might turn out to be overlapping signals from neighboring objects, it's likely there are at least some truly new exotic cosmic accelerators in the data set awaiting follow-up observations.

One particular mystery source seems to align with an object called 2FLE J0340.8+5258, which seems to also have been detected by an observatory in China and appears to be capable of generating light across nine orders of magnitude in energy.

Fermi-LAT itself seems to have reached its limit with this new data set. The researchers have likely squeezed everything they could out of the decades of data from this satellite, which was originally launched in 2008.

However, there are other gamma-ray missions coming online, including NASA's Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI), which is designed specifically to look for gamma rays in the 0.2–5 MeV range using a special type of germanium detector that has only become available in the last few years. Combining that new data with the decades' worth of Fermi data might finally shed some light on one of the longest-standing blind spots in the extreme physics of the universe.

More information

A. Adelfio et al., The Second Catalog of Low-energy Fermi-LAT Sources, The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series (2026). DOI: 10.3847/1538-4365/aeb54d

Provided by Universe Today

Source: Phys.org | Published: 2026-11-21 13:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: The Secrets Hiding in a Duck-Billed Dinosaur’s Beak
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Hadrosaurs might not be the most popular dinosaurs among children, but they were extremely popular with natural selection. These duck-billed dinosaurs were some of the most common types of herbivores living during the Cretaceous period, and as such, they’re well-represented in the fossil record. Remarkably, we’re still learning new things about them and their eponymous bills.

For more than a decade, paleontologists puzzled over a series of bony projections around the front rim of the upper jaw of Tethyshadros, a genus of duck-billed dinosaur first discovered in Italy’s Villaggio del Pescatore. At first, they were believed to be a set of comb-like teeth, but now a new analysis published in Royal Society Open Science is revealing that they were far more complicated.

Read more: “This Bizarre Jurassic “Squid” Swam the Ancient Seas of Wyoming”

An international team of paleontologists conducted extensive micro-CT scans of the upper and lower jaw from a specimen named “Antonio,” the holotype of the genus. They determined that the mysterious spikes weren’t teeth at all—they weren’t even visible from the outside. Instead, they were a kind of scaffold supporting the dinosaur’s beak.

Made out of keratin (the same substance as fingernails), the beak had a complex network of minuscule bony channels feeding into it which housed nerves and capillaries. “What looked like a bizarre toothed or spiked beak may actually be the bony footprint of a much more complex living organ,” study author Marco Muscioni of the University of Bologna explained in a statement.

According to the team, it’s likely Tethyshadros’ beak functioned as a Swiss Army knife of sorts. A network of nerves wired it as a useful sensory organ for foraging, blood vessels indicate it could have helped radiate heat from its brain, and it was still sturdy enough to withstand the wear and tear grazing on gritty vegetation (in fact, it bears some resemblance to a cow’s hoof).

“Tethyshadros continues to surprise us,” study author Federico Fanti of the University of Bologna said. “The Villaggio del Pescatore fossils are among the most complete dinosaurs ever found in Europe, but new technologies are showing that even specimens we have studied for years can still preserve completely unexpected information.”

Enjoying Nautilus? Subscribe to our free newsletter.

Lead Image: Davide Bonadonna

item.title: International talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control on the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am on Saturday morning, after all night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.

Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the Review Conference on Conventional Weapons at the UN in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.

The mandate simply asks countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.

Although Russia led the objections using uniquely obstructive stalling tactics from the opening day, other military powers who have all invested heavily in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.

Some argued that international humanitarian law is sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges.

European and Nato states, including Ukraine, as well as China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.

The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons was discussed in the meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.

South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.

The CCW is a particular UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.

Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said the world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week.

“Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”

Diplomats inside the negotiations said that Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.

The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.

Speaking at a different conference, organised by Atlantic magazine, the former US national security adviser John Bolton said: “We are moving closer and closer to almost totally unmanned warfare in the battle field. I am not sure we need manned aircraft anymore if we have the right drone technology.

“The boundaries western civilisation tried to draw between war and civilian life are disintegrating.”

Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.

Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that the states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years already, and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.

Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, told the Guardian that autonomous weapons needed binding law.

She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months, and dismissed the US’s proposal for five years to sort out a mandate.

A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.

“These are not weapons of the future that are being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems,” Brazil’s delegate told the floor on Wednesday.

Source: The Guardian Science | Published: 2026-11-21 13:15 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says

The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.

That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas.

Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.

"In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit.

He didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX plans to shift most Starship launches to its new Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.)

Musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.)

The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle.

Before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions, and it had reflown a booster twice. But the company had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly.

So snagging Ship on the first try was a very big deal, according to Musk.

"Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how important this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday.

And SpaceX is very serious about Starship reuse. Musk has said that the company wants to launch about 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030.

This mind-boggling cadence will help the company build out two enormous megaconstellations in low Earth orbit — the next iteration of its Starlink broadband network, which will consist of about 100,000 satellites, and its Starmind AI data-center constellation, which will be 10 times bigger than that.

Assembly of that new Starlink network is already underway. Ship carried 26 of the next-gen internet spacecraft up for the first time on Flight 14, which launched on Sept. 28, and repeated the feat on Flight 15.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

item.title: How to use your phone if the grid goes down
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information, clear explanation

You probably don’t need reminding about our intense reliance on our phones for communication—so what happens when the networks that those phones rely on go down? Power and tech outages continue to cause disruptions, and that can leave you stuck when it comes to staying in touch with others.

There are options available to you though, both in terms of what you can do on your phone, and what you can use instead of it. You’ll need to make sure the people you’re chatting with have set up the same options, so it’s worth mentioning at the next family or friends gathering.

Power outages can be different in scope and type, but for the purposes of this guide we’ll imagine a localized power grid collapse that has knocked out your Wi-Fi router and your local cell tower—but not a global shutdown that’s taken out all infrastructure, including the ground stations communicating with satellites in orbit.

How to communicate with your phone during an outage

If you’ve acquired a phone from Apple, Samsung, or Google in the last two or three years, it comes with satellite communications built in, so you can still text friends and family if the cell towers go out (calling isn’t an option, due to bandwidth). The feature should kick in automatically in Messages on iOS, or in Google Messages on Android, provided your carrier supports it—you’ll just see a prompt on screen.

Follow the instructions to find a satellite and start texting. There’s nothing to enable or turn on, but if you want to test it out beforehand so you know it works, open Settings then pick Apps > Messages > Satellite Connection Demo (iOS), or Safety and emergency > Satellite SOS (Android).

There is another option on your phone, which is to try a peer-to-peer messaging app. These apps need to be downloaded in advance and work over Bluetooth to send messages in a mesh created by the devices themselves. That means a limited range, but you don’t need any Wi-Fi or cellular connectivity.

One of the best apps in this category is Bridgefy, which you can get for Android and iOS. It’s free to use, simple to operate, and has a range of around 100 meters (or 330 feet). You don’t have to wait until the power goes out to use it either, because you could set up a mesh chat when you’re out camping, or taking a trip with family.

Alternative devices to replace your phone for emergencies

Unless you do a lot of outdoor, off-grid adventuring, you might not have realized just how many devices now exist that can keep you connected even without access to Wi-Fi or cellular networks. Some of these options work via the same satellite networks as your phone.

Have a look at the Garmin InReach Messenger Plus, for example, a $299.99 communicator you can use whenever cell networks are down (or just out of range). You’re also going to need an active subscription. They start at $7.99 a month, but once you’re set up you can connect to the wider world from just about anywhere.

Then there are the more straightforward walkie-talkie devices, which operate over radio signals across a range of a few miles. That might just be enough if you’ve got friends and family you need to contact when the power’s out. There are plenty of devices to choose between, but the Motorola T802 Talkabout is a good example and under $100 for a pair.

Don’t forget a battery-powered radio either. It won’t let you message anyone directly, but it will mean you can stay up to date with what’s happening out there in the world, and it might give you an idea of when the power’s going to come back on. You can even get models that work via solar or hand-crank power, like this $30 emergency radio.

General tech tips for a power outage

All of your phones and other devices will need power if they’re going to keep you in touch with other people—otherwise you’ll be relying on smoke signals and postal couriers. So it’s wise to invest in a portable power station ahead of time. Something like the $289 Jackery Explorer 300 would do the job.

Obviously you’re going to want to charge up these hefty power stations before the electricity gets cut, otherwise they won’t be much use. But you’re actually not as reliant on the power grid as you might think. Many models (including those offered by Jackery) have solar panel add-ons you can invest in as well.

Even with a backup supply in place, it’s a good idea to try and conserve power on your gadgets as much as possible too. Your phones, tablets, and laptops will all have low power settings you can make use of, but there are standard tips that apply across just about every gadget. Reduce screen brightness and volume as much as possible, and enable airplane mode where you can.

When you do have power and Wi-Fi available, make sure you download as much essential info to your phone as you can, so it’s still there when an internet connection isn’t. This is particularly useful for maps: Both Google Maps (Settings > Offline maps) and Apple Maps (Profile picture > Offline maps) let you do this.

item.title: How red squirrels made island their home
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

How red squirrels made island their home

With growing concerns that red squirrels could soon become extinct in England, one Channel Island is a corner of the British Isles where they maintain a stronghold.

Jersey is home to a thriving red squirrel population, thanks to the complete absence of grey squirrels, which carry a virus deadly to their red cousins.

Red squirrels are endangered in the UK, with about 120,000 to 160,000 left in the wild and various projects are aiming to boost those numbers.

There have some strongholds in England, external, particularly islands, and 75% of the British population is in Scotland, external.

However, despite not being native to Jersey, Henry Glynn, an ecologist with the National Trust of Jersey, said they "really are iconic for Jersey".

He said: "When you speak to people who have come over to visit the island from the UK, a lot of them will say that one of the things they want to do whilst here is to see a red squirrel, because they're so rare and so difficult to see in large parts of the UK.

"That is actually really special for them."

Red squirrels are not native to Jersey, having been introduced in 1885.

However, Glynn described them as "naturalised", having become "assimilated into the natural environment" over many years.

The animals have previously featured in Visit Jersey, external tourism campaigns, including one fronted by conservationist Ben Fogle.

The National Trust of Jersey said the island was an "important refuge" for the red squirrel, where they were "fairly widespread, external".

It said the inland valleys and woodlands were the best places to spot them.

The species is legally protected, which means it would be a criminal offence to harm them.

Nina Powell, senior animal carer at the JSPCA [Jersey Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals], said Jersey has a "good population" of squirrels and that "you can see them almost anywhere".

While the primary reason for their success is the lack of grey squirrels, Powell said they also thrived "because people look out for them".

She said: "A lot of people do support them, put out feeders and stuff like that.

"Their habitats are decreasing everywhere... but we do have quite a lot of nature reserves.

"In some places, we've got rope bridges which really help them cross the roads, and our speed limits are quite low, so that helps them as well".

She said the JSPCA had handled 50 red squirrels so far this year, including hand-raising eight babies, called kits (kittens).

She said: "We want to keep all animals as wild as possible, so we try and be as hands-off as possible.

"Some of them don't like us... some of them are quite sweet. They really do vary in personality."

Glynn agreed that their success had come in part because of the efforts of islanders.

He said: "They're really beloved amongst the local community as well. A lot of people put out squirrel feeders or love to see them in the garden.

"We get lots of reports from people who just want to tell us they've seen them because they're so happy to have them around."

Source: BBC Science & Environment | Published: 2026-11-21 12:18 UTC | Difficulty: 50/100

item.title: Despite soaring demand for GLP-1s, many eligible patients are unable to access these drugs for weight loss
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Despite soaring demand for GLP-1s, many eligible patients are unable to access these drugs for weight loss

In just a few short years, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have surged in popularity across the United States, transforming from specialized treatments for type 2 diabetes into revolutionary therapeutics for weight management, cardiovascular health and other emerging uses. But not all populations are benefiting from this expansion. As GLP-1 use has increased, disparities in access to these drugs have widened significantly, according to a new study led by researchers at Boston University School of Public Health (BUSPH).

Published in the journal Health Affairs Scholar, the study found that the percentage of patients with overweight or obesity and without type 2 diabetes who filled prescriptions for semaglutide (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy) and tirzepatide (sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound) within six months of becoming eligible surged from 1.9% in 2021 to 16.6% in 2025.

But prescriptions for these medications were lower among men, Black or Hispanic patients, younger or older patients (ages 18–34 or 55–64), patients in a lower BMI category and/or patients whose health care provider was located in a neighborhood with lower socioeconomic status (SES), measured by education levels in the provider's ZIP code.

These disparities widened over time and were particularly pronounced in 2024 and 2025, after semaglutide and tirzepatide received formal approval by the Food and Drug Administration for chronic weight management in 2021 and 2023, respectively.

By mimicking a natural hormone that helps regulate insulin, blood sugar, appetite and digestion, GLP-1s can help people achieve dramatic weight loss, particularly those who struggle to lose weight through traditional diet and exercise. Health experts worry that persistent challenges with GLP-1 accessibility and affordability are hindering large swaths of eligible people from receiving life-changing and potentially lifesaving treatment.

"Our study focuses on a population that is especially vulnerable to inequities in GLP-1 access," says study senior author Dr. Andrew Stokes, an associate professor of global health at BUSPH, who studies population health, aging and mortality, including inequities in GLP-1 access.

"We have better treatments for obesity than ever, but access to them hasn't caught up. It is much easier for people with diabetes to get these drugs covered by insurance. But for people living with overweight or obesity, coverage is very difficult to obtain—even when they qualify—because providers and insurers don't always view these as conditions that merit treatment. This is a population that has been left behind."

As these medications continue to gain prominence, the findings underscore the need for health care providers to receive appropriate training and resources about prescribing GLP-1 treatments, as well as the need for improvements in insurance companies' drug benefit design to ensure that people who qualify for these treatments can easily access them.

"GLP-1 receptor agonists are moving into routine care very quickly, but without deliberate action, these drugs risk widening the health inequities that obesity already reflects," says study lead and corresponding author Dr. Minh Trung Le, a research data analyst in the Department of Global Health at BUSPH at the time of the study.

Stokes and Le utilized medical claims data from a national database that includes closed claims for more than 175 million patients. For the analysis, they examined health information, GLP-1 treatment and health care provider locations among 512,389 eligible, commercially insured patients ages 18–64. The analysis did not include patients covered by Medicaid or Medicare, people without insurance or prescriptions obtained through direct-to-consumer channels.

Despite the nearly ninefold rise in GLP-1 prescriptions among eligible patients during the study period, the researchers point out that the vast majority of eligible patients still do not receive these prescriptions for weight management. People with employer-sponsored and other commercial insurance are more likely to have access to GLP-1s.

That racial disparities in access to these medications were still evident among the study's commercially insured participants underscores the long-standing structural barriers to health care that Black and Hispanic patients experience, even as they are burdened by obesity and other health conditions at greater rates than other populations. Black and Hispanic patients are more likely to face biases and stigma in health care, mistrust of the health care system and higher medication costs, all of which can exacerbate racial disparities in GLP-1 uptake.

The expansion in GLP-1 medication use also disproportionately benefited patients who saw providers in higher-SES neighborhoods. These SES disparities were smaller in the beginning of the study period but widened over time and were larger among patients in lower BMI categories. These disparities were also particularly pronounced among men, which the researchers say may reflect men's lower likelihood of seeking weight-management care.

"Patients seen at clinics in lower socioeconomic neighborhoods had about 35% lower odds of being prescribed semaglutide or tirzepatide in 2024–2025; early on, that gap was about 15%," says Le. Insurance coverage alone doesn't close the gap, he says. "We need to look at how drug benefits are designed, including prior authorization, step therapy and out-of-pocket costs that land unevenly on different patients. We also need to give under-resourced practices real support, such as help with prior-authorization paperwork, so that a clinic's administrative capacity doesn't decide who gets treated."…
