item.title: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: light-hearted, but not particularly informative

Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work

- Published

There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's.

Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish.

From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive.

"We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah.

She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left".

'Suss out the smelliness'

Casey, a content creator for an energy company, says he used to eat tuna at his desk but has since "reformed".

He says you have to "suss out the smelliness" and then decide if it's acceptable to eat at the desk.

But fish isn't the only food causing office friction and Casey says his regular snack of cinnamon pretzels has been causing "quite a bit of havoc".

"The sugar's going everywhere and it's getting in my laptop keys," he admits. No-one in the office has commented on it yet but he says he's hiding the crumbs by "shuffling them off the desk".

Boiled eggs also split opinion. Laura, who works in finance, says she's been teased by colleagues for eating them.

"In my defence, it was high protein, it was cost-effective and healthy â I swear by a good boiled egg."

She thinks that no food is off limits at the desk. "Coming from an Asian background where you'd eat fish for breakfast I am very open to it being eaten."

Ashlea Fisher, who runs her own recruitment company, has tackled the issue of smelly food in the office head on when she asked a member of staff to stop bringing in fish after "the smell was so bad that a pregnant colleague was feeling physically sick".

"I'm a big believer in being able to have an honest conversation with your team," she says, and suggests that other people in her position should approach a conversation lightly and be conscious of not embarrassing colleagues.

"Nobody should feel judged for what they eat, and we should respect different cultures and dietary requirements, but being mindful of the people around you is simply good workplace etiquette."

Do you take a lunch break?

While what we eat in the office at lunch can cause tension, there's also the question of whether we're even taking the time to enjoy our lunch in the first place.

In a world of back-to-back meetings and overflowing inboxes, it's easy to skip our break and shovel down a sandwich with one hand while replying to emails with the other.

A 2025 report by Just Eat found that the youngest workers, Gen Z, were the most likely to take a full break, with 56% doing so.

However, the next generation up, millennials were more likely than any other to eat lunch at their desk.

"While it can be convenient to eat at your desk, it's not best practice to remain glued to the screen all day," says Alan Price, an employment law and HR expert, and CEO of BrightHR.

"Taking a break isn't just an employment right, there are proven benefits for both physical and mental health."

Laura, whose working day can occasionally finish at 2am, says stepping away from her desk is a non-negotiable and she makes a point of taking an hour for lunch, describing it as "essential for maintaining my sanity".

"I take my lunch break as much as possible, for the sake of my eyes and mental wellbeing," she says.

But others are less precious about it. Content creator Manny says he has lunch at his desk "most of the time".

His work is task-based and his company operates a policy of "do the work when you want to do it".

"Usually you just take 20 minutes to eat something, but on another day you might take an hour. You just kind of feel it out," he says.

item.title: Judge extends deadline for Trump’s deposition in $10bn BBC lawsuit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: legal news, but not directly related to business

Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge, gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned.

But on Tuesday, the president got something of a reprieve when Jeffrey Kuntz, a federal district court judge, approved a joint motion by the parties and extended the deadline for Trump’s deposition until 22 January. The judge also pushed back the deadline for discovery in the case from 18 December to 29 January.

Trump had originally agreed to sit for a deposition on 16 October, but his team backed out, citing “matters of national importance”. That led the BBC to file a motion to compel Trump to sit for a deposition in a timely fashion.

According to the joint motion filed on Monday, the BBC has agreed to the Trump team’s proposal for the president to sit for a deposition between 11 January and 22 January after his representatives said he was unavailable to do so this year “due to his schedule and the nature of his profession”. As that timeline nears, the parties will meet to select a date and identify a secure location for the deposition.

“It is Trump’s case, so he should expect to be deposed,” Kuntz wrote in his order. “It appears he acknowledges that reality.”

The judge ordered the parties to schedule Trump’s deposition by Friday at noon. Kuntz scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

So far, Trump’s lawyers have deposed seven defendant witnesses. As part of the agreement between Trump and the BBC, the president’s lawyers will not depose Samir Shah, the BBC chair, or a former BBC director-general – nor any current or former BBC employee – until the president sits for questioning.

While Trump’s seven-hour-long deposition will be videotaped, it will only be available to attorneys for the parties.

In addition to Trump, the BBC might also be able to depose his daughter, Ivanka Trump, his son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner. “Defendant is currently conferring with President Trump and these non-parties regarding the subpoenas directed to them, given that these non-parties may be objecting to, or moving to quash, those subpoenas,” the parties wrote in their joint motion.

Last week, Kuntz, a Trump appointee, refused the BBC’s request to dismiss the case, though he threw out the president’s contention that the broadcaster violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.

“BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a 70-minute-long speech into 12 seconds,” the judge wrote in his ruling. “But the court is not persuaded.”

item.title: New net-zero community will become Michigan’s first virtual power plant
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear reporting on a significant environmental development

Mitch Hall and his wife, Lori, live in one of the most sustainable communities in the U.S. Their town house is among a few dozen residences constructed so far at Veridian at County Farm, a fossil-fuel-free, net-zero-energy development in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Homes here make about as much solar energy as they consume, with the help of batteries that save solar power for use in the evenings.

Now, the couple is eager to share the benefits of their clean energy infrastructure with the wider grid.

In the coming weeks, Veridian households can enroll in Michigan’s first residential pilot of a virtual power plant; Detroit-based utility DTE Energy will then be able to remotely control the network of residents’ home batteries to inject their stored solar power onto the grid when operators need it most.

“This pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability,” Joi Harris, president and chief executive officer of DTE Energy, said in a statement. VPPs can smooth out demand peaks, reducing the utility’s need to invest in grid-infrastructure upgrades and generate kilowatt-hours with expensive fossil fuel peaker plants, both of which would pile costs on consumers.

The initiative “should work well for the residents, too,” Hall said. “DTE will pay us a little bit to be part of this project.” Because the utility will pull battery power automatically when the grid is strained and electricity prices are likely to be highest, “a neat part about the virtual power plant is you don’t have to spend a lot of time learning and trying to optimize,” he noted. “DTE will manage that battery for you.” (DTE did not respond to Canary Media’s request for exact figures on how much it would compensate customers in time for publication.)

VPPs have existed for years but have been slow to gain widespread traction because of a host of factors. Utilities often haven’t been incentivized to embrace the approach, while home solar and batteries remain too expensive for many households in the U.S. But as electrification and the data center rush spur unprecedented demand, VPPs are taking off as a fast way to get power on the grid. Earlier this month, the Brattle Group estimated that 524 gigawatts of distributed energy resources harnessed in VPPs could save households on average $122 per year by 2050.

Currently, “there’s immense untapped capacity,” said Kevin Brehm, manager in the carbon-free electricity practice at clean energy think tank RMI.

Matt Grocoff, the founder of Thrive Collaborative, started to consider a VPP pilot at Veridian in 2019. He wanted the neighborhood to mimic an ecosystem — a resilient web of relationships in which individual organisms do more than just extract resources. For example, a tree in a forest turns sunlight into nutrients and shares them symbiotically with a vast, interconnected underground web of fungi.

Likewise, with a VPP, each Veridian home “can be producing energy that it needs and mutually beneficially sharing it across a network of energy rather than a linear grid that flows in only one direction,” Grocoff said.

DTE expects nearly 100 battery-equipped Veridian homes to ultimately participate in the pilot. So far, 44 market-rate homes with solar and batteries have been built, out of 120 planned, as have 50 affordable housing units that don’t have batteries yet, according to Thrive Collaborative. Battery manufacturer Sonnen USA, maker of the home storage systems installed at Veridian, is helping DTE operate the pilot using Sonnen’s proprietary software.

“Veridian is a test bed,” said Geoff Ferrell, executive vice president of Sonnen USA’s VPP business unit. The initiative, which is expected to be able to deliver up to about 300 kilowatts for three hours, will give DTE a clearer picture of how much power the home battery fleet can actually generate and when, providing “a really great basis” for a scaled-up program, he noted.

Ferrell points to another Sonnen-facilitated VPP that also sprang up as a humble pilot project, but rapidly mushroomed into a full-scale program because of early positive results. That initiative started in 2017 with a new apartment building topped with solar, Soleil Lofts outside Salt Lake City.

Sonnen hadn’t even finished installing batteries in each of the development’s 600 units when the utility Rocky Mountain Power and the state utility commission decided that the initial data was promising enough to merit extending the program to every residential customer in the utility’s territory, Ferrell said. Today, about 7,900 homes and businesses participate in the program, now called Wattsmart Battery, in Utah, Wyoming, and Idaho.

Given the success of that VPP and many others, Brehm would like to see more utilities go full throttle at the outset.

“Do you need another pilot?” he asked, noting that numerous VPP programs exist for utilities to model their own programs after.

But for utilities that do approach VPPs with caution, Rocky Mountain Power’s pilot is a good model, according to Brehm. The utility’s employees were able to rapidly understand how the residential battery fleet worked and how to deploy it, he said, “so that they could integrate these batteries into their operations initially, and subsequently [into their resource-capacity] planning.” He’d like to see DTE do the same.

The VPP pilot at Veridian is already starting to inspire developers and utilities outside Michigan, including the development Peace Hill in Townsend, Washington, said Grocoff of Thrive Collaborative.

“We’re getting calls from all over the country,” Grocoff said. “It’s really exciting.”

Source: Grist | Published: 2026-11-21 14:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The scientists fighting to help Maui wildfire survivors heal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting on a critical issue with clear detail

Early on a Saturday morning in May, Ruben Juarez took the 45-minute flight from Oʻahu to Maui, just like he’d done dozens of times over the past three years.

This one felt different.

Juarez landed in Kahului Airport with his partner, Alika Maunakea, and drove on a long winding highway beside the piercing blue ocean until they reached the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center.

A cool breeze wafted in from the Pacific less than half a mile below as they set up stations for blood collection, lung function tests, and mental health check-ins, directing a team of Ph.D. students and local healthcare providers. Then they waited for the fire survivors to arrive.

On August 8, 2023, Maui was hit with the deadliest wildfires the U.S. has seen in over a century. They killed at least 102 people, displaced nearly 13,000 residents, and destroyed more than 2,200 buildings. Three years later, just 15 percent have been rebuilt.

Juarez, an economist, and Maunakea, a biomedical scientist, never expected to focus on disaster recovery. But after the fires, they were thrust into the space by the overwhelming scale of need. The two University of Hawaiʻi professors dreamed up the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, as a form of rapid response: an effort to track the impacts of the fires on survivors’ health.

Three years and 2,500 participants later, the study has blossomed into a combination of research and intervention, a web of community organizations working together to give participants not just free testing but also therapy, food assistance, cash support, and help connecting with doctors and insurance. Some even say the study saved their lives.

The researchers hope MauiWES could become a national blueprint for public health response after disasters. Experts across the country are paying attention. One longtime disaster researcher, David Eisenman at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the study’s holistic approach is “singular.”

But critical federal support to keep the effort going for at least a decade was running out, and its renewal was uncertain — grant applications had been met with silence for months. And just two weeks before Juarez and Maunakea landed on Maui, state funding they were counting on fell through.

Now, here they were at what might be their last big event to understand how survivors were doing and what help they needed.

Juarez was distraught: It felt like the end. But Maunakea, usually the pessimist of the pair, refused to believe it. He felt the study had to continue. The need was too great. They would find a way.

At the health center that Saturday morning, Maunakea greeted Lisa and Nilsson Panis, a pair of siblings born and raised in Lahaina. As he checked them into the study, he explained what they’d do that day. Urine samples to track environmental exposures. Saliva collection for biomarkers of stress and aging. Blood tests for metabolic function. Two assessments of lung health. Recordings of blood pressure, height, and weight. A mental health screener.

At the end of it all, they’d meet with a volunteer physician who would help them understand their test results, and they’d each walk away with $100, compensation for their time.

“We’re trying to do this every year,” Maunakea told the Panises.

He was determined to make that happen.

The lobby of the health center had a dark stain on its ceiling where water had leaked in just a month before.

The building — run by the state’s Department of Health and loaned to MauiWES for the weekend — sits near the base of the sprawling West Maui mountains. That weekend, the foothills above the center were covered in dry, yellowing grass that was nonetheless much greener than usual, courtesy of recent Kona low storms.

The storms swept water damage into construction sites and homes that had just been rebuilt. They busted up highways and caused torrential flooding, triggering millions of dollars in damage across the county. They also kicked off an unusually verdant spring, with flowers blooming on the trees outside the center and along the highway below. Wetness that early can heighten the fire risk later in the year, fueling grass and brush growth that dries out and becomes plentiful tinder, susceptible to heat and strong winds.

Lisa Panis, a participant in the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, has struggled with her mental and physical health since the fires, and her family is still in temporary housing. Keerti Gopal

Lisa Panis had an appointment with MauiWES that day, but she was hoping they’d have room for her older brother, too. In a fluorescently lit room just beside the center’s main lobby, she introduced Nilsson to Maunakea and explained that he had been a first responder after the wildfires, cleaning up debris in the burn zone. Maunakea immediately instructed the Ph.D. students working the check-in desk to sign him up, along with Nilsson’s girlfriend, another survivor.

MauiWES had limited resources, especially with funding so up in the air. But on an island already suffering from a severe healthcare provider shortage, Maunakea and Juarez didn’t like turning anyone away.

Maunakea listened to Nilsson explain what his life looked like in the months after the fires:12-hour days, seven days a week, clearing the burn zone for a construction company. He wore full-body gear to keep as much of the dust out as possible, but he still ended each day coated in grime. Though he’d never been tested, Nilsson felt confident the constant inhalation of ash and the debris that covered his body as he worked had impacted his health.

“We tried to push all the dust down with water,” Nilsson said to Maunakea, describing the cleanup. “But you cannot get everything.”

“Are you still doing that, or pau?” Maunakea asked.

“Pau,” Nilsson replied. Finished. Now he was working as a mason, bringing his sister on whenever he could. It wasn’t steady. He hoped jobs would pick up in the summer.…

Source: Grist | Published: 2026-11-14 14:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://grist.org/wildfires/the-scientists-fighting-to-help-maui-wildfire-survivors-heal/

item.title: Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: important topic with clear reporting and useful context

The annual United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change gathering drew historic levels of Indigenous attendance in Belém, Brazil last year, leading some to dub it “the Indigenous COP.” But the event was marked by frustration and protest, with many Indigenous leaders calling it little more than a continuation of a longstanding pattern of exclusion from international negotiations.

This year’s gathering in Antalya, Turkey, is billed as an “implementation” conference focused less on sweeping new pledges than on the procedural work of turning previous agreements into action. For Indigenous advocates, that makes COP31, which started November 9, a test of whether the promises made last year translate into tangible changes, including greater authority over climate action.

“It is still a struggle,” said Edward Porokwa, who is Maasai and a member of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. “I’m yet to really determine whether there will be any more progress that is made in terms of realization of the rights of Indigenous people.”

Indigenous advocates are pressing governments to follow through on their commitments to secure and strengthen Indigenous land rights on 400 million acres in tropical forest countries, provide $1.8 billion in funding, and respect rights to free, prior, and informed consent in the energy transition.

Despite those pledges, funds have been slow to reach affected communities and Indigenous land defenders say their rights and lives remain under constant threat. Porokwa said that he feels that responsibility to address climate change continues to fall on smaller countries and Indigenous peoples.

The stakes have been particularly stark over the last year. In Nepal, massive floods and landslides in August killed more than 1,500 people and destroyed entire villages. In Canada, a historic wildfire season saw millions of acres burned, causing thousands of evacuations. And in Indonesia, wildfire smoke alone has caused thousands of deaths and led to school closures and other emergency measures across Southeast Asia.

“The recent large-scale mountainside collapse on the border of Nepal and Tibet should serve as a wake-up call to the global community,” said Biswash Chepang, who is a founder of the Institute for Indigenous Affairs and Development in Nepal.

Climate-driven threats to Indigenous peoples and their lands continue to mount as a historically powerful El Niño threatens to drive famine, heat-related deaths, and other catastrophes across the globe.

The conference comes in the wake of a recent United Nations report that said it will be virtually impossible to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees, the goal set under the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement. Indigenous delegates find that reality particularly frustrating because they see it as a direct result of decision makers ignoring their knowledge and all the ways their stewardship has been proven to benefit the environment and climate.

“For over 30 years we have brought Indigenous knowledges and sciences to these negotiations,” Māori activist Quack Pirihi said in an opening statement on behalf of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. “Yet emissions continue to rise, putting 1.5 degrees C beyond reach.”

While the work of reducing emissions and protecting Indigenous rights in the energy transition continues, securing funding for nations and communities most impacted by climate disasters is also a priority. In October, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage approved $21.6 million for Nepal — its first disbursement and less than 1 percent of the nearly $5 billion in damage the country sustained. But the process to receive and administer those funds is ongoing, and Indigenous leaders say the fund must work faster. Their push comes as wealthy countries face renewed scrutiny over climate-finance pledges they have failed to deliver.

“Loss and damage is not simply a question of humanitarian assistance,” Chepang said. “It is also a question of climate responsibility, historical emissions, equity, and the right of affected communities to recover with dignity.”

Indigenous peoples also hope to hold polluters to account. Bianca Ranson, who is Māori and a board member of the Aotearoa Climate Action Network, is attending COP31 in part to highlight the landmark climate case her father Mike Smith led against major emitters in New Zealand. The case, which uses Māori customary law, has been blocked by the national government.

Despite the logistical, financial, and political hurdles of attending an event like COP, Ranson said there is value in global spaces. “I think that with the geopolitical moment that we’re in, with the rise of the far right and fascism and war, and the struggles that Indigenous peoples are facing across the globe, it’s a really important place for us to be able to come together to connect, to strengthen our solidarity,” Ranson said.

As negotiations continue through November 20, Indigenous advocates will continue their push for all the discussions to lead to tangible actions. “Now I think it is not time only to talk about the commitment,” Porokwa said. “It is time to change the commitment into practice.”

item.title: The affordability election delivered billions for public transit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information on a significant environmental issue

In an election dominated by concerns about affordability, voters across the country overwhelmingly agreed to raise taxes to preserve or expand public transit.

Out of 27 ballot measures supporting transit, 22 passed on November 3, representing $27.4 billion in funding to rescue faltering systems and expand or build new ones. Some of the biggest wins of the night included voters in the San Francisco Bay Area staving off enormous cuts to Bay Area Rapid Transit and other regional systems, Coloradans backing new regional rail, and residents of Seattle and nearby Pierce County favoring expanded bus service.

“It’s an indication that the public is willing to pay for these public transit improvements,” said Sohail Husain, a policy analyst at the Eno Center for Transportation. “That’s very telling –– especially in a world like today where people are concerned about affordability. I think people are still also concerned about mobility and having options to move.”

Public transit has now fared well in the red wave of 2024 — when 19 out of 25 measures supporting transit passed — and this year’s blue wave. Although few candidates campaigned on the issue, the results could significantly alter policy. At the state level, transit advocates see opportunities to advance projects or simply get the government out of the way. Meanwhile, a Democratic majority in Congress will shape a major transportation infrastructure law that is up for renewal. Together, the results could remake how Americans get around.

States have broad discretion to fund transportation as they see fit, which is why Democratic wins in red states and Democratic control of the governorship and both legislative chambers in 22 states have many public transit advocates excited about what comes next.

Pennsylvania is one of those states. It has endured a bitter battle over the finances of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, which serves the Philadelphia area. When the agency faced 45 percent service cuts last year, Governor Josh Shapiro directed the state Department of Transportation to allow the agency to shift nearly $400 million from its capital to operational budget. He also made another $220 million available to the system.

Now, with Democrats taking control of both chambers of the state legislature, transit advocates say SEPTA can look beyond self-preservation. Stephen Bronskill of Transit Forward Philadelphia pointed to projects including trolley modernization, new fleets to replace vehicles from the 1970s, more frequent regional rail service, and fully accessible stations.

“This is a once-in-a-generation moment to invest in public transit –– safe, reliable, accessible transit that Philly needs, but all of Pennsylvania deserves,” he said.

The prospects are less straightforward in Texas, where Republicans still control the Senate. Jay Blazek Crossley, executive director of Farm&City, a nonprofit focused in part on road safety, has spent more than a decade trying to nudge GOP lawmakers toward less violent and less polluting transportation options. Every legislative session has seen him unsuccessfully push legislation that would make it easier for cities to reduce speed limits on residential streets. He sees new hope for that measure and, more broadly, a future that might include additional public transit funding, which accounts for just 0.72 percent of the transportation department’s budget. State Republicans have generally been more interested in moving more cars more quickly, primarily by building bigger highways, while pushing back against some city-led public transit efforts.

“At the very least, the state, I believe, will get out of the way on things like building good light rail and transit,” he said.

There’s hope for bigger projects too. State Representative John Bucy III has again filed legislation directing the Texas Department of Transportation to find a public-private partnership for a high-speed rail line linking Dallas and San Antonio. He believes the bill will appeal to lawmakers whose constituents would benefit from an alternative to driving on the heavily congested Interstate 35 corridor.

“I think the voters spoke loud and clear that they want a Texas government that is going to work on kitchen table issues,” he said. “I think that’s healthcare, education. It’s also mobility and transit, and how do we get around this big, vast state?”

Georgia is another state where Democrats took the governorship and flipped the House, but Republicans still control the Senate. That could be a challenge for Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who has called for dedicated state funding for the Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority and other systems that have historically relied heavily on local and federal support.

The election could have even greater implications at the federal level, where Congress must soon decide how much spending to allocate to transit and passenger rail. The BUILD America 250 Act passed out of a key House commitee with bipartisan support in May, but left public transit advocates concerned about funding cuts. With Democrats taking control of Congress, the legislation is likely to look different. Representative Jerry Nadler of New York, the lone Democrat on the committee to oppose advancing the legislation, sees an opportunity to change its direction.

“Unlike the current Republican proposal, next year’s bill should not prioritize one mode of transportation at the expense of others. This bill must make robust investments in rail and public transit, to connect communities, create good-paying jobs, lower transportation costs for families, and reduce the cost of moving goods across the country,” he said in a statement.…

item.title: The cozy radicalism of repair cafés
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting topic with clear reporting and useful context

On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with tool boxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.

That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.

“This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus said, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”

Lilly Pettus’s broken chair gets a hand from attendees at the Decatur repair café. Nearby, a sign tracks repair progress during the event.

This is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café, one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies selling everything from hiking boots, smartphones, and hot water boilers, that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throw-away economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change.

Yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés as more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy.

At the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through.

Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus said. “We are a big family.”

The newlyweds settled on a simple table and six chairs — two “host style” with arms, four without — from the local Ethan Allen store. The furniture came to feel more like home than the many houses where Pettus, her husband, and their children lived. They moved the table and chairs with them from Florida to Connecticut, then to Indiana, Michigan, Texas, and finally to Georgia. “ I don’t know anyone’s chairs that I like more than my own,” Pettus said.

But after absorbing shakes of laughter during countless games of Hearts, and fidgets of anxiety at family meetings about upcoming moves, one of the chair’s joints finally cracked. “We had the chair just sitting in the corner,” Pettus said, “but no one actually sat in it.” She didn’t know how to fix the chair, but if she sent it to a landfill that would mean trashing a reminder of her fondest memories from the last 30 years.

Pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house, Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair, and decided to give it a second chance.

“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely,” said Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a new item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.”

Postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future. “Markets are flooded with trash — with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma said. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.”

Repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste — the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft — according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families.

Postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair.…

item.title: This surprise cost could derail your heat pump or EV charger installation. Here’s how to avoid it.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information on a practical environmental issue

“Electrify everything” has become a mantra in the fight against climate change. Switching a home’s heating, cooling, and other energy-intensive loads from fossil fuels to electricity could drastically reduce planet-warming emissions. But electrification has often run into a major, and expensive, hurdle: upgrading a home’s electric capacity.

A home’s connection to the grid is rated by amperage, or amps, which caps the amount of current it can safely draw at once. The standard for houses built in the last few decades is generally 200 amps. Many older residences, however, have a lower limit because they were constructed when electricity powered little more than the lights, refrigerator, microwave, and perhaps the dryer. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that roughly a third of homes in the United States have panel capacity of 100 amps or less. In the Northeast, that share rises to closer to half.

As people install heat pumps, induction stoves, and EV chargers, they can run into a couple of potential issues. Their electric panel may simply run out of slots to install more circuit breakers, in which case the relatively easy fix of adding a subpanel often does the trick. But sometimes homeowners run into a bigger problem, where an electrician says all the new loads will push them past their home’s peak power limits.

Upgrading an electrical service can start at a few thousand dollars and quickly skyrocket, particularly in rural areas or places where power lines run underground. “We’ve seen estimates of $10,000 to $20,000,” said AJ Rossman, an electrical engineer with VEIC, a contractor that runs much of Efficiency Vermont’s state program.

The exact scope of the problem is unclear. There is scant data on how many service upgrades are done each year, let alone those that may have been recommended and never made due to the cost. But the Lawrence Berkeley research suggests there may be thousands, if not millions, of homeowners who are told they need to upsize their service as they electrify.

The good news is, there are workarounds — if you or your electrician know where to look. It’s a lesson my wife and I recently learned.

When we moved into our Burlington, Vermont, home, natural gas powered the furnace, stove, and dryer. We knew we’d eventually want to electrify, so I had our service increased from 150 amps to 200. Because we needed the upgrade as part of other work, the bill wasn’t horrible.

The change allowed us to install an EV charger, switch to heat pumps, get an induction stove, and plan for an electric dryer. We were happy to have a home largely free of fossil fuels.

Then we decided to build an addition.

Our plan for an extra 800 square feet would require two more small heat pumps along with lighting, outlets, and ditching our gas dryer. None of this was much of a concern until our electrician did the math. He determined that the laundry room swap alone would push our theoretical load to around 192 amps. Upgrading to 300 or 400 amp service would require trenching a new underground line and possibly even overhauling the transformer serving our block. It could cost us well over $10,000.

I panicked and started digging for answers. I had heard about a growing array of products designed to help people in my situation. For example, a friend had installed a smart panel that monitors how much electricity each circuit is using to ensure demand does not exceed the home’s capacity. If things get close, the panel shuts off lower-priority breakers as needed, then turns them back on when it’s safe.

This was appealing, but expensive. Converting my panel would have cost around $4,000 in materials alone. Even options that control a few circuits starts at about $2,000. With labor, the outlay seemed almost as staggering as a service upgrade.

I came across a cheaper category of devices called load-sharing switches, or smart splitters. They allow two high-demand appliances to share the same circuit, with just one running at a time. That means only the heavier load counts in a home’s demand calculation. Each switch cost around $800, depending on the brand. The issue was that we would probably need at least two to bring our calculated load below 200 amps. That was certainly an improvement, but it still wasn’t cheap and it left little wiggle room for the future.

There must be a better option, I thought. So, as a last-ditch effort, I called my utility provider, who I assumed may have other customers in a similar position. An advisor immediately asked me a question I had taken for granted: Is your electrician sure you need an upgrade?

When my electrician had calculated how much power my house would need, it appears he used the National Electrical Code’s standard method. Simply put, this approach uses the rated loads of all the electrical items in a home to calculate its theoretical load. Using one of the many online calculators to replicate his work, I arrived at the same conclusion: I was already taking up about 187 amps and the addition would push me to around 227 — beyond the panel’s 220-amp limit.

But Burlington Electric told me there was a lesser-known section of the code that could give me a very different answer. Commonly referred to as Section 220.87, even though it was recently moved to section 120.87, this method uses a year’s worth of utility data to identify a home’s actual peak demand instead of relying on hypothetical usage. Like 73 percent of residences around the country, my home has a smart meter, so it was relatively easy to request that information from my utility. A spreadsheet arrived the next day.

The file was thousands of rows long, so I put it into TrueLoadapp.com, a tool electricians can use to evaluate a customer’s load using this alternative method. It parsed the data to find my peak, which came on January 20, when my home topped out at just under 62 amps. The code mandates a 25 percent buffer when calculating usage, which bumped me about 77 amps.…

Source: Grist | Published: 2026-11-12 09:45 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Climate progressives won the midterms without saying ‘climate’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting political angle on environmental issues

On October 20, the two candidates running to represent Michigan in the U.S. Senate, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, took questions for an hour at the Detroit Economic Club. El-Sayed, the Democrat who had previously run for governor, made a name for himself years ago by connecting public health to the climate crisis. He published a fierce defense of the Green New Deal at the time, touting its economic, health, and planetary benefits. But last month at the Detroit Economic Club, El-Sayed didn’t mention the Green New Deal at all.

Instead, the only mentions of such a plan came from his opponent, who used it as an attack on El-Sayed and the Democratic party as a whole. “We need to make sure we don’t have the largest tax increase in the history of the country,” Rogers said, “which is, that’s what the other team is talking about doing.”

A vote for El-Sayed would ring in an era of “big government, government control, more rules, more regulation, another Green New Deal,” Rogers continued. It’s become a common refrain since President Donald Trump’s effort to rebrand the climate movement’s push for widescale public investment in renewable energy as a “Green New Scam.”

Two weeks later, El-Sayed handily won the race.

Even though many of the newly elected Democrats did not talk about the Green New Deal by name, the think tank Climate and Community Institute describes El-Sayed as belonging to a new class of green economic populists who are running for public office (and winning) by connecting the need for climate action to soaring utility bills and the hoarding of wealth by a handful of individuals and companies.

El-Sayed “clearly gets it,” said Patrick Bigger, research director at Climate and Community Institute, or CCI. The senator-elect’s platform, which proposes stricter regulations on data centers and energy companies, is “really exciting,” he said. These are promising climate agenda items — even if Democrats don’t explicitly call them that. For example, voters may oppose data centers in their backyard for any number of reasons, but some number of them are required for our digitalized reality and progressives now have an opportunity to take the companies behind them to task and get them to commit to reducing their strain on the local environment. Likewise, where voters came out in support of lowering utility bills, electeds now can talk further about investing in cheaper renewable energy systems like solar and wind power.

Bigger led a recent analysis that scored candidates in this year’s primary and midterm elections based on three questions: Is the candidate pushing for renewable energy or other climate actions? Do they name the rising cost of living as a voter issue, and have a plan to lower those costs? Do they articulate a populist vision by blaming wealthy corporations and powerful individuals for both the climate and affordability crises? CCI argues that candidates like El-Sayed who check all three boxes are the climate champions of the moment.

Other progressives named in the report include Will Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, the climate group that first sounded the alarm for a Green New Deal in 2018. Lawrence, who will represent Michigan’s 7th District in the next Congress, points to his history of climate organizing on his website: “I will be among the most knowledgeable and dedicated members of Congress on water, climate and energy policy,” he writes. “I will fight for investment to secure the climate we depend on, adapt to the changes we can’t prevent, and finally drive our electric bills down.”

These “new folks headed to the House and the Senate who are really on board with a robust transformative approach to climate,” said Bigger, represent “a major shift.”

But not all climate progressives heading to Washington next year are so allergic to calling it the Green New Deal: Representatives-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York City name it specifically on their campaign websites and in the press. Still, this new wave of climate leaders may feel it’s time for the decarbonization agenda to get a refresh; Valdez and Avila Chevalier’s websites also include mentions of “a livable planet for all” and “a livable world for everyone,” respectively. In part, this diversity of messaging tactics reflects the fractured nature of the climate movement since Trump retook office with a checklist of Biden-era environmental regulations to roll back.

If progressive Democrats’ messaging on climate has shifted, said Aru Shiney-Ajay, executive director of the Sunrise Movement, it’s because the terrain they’re fighting in has changed, too. “I think, as the climate crisis gets worse and worse, it’s becoming increasingly clear that the strategy, policy-wise, needs to be incorporating climate change into every single aspect of what we’re doing,” she said. In other words, climate policy should not be framed as a separate issue from the economy, infrastructure improvements, or foreign policy. “It should be the defining framework within which we have to think about how we run our society,” said Shiney-Ajay.

In 2018, the Sunrise Movement burst onto the national stage by protesting outside House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi’s office — with the Green New Deal as their top priority. Just seven years later, members of the Sunrise Movement voted to reorganize around the priority of fighting authoritarianism and, in particular, the second Trump administration. Shiney-Ajay acknowledged that the climate movement has suffered in recent years.

But that doesn’t mean that the public has become disengaged from the climate crisis. In fact, voters across the political spectrum are more attuned to it than ever. “People are actually really hungry for something to do about climate change,” said Shiney-Ajay. “I think we will actually see a lot of momentum around stopping the climate crisis. And I certainly hope to build a movement that makes that possible.”…

item.title: Climate change is coming for the cactus. Yes, the cactus.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique angle on climate change impacts

The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive — they thrive and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.

Yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled not just a future of relentlessly rising temperatures, but the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.

“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you can throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing — and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly — but they’re not that different from other plants.”

That means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year. Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive, like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet said. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”

Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet said. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”

Instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.

Really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet said. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”

Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought — the lack of water may not kill them immediately, but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.

Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” said Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”

Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”

Still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.

In the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.

Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni said. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There’s a lot of people in the countries that are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”

Source: Grist | Published: 2026-11-12 09:15 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Gravy-Braised Turkey
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, detailed cooking instructions

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Recipe information

- Total Time 4 hours 30 minutes

- Yield 8 servings

Ingredients

Preparation

- Step 1 Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.) Step 2 Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly). Step 3 Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper. Step 4 Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes. Step 5 Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

item.title: Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original recipe, clear instructions

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Recipe information

- Total Time 35 minutes

- Yield 6–8 servings

Ingredients

Preparation

item.title: Thanksgiving Cornbread
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original recipe, clear instructions

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

Recipe information

- Total Time 1 hour 15 minutes

- Yield 12–18 servings

Ingredients

Preparation

- Step 1 Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl. Step 2 Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat. Step 3 Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan. Step 4 Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter. Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

item.title: A Beautiful Cabbage Galette
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original recipe, clear instructions

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

Recipe information

- Total Time 2 hours 40 minutes

- Yield 6–8 servings

Ingredients

Crust

Filling and Assembly

Preparation

- Crust Step 1 Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain). Step 2 Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours. Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

- Filling and Assembly Step 3 When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside. Step 4 Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool. Step 5 Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine. Step 6 Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet. Step 7 Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.) Step 8 Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving. Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

item.title: Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original recipe, clear instructions

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

Recipe information

- Total Time 2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

- Yield 10–12 servings

Ingredients

Dough

Filling and Assembly

Preparation

- Dough Step 1 Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size). Step 2 Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain). Step 3 Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours. Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

- Filling and Assembly Step 4 Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes. Step 5 Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes. Step 6 Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes. Step 7 Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes. Step 8 Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes. Step 9 Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Step 10 Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving. Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.
