item.title: Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original recipe, clear instructions

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

Notes:

- You can substitute bone-in chicken thighs and legs and increase the cooking time by 10 to 15 minutes.

- Use tortillas instead of naan or roti in a pinch.

Recipe information

- Total Time 4 servings

- Yield 1 hour (plus 1 hour for marinating)

Ingredients

Garam Masala

Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions

Chicken Kari

Preparation

- Garam Masala Step 1 In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine. Step 2 Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool. Step 3 Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid. Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

- Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions Step 4 To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt. Step 5 In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture. Step 6 Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

- Chicken Kari Step 7 To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight. Step 8 In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes. Step 9 Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through. Step 10 Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread. Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

item.title: Cranberry Meringue Pie
item.description:

Why it is here: original recipe, clear instructions

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

Recipe information

- Total Time 3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

- Yield 12 servings

Ingredients

Crust

Filling and Assembly

Preparation

- Crust Step 1 Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size). Step 2 Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain). Step 3 Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours. Step 4 Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours. Step 5 Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool. Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

- Filling and Assembly Step 6 Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool. Step 7 Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day. Step 8 Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more. Step 9 Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

item.description:

Why it is here: in-depth analysis, expert insight

During during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America, I was joined by art advisor Sophia Cohen to explore one of the hottest topics in the art market today: the next generation of collectors.

Cohen is the founder of Siren, an art advisory and curatorial consultancy. She started her career working for dealer Gavin Brown, who, Cohen explains, taught her about the importance of being with artists of your own generation and how an art dealer can function as an important steward for the artists they represent. When Brown’s gallery closed in 2020, Cohen pivoted to Gagosian (“the exact opposite,” in her words), where she spent six years, eventually becoming an associate director. Cohen is also one of four co-chairs leading the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Vanguard Council, an invite-only group of next-generation patrons.

At our talk on Friday, November 13, at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Cohen spoke about the advice she gives to young collectors about when and how to buy, and why it’s sometimes important to make mistakes. She also gave insight into her own collecting, and discussed how today’s patrons are structuring their giving. Watch the video above to see the whole conversation.

item.title: Ireland’s Experiment in Paying Artists a Basic Income Is Working as Intended For Artists
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, policy impact

Life was pretty rosy for the 2,000 Irish artists who landed a spot on Ireland’s Basic Income for the Arts (BIA) pilot scheme. For three years, from 2022 to 2025, €325 arrived in their bank accounts every week. The money was intended to provide a dependable income, reduce the need to take on unrelated jobs to cover living costs, and give artists more time to concentrate on making art. Judging by the recipients I spoke earlier this month at Dublin Gallery Weekend (DGW), the pilot was a success. And since the BIA was made permanent in February, thousands more artists are hoping to reap the rewards.

“Basic Income for the Arts is a game changer, and now it is here to stay,” Ireland’s minister for culture, communications, and sport, Patrick O’Donovan, said in February.

Now in its fourth year, DGW was launched in 2023 by the city’s commercial galleries to raise the profile of its contemporary art scene. Organized by the Contemporary Art Gallery Association (CAGA), this year’s four-day program brought together galleries and cultural institutions for exhibitions, talks, screenings, and performances. A major addition was the inaugural Francis Bacon Awards for Irish Visual Arts, a €40,000 prize fund supported by Château La Coste. Painter Patrick Graham received the €25,000 Lifetime Achievement Award, while Belfast-born artist Cathy Wilkes took the €15,000 Mid-Career prize. Both will stage solo exhibitions at Château La Coste in Provence, France.

While the artists I spoke to described the BIA as a major boost to their working lives, I found little evidence that it has fundamentally changed Dublin’s contemporary art scene. None of the dealers, curators, or museum directors I spoke to suggested that its impact had been felt on a wider scale across the city’s galleries or commercial market.

Applications for the BIA’s new three-year round opened in May, with previous recipients eligible to reapply for one of the 2,000 available places. Around 10,000 artists applied, making competition fierce for a program to which the Irish government has committed €18 million.

“Over the course of the scheme, my practice flourished,” Dublin-based artist Gearóid O’Dea, who was selected for the pilot, told ARTnews. The funding allowed him to curate an exhibition based on Samuel Beckett’s work that travelled to Berlin, and collaborate with four other artists through the Glue Factory collective. He said the financial support made it possible to bring artists together and exhibit internationally without constantly having to find other jobs to make ends meet.

Cork-born Elinor O’Donovan, who is now studying for a master’s degree in Gothenburg, Sweden, also received the pilot payment. She told ARTnews that “it completely transformed my ability to work as an artist.”

Before joining the scheme, O’Donovan worked part-time as a receptionist alongside her artistic practice. The weekly payment allowed her to give up the job and concentrate on making art full-time. “Knowing the money was coming for three years was a big relief,” she said. “My psychological wellbeing improved because there was security.”

Lauren, another former recipient who is now based in London, said the payment arrived at a pivotal moment in her career. Having just completed her undergraduate degree, she had secured a graduate residency at the Royal Hibernian Academy in Dublin, where she was given a studio and access to painting classes. The BIA helped her develop her practice and take up further opportunities, including residencies and exhibitions. She has since secured funding to continue her studies in London. “There’s kind of nothing I haven’t done in the last four or five years that hasn’t, in some way, been impacted by my experience with the basic income,” she told ARTnews.

Despite the BIA’s unprecedented support for artists, not everyone is waxing lyrical about it, including some who benefited from the original pilot. Tadhg Ó Cuirrín, a visual artist who received the payment and works with the artists’ trade union Praxis, believes the government has missed an opportunity to build on its success. More than 10,000 artists applied for the new round, yet the number of places remains unchanged at 2,000. Recipients will also be limited to three years of support in every six-year period.

“It feels less like a base income per se and more like a kind of a multi-annual grant chosen by lottery,” he told ARTnews.

Although the program is now permanent, individual artists are not guaranteed support beyond three years. Artists must meet the scheme’s eligibility criteria, after which places are allocated through a lottery, with selection also taking demographic representation into account. Ó Cuirrín argued that the three-years-on, three-years-off model reinstates the financial insecurity BIA was designed to address. Artists risk losing their income just as their practices are beginning to flourish.

O’Dea has reapplied for the new round but is still waiting to hear if he’s been selected. He said the prospect of losing the regular income has brought financial anxiety back into his life.

The transition has also caused difficulties for artists who relied on other forms of state support. Michaële Cutaya, a spokesperson for Praxis, previously told The Art Newspaper that some former recipients have had to return to other work to cover their living costs. “If you have to then take on a different kind of job, it’s really disruptive,” she said.

Noel Kelly, chief executive of Visual Artists Ireland, said he welcomes the permanent scheme, but pointed to practical problems. BIA payments can affect artists receiving means-tested benefits, including disability allowance, while some applicants’ immigration status may prevent them from registering as self-employed, a requirement for participation.…

Source: ARTnews | Published: 2026-11-21 13:19 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Maren Hassinger Won’t Be Weighed Down
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: biographical context, art appreciation

Maren Hassinger’s retrospective at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) has a radiant warmth about it—surprisingly so, given that it’s a show made mostly of gray metal sculptures whose edges could prick you raw. This warmth owes a lot to the photographs, printed mural-sized and filling vitrines, taken by her long-term collaborator Adam Avila. Scattered throughout, they show Hassinger dancing, beaming, and/or hamming it up for the camera, often mirroring her sculpture’s forms with her body. But it owes, too, to the ways she rose to meet her career’s surprising twists and turns.

Rejected in college from Bennington’s dance department in the 1960s, Hassinger was pushed toward sculpture by a teacher who noticed her gift. “My love of motion,” she says in the catalog, carried her from one to the other. Clement Greenberg was a guest at her senior thesis critique: He had “the gift of gab, but was a bit of a bully” she remembers with accurate alliterations. He would not be her last mean man.

In graduate school, at UCLA, Hassinger was rerouted once again after finding the sculpture program to be a boys’ club. As she remembers it, not one single woman was enrolled. So she found a home in fiber, a typical tale, and made it work: “Truthfully,” she admits in the catalog, “I was just trying to get a degree so I could teach and make art.” But she found herself too impatient for the loom and uninterested in making fabric. So she gathered fibers out in the world, chancing upon a weighty rope in a shipyard. It was made of blonde hemp but discolored by oil. Playing around, she eventually unraveled some of its strands before tying segments into a series of loose, giant macrame knots that greet visitors to BAMPFA, where they lie on the ground as if waiting to be pulled tight.

Hassinger would marry craft techniques with industrial materials henceforth—a revealing portrait of women’s changing work in her time. She became such a regular at one LA wire shop that they featured her on the cover of their trade magazine. Soon, she was incorporating elevator cables—effectively wire ropes, their cords twisted together—into what would become her best known works. Leaning (1980) sees cables with frayed ends bundled in some two dozen bouquets. Only the central arrangement has a flat bottom and sits sturdily; the rest are free to lean.

Fiber meets metal in River, a 2,000-pound rope-chain Hassinger made as an ambitious graduate student in 1972. But where was a student to store such a behemoth? Recognition would not come until much later—as the title of her work Wallflower series (1975) attests—so she let River go, then finally remade it in 2011 for a Studio Museum acquisition. (Good thing she had so many photographs). A few other works at BAMPFA are recreations, too, but after school, she mainly made sculptures that could be coiled up and made compact: a resourceful response to the realities of real estate.

To see Hassinger’s work is to think about the act of making it. It shows you: Knots are blown up big so that you can see each twist and turn. Her titles are often verbs, as with Whirling (1978), Walking (1978), and Leaning (1980). “When she talks about the work, she moves” explained Margot Norton, who co-curated the show with Anthony Graham.

Hassinger met the obstacles that came her way, as a Black woman born in 1947, with poetry and practicality in equal measure. Of her turn to newspaper, which she twisted and knotted for a cascading 2008 installation, she explains that the material “is very handy and cheap [laughs].” But it also must have been cathartic to rip the headlines into strips. Her resourcefulness and resilience define the show, which sees her rethink sculpture without storage, fiber without fabric, choreography without corporeality.

Hassinger hardly did it alone. “Working alone is so antisocial” as she quips in the catalog. When Senga Nengudi first saw Hassinger’s work in 1975, she was thrilled to see another Black woman working with sculpture and performance, then looked her up. They became fast friends. With David Hammons, Nengudi then suggested that Linda Goode-Bryant show Hassinger at her gallery, Just Above Midtown (JAM). That show’s main work, Beach (1980), is installed at BAMPFA, too.

When Hassinger’s cohort of Black LA artists—known as Studio Z—lacked opportunities, they invented their own, as when Hassinger, Nengudi, Ulysses Jenkins, and others performed at the 1982 opening of “Afro-American Abstractions.” They had neither hung work on the walls nor been included in the checklist, but they did call up the Los Angeles Municipal Art Gallery to accept a nonexistent invitation: “We are so thrilled to be doing the opening performance!” they informed whoever answered the phone.

In the 1990s, Hassinger found herself without a studio. Starved for space, she turned to video. Birthright (2005) is nothing like her sculptures, but it will forever change how you see them. Onscreen, the artist interviews her uncle about her family tree. She learns that her grandmother, Puddin, had been the product both of incest and an interracial affair. Puddin’s parents hadn’t known that they were nephew and aunt, because Puddin’s father was born out of wedlock to his lover’s father who had a secret Native mistress.

Once the affair was discovered, Puddin was given away to a plantation caretaker who had been enslaved, and her father was lynched by a white mob. Puddin’s son—Hassinger’s dad—never talked about any of this: He was abandoned too by Puddin, then struggled to relate to women, cutting Hassinger out of the will and passing down patterns. “My legacy was to feel unloved,” the artist concludes in the video. But then the show keeps going.…

Source: ARTnews | Published: 2026-11-21 10:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/aia-reviews/maren-hassinger-bampfa-retrospective-berkeley-1234806748/

item.title: ‘Napping together on the reeds, the swans appeared luminous’: Noah Forster’s best phone picture
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: personal narrative, artistic expression

Twenty-one-year-old Noah Forster had always thought swans were beautiful, but it was his girlfriend Cecilia is the one who made him really notice them. The pair began dating two years ago, but now live 70 miles apart; he is a welder in Newark-on-Trent, she is studying law in Leeds.

“The distance can be difficult, but we try to talk as much as possible,” Forster says. “It’s taken me a while to save up for a driver’s licence and car, so I have a daily walk from my home and across the River Trent to get the 6am train to work. We like to send photos of our day to each other, and I took this photo on an exceptionally cold and frosty morning in November, walking across the river to get to work. I saw these swans near the castle. Napping together on the reeds, they appeared luminous.”

“Me and you,” he wrote in a message to Cecilia, attaching the image. “I know she loves swans, but I also knew she was most likely sleeping herself!” he says.

Later, Cecilia encouraged him to submit the photo to be considered for the Smart Shot column. “I decided to keep the name of the image the same as the caption I sent to her, because it represents the calm and peaceful feeling you have when you are with someone you trust. I hope it makes others think about their special person who they feel safe with.”

item.title: Hail to the Squash King
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: vague, lacks depth

Hail to the Squash King

Swimming in a Peter Bradley color field. Leaping from dot to dot on a Howardena Pindell speckled canvas. A Peter Jemison horse prances toward me. A Pepsi Cherry truck pulls over as I’m having deep thoughts about authenticity.

In the morning glow, a pretty woman walks down the sidewalk with a carton of a dozen eggs. A faded black-and-white Marilyn Monroe poster greets customers at the Organic Deli. A photo in the paper shows the presidents of the United States, China, and Russia against a giant painting of the Great Wall. A Madonna song whispers, “Express yourself, express yourself.”

A well-dressed man cycling to work is nice to look at. A Hilma af Klint painting sells for $12.7 million at auction, 16 times its highest estimate. Meanwhile at the supermarket, just three small items set me back $100. How could that be? If the middle class had any guts, they’d be out there on the streets burning effigies of Adam Smith and Sigmund Freud. But they’re not; they’re waiting 40 minutes in line across the street just to buy a bagel.

At the Ace Hotel, I read something I’ve written for the new edition of The Other Almanac. I wear my heart on my sleeve in front of strangers. The next speaker is a whale necropsy expert. At the end of the evening someone is crowned “Squash King.”

A golden sunset falls over the glass towers of Long Island City. The Kosciuszko Bridge is lit with cotton candy colors. Fog in Downtown Brooklyn, or is it smoke? I can’t really tell. In Chelsea, I follow a group of people into an art gallery just to see what they’re into. It turns out to be a big mistake.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever

In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die. | Moustafa Bayoumi

item.title: ZHA completes “secular” Théâtre Royal de Rabat in Morocco
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: high-quality architectural design reporting

ZHA completes “secular” Théâtre Royal de Rabat in Morocco

UK studio ZHA took visual cues from the riverbank site of this national theatre in Morocco when designing its sweeping exterior form, which encases a trio of performance spaces.

Named Théâtre Royal de Rabat, the performance venue for artists and musicians is located between the cities of Rabat and Salé near to the recently completed Mohammed VI Tower, which is the country’s tallest building.

It is the first project completed by ZHA, formerly Zaha Hadid Architects, in Africa.

ZHA revealed its proposal for Théâtre Royal de Rabat in 2010. At the time, the studio’s founder, Zaha Hadid, described the design as “secular”.

“It is uplifting to go into a great space, a heavenly space,” Hadid said.

“As a performance venue, the Théâtre Royal de Rabat is secular, but it has the capacity to transport the audience to an imaginary space and time.”

Théâtre Royal de Rabat’s design draws on the topography of its site on the banks of the Bouregreg River, which runs between the two cities.

It contains three performance venues, with its main space being a 1,821-seat theatre, simply named the Auditorium.

This venue is lined with crystal-like, faceted surfaces that the studio modelled on muqarnas – a traditional type of three-dimensional ornamentation found in Islamic architecture.

The walls also double as an acoustic treatment, developed by ZHA with acousticians at Arup “to deliver the highest quality of sound to every seat in the hall”.

The second venue is the Studio Theatre, an adaptable space with retractable seating that ZHA described as “offering a variety of configurations from a flat-floor to a stage with proscenium arch”.

It has a capacity of 250 people and is primarily intended for experimental performances and rehearsals. However, it can also be transformed into a space for events such as talks and educational workshops.

The final performance space is the Amphitheatre, an open-air venue accommodating 7,000 spectators for large public events.

The Amphitheatre and Studio Theatre have not yet been revealed in photos.

Completing the building is a triple-height foyer, described by ZHA as “canyon-like”. It is animated by interlocking staircases that emulate draped, flowing fabric, culminating at a restaurant with views of the river outside.

“Designed as a space for transition and reflection, the foyer encourages curiosity and dialogue to unfold before and after each performance,” said ZHA.

Théâtre Royal de Rabat uses a mix of air-source heat pumps, ground-source cooling and radiant heating as part of its heating and cooling system, alongside natural ventilation. A rainwater collection system is used for the bathrooms and landscape irrigation.

Elsewhere, ZHA recently completed a performing arts centre in China crowned by a trio of swooping, interconnected volumes informed by traditional Cantonese opera costumes

Another landmark performance venue that recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Opera House by Snøhetta, which incorporates a giant spiral staircase.

Photography by Hufton+Crow

Source: Dezeen | Published: 2026-11-21 11:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Google's Yi Xiang on how to build a design career across global borders
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: insightful career advice with global perspective

Google's Yi Xiang on how to build a design career across global borders

The senior UX designer reveals the lessons that moving between different cultures has taught him.

Ever dreamt of working abroad? I did, back in the early 2000s, and it led to a three-year career break from journalism to teach English in Japan. I loved every minute of it, but it also taught me something profound.

Previously, when people banged on about Asian cultures being totally different from the West, I'd taken it with a pinch of salt. People are the same everywhere, I'd thought. But living in Tokyo, I discovered that cultural differences really are a thing.

The Japanese people I made friends with really did seem to focus more on the collective than the individual, which meant living and working there was quite a culture shock. For me, it was a good shock, but I could also understand why some fresh recruits only spend a couple of days in the country before hurriedly booking the first flight back to the UK. The shift in behaviour and attitude can be... a lot.

I was thinking about this when I started chatting to Yi Xiang, a senior UX designer at Google, whose work has been recognised by the iF Design Award and A' Design Award, and who's turned his personal portfolio into an ever-evolving home for creative coding experiments.

Putting my own experience aside, Yi's career path has taken him to four distinctive places around the world, each with its own strong and unique culture.

Born in Jiangsu, China, Yi began his journey with a degree in interactive arts and technology at Simon Fraser University in Canada. Later, he earned a Master's in interaction design at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University.

His design career then took off in mainland China, where he worked at R/GA in Shanghai before moving to TikTok, where he worked as a product designer on TikTok.com. Then in late 2025, he relocated to San Francisco's Bay Area and started working in Silicon Valley.

Despite all this experience, Yi admits he wasn't very familiar with the US job market or its work culture when he arrived. I wanted to know more about how he navigated that shift.

Building a relationship with place

Arriving somewhere new typically means a struggle to fit in. But Yi takes a philosophical approach. While he admits to moments of unfamiliarity, he doesn't think he has to become a particular kind of person to 'belong' anywhere. "People build a relationship with a place in different ways," he says. "Keeping your own background and habits doesn't prevent you from contributing."

What attracted him to Silicon Valley, he says, was the number of talented people working in a world where design meets tech. He wanted to learn how they think and work, and challenge himself. So he's been actively seeking out designers with local experience and asking them for honest feedback to understand where he still needs to improve.

"It's not about assuming I belong," he explains, "but about continuously learning and pushing myself to become a designer who can contribute at that level." For him, confidence isn't about faking it till you make it. "My confidence comes from learning, feedback and making things, rather than simply telling myself that I'll be fine," he says.

American vs Chinese differences

Language has, he says, been a challenge at times. "Being able to express an idea is one thing; helping people from different backgrounds understand it and contribute to the discussion is another," he reasons. Yet Yi is wary of making broad generalisations about Chinese and American design as a whole.

The differences he's experienced, he says, have as much to do with the specifics—the stage he's at in his career, the teams he's working with and the products he's designing—as they do with geography. Underlying it all, he adds, good design shares the same underlying principles everywhere. It's just the details that need to change for different contexts.

Some of the obvious differences are rooted in language itself. Chinese, he notes, can say a lot in relatively few characters, but those characters themselves can be visually complex, which affects choices around type size, weight, line spacing and hierarchy.

Other languages bring similar challenges, longer labels to right-to-left reading in Arabic. The overall challenge then lies in recognising that "internationalisation means maintaining coherence, while making room for those differences."

Yi adds that some Chinese digital products prioritise speed and breadth of function, while some Western ones focus on motion and micro-interactions. But overall, it's not a big concern. "What interests me is how thoughtful details can make an efficient experience feel more human, without getting in the way of what people came to do," he says.

Portfolio as laboratory

While Yi is firmly focused on his career, he's smart enough to know that side projects can only help, not harm, those efforts. Hence the work he puts into what he calls his portfolio, even though it's less an archive of past work than a laboratory of current experiments. With these, he's heavily leaning into AI-assisted coding, which he says has let him build ideas that had sat in his head for years.

Serving as both a hobby and an investment in his future practice, these experiments include Transitery, an open-source collection of transition animations, and Vibe Text, which renders typed words in materials ranging from wood to jelly.

Yi makes it clear, though, that doesn't let the AI have the final word. "Generating something is only a starting point," he says.

Source: Creative Boom | Published: 2026-11-17 07:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Sheep, polka dots and graphic wanderings: inside Ines Launay's playful world of illustration
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: engaging profile of an illustrator with personal story

Sheep, polka dots and graphic wanderings: inside Ines Launay's playful world of illustration

The French illustrator draws on everything from trail running and wooden toys to everyday encounters, piecing together charming, colourful compositions that celebrate the joy of making things.

Sheep, wooden toys, polka dots and foam – these are just a few of the things that French illustrator Ines Launay keeps close at hand when she's making work, alongside a fondness for wandering, textile crafts, costumes and the occasional absurdity. It's a wonderfully peculiar collection of interests, but one that makes perfect sense when you look through her portfolio, where loose pencil marks, wonky characters, and little snippets of everyday life come together in playful, unexpected ways.

In one illustration, a group of people gather outside a Japanese shopfront, surrounded by bicycles, colourful signs and tiny details that keep you looking for ages and ages. Elsewhere, illustrated pages are filled with handwritten notes, miniature figures, landscapes and the odd speech bubble, resembling a cross between a travel diary, a comic and a collection of memories. There's a lovely handmade quality to it all, with the warmth of coloured pencils and the inky brushstrokes giving her work a deliciously tactile feel.

For Ines, drawing has been a constant since childhood. Growing up in a small town in central France, she was introduced to art by her grandparents, who both painted, while her grandmother also ran small modelling workshops. She took drawing classes for several years, though she remembers them more as afternoons spent drawing with friends than formal lessons. "Like many children, I loved drawing," she recalls. "For me, it was a way to exist, and I never really stopped. Today, drawing is part of my daily life, part of who I am, and part of how I see the world."

After studying illustration in Paris for three years and graduating in 2024, Ines has been figuring out how to fit her creative practice around a full-time job, which currently pays the bills. It's a balancing act that also involves her love of sport, particularly trail running, hiking and cycling, activities that regularly find their way into her drawings through the places she visits and the thoughts she has along the way.

With limited time to create, she's developed a process that involves making small separate pencil drawings before assembling them digitally. Rather than starting with a fully formed composition, she lets the individual elements accumulate and works out how they might fit together afterwards. "The final piece is often just the result of a graphic wandering," she explains. "I find it very hard to imagine one image as a whole, something complete on its own. That's also why I draw small separate pieces first, and only afterwards I think about what to do with them."

It's an approach shaped partly by two artists she particularly admires, Paul Cox and Sammy Stein, whose work opened her eyes to different ways of telling stories through images. "Their work spoke to me right away, and when I feel creatively lost, I like to go back to it," says Ines. She also recalls Sammy's observation that comics are, "in part, graphic design", an idea that resonates with her own interest in composition and the relationship between individual drawings on the page.

Two projects that capture these interests particularly well are Levain, her 2024 graduation project, and Sur les pas d'Ella Maillart, an illustrated travel notebook. The former is a graphic novel about three friends experimenting with different ways of living and inhabiting the world, presented through an intriguing mixture of landscapes, small figures and colourful graphic arrangements. The latter follows a journey through Switzerland in the footsteps of adventurer and travel writer Ella Maillart, undertaken with Louane Carmona and Coline Balfroid, who made an accompanying video documentary.

The pages of Sur les pas d'Ella Maillart are packed with delicate pencil drawings, handwritten observations and little scenes from the journey, with the informal quality of a sketchbook that someone has kindly invited you to flick through. "Graphically and narratively, they have plenty of flaws, but I learned a lot from them, and it's so rewarding to create a finished object – not just an image shared on a screen," Ines says. "On one side, there's the travel-notebook format, where I tell the story of my adventures – whether trips or races. On the other, there's a more experiential side with Levain, which holds my fads and my questions."

While her illustrations have an unmistakable sense of curiosity and play, Ines is also candid about questioning the purpose of making art, particularly when the world can feel so overwhelming. "With everything happening in the world, everything quickly feels pointless," she says.

Yet looking at other people's work still gives her "that little spark of curiosity, that boost of motivation, that feeling of joy and pleasure that I need every day." Perhaps that's what makes her work so appealing. Whether she's recording a journey, experimenting with an arrangement on pencil sketches or following an idea to see where it goes, there's something infectious about her willingness to keep making and trying things out.

Source: Creative Boom | Published: 2026-11-17 06:45 UTC | Difficulty: 50/100

item.title: This non-alcoholic aperitif packaging was made with real plants, sunlight and embossed glass
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting packaging design with sustainable approach

The zero-alcohol drinks market has come a long way. Nowadays, in all but the most traditional "old-man" pubs, you're sure to be able to get at least one alcohol-free beer, and possibly several, while the big supermarkets are packed with them.

Other alcohol-free alternatives, however, are taking longer to make an impact on both the trade and the public. So it's great to see Love, the creative agency based in Manchester and New York, working with Everleaf, the premium non-alcoholic aperitif founded by conservation biologist and bartender Paul Mathew, to push things forward.

Having made inroads into bars and restaurants, Everleaf wanted to win over shoppers too. So it asked Love to give its branding and packaging a thorough going-over.

The brief was to craft a more distinctive consumer brand that conveyed both the drink's premium quality and its close relationship with nature. Rather than starting from scratch, Love decided to refine and build on the brand world Everleaf already had.

A new bottle design

The highlight is a redesigned Everleaf bottle. With a softer, more curved shape, it features embossed acacia leaves around the base, a subtle texture at the neck and a leaf mark moulded into the glass at the shoulder. This design isn't just nice to look at: it's beautifully tactile and makes you instantly want to pick it up and run your fingers over it.

The neck is now longer and easier to grip, and colour coding on the label and a coloured disc on the cap make it quicker to tell the three flavours apart: blue for Marine, orange for Forest and pink for Mountain.

Printed by the sun

Love also created new botanical artwork in-house using cyanotype. This vintage photographic process, dating back to the 1840s, involves placing objects on light-sensitive paper and leaving them in sunlight to create a silhouette.

In this instance, the team arranged real plants on the paper, exposed them to the sun and then scanned and refined the prints.

On the labels, these soft-edged silhouettes appear in washes of colour behind a newly crafted wordmark, with an effect that sits somewhere between a botanical print and a pressed flower. Each flavour has its own pair of plants: saffron and orchid leaves for Forest, rosehip and cherry blossom for Mountain, and seaweed and olive branch for Marine.

Wider packaging

The visual system also appears on cartons and shipping boxes. The single-bottle cartons are white, with the cyanotype artwork reproduced as a halftone print in each flavour's colour, alongside evocative descriptions. Mountain's carton, for example, reads: "Blossom, sharp air and anticipation brought in on the breeze."

The shipping boxes are made of kraft-brown cardboard printed in a single dark colour, with foliage silhouettes spilling across the surfaces and a QR code inside the lid. A restrained approach to colour and low ink coverage gives everything a sophisticated, grown-up finish.

Sustainability was a big part of the brief, with Love's in-house sustainability manager working alongside its structural, design and illustration teams.

The new bottle is 23% lighter than its predecessor, weighing just 385g, down from 500g. It's made from 100% post-consumer recycled glass, and the labels use wood-free stock made from 100% recycled pulp, as before; secondary and tertiary packaging is made from recyclable cardboard and finished with single-colour, low-ink print.

Aiming for growth

"The aim of this refresh was to solidify our position as number one in the on-trade, while helping us expand into the off-trade for continued growth, gaining brand affinity and loyalty with new consumers in the process," says Everleaf founder Paul Mathew.

"The repositioning and beautiful new bottle design deliver a tactile, premium feel that reinforces our luxury brand positioning and reflects our desire to make delicious drinks that connect people with the natural world through aroma, flavour and texture."

Nick Johnson, senior design director at Love, adds: "Everleaf didn't need reinvention; it needed its natural brand world to work harder. We used real plants, sunlight and glassmaking craft to create a pack that feels more tactile, distinctive and premium, while the longer neck and clearer colour coding make it work better for bartenders too."

The new packaging is rolling out across bars and restaurants, Everleaf's own website, Ocado and Majestic. From the looks of it, it should do a fine job of catching the eye in the supermarket aisle too.

Source: Creative Boom | Published: 2026-11-17 06:30 UTC | Difficulty: 50/100

item.title: ESR x Craig & Karl Bring a Pocket Full of Joy to Everyday Technology
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: creative collaboration in tech accessories

The objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize. From the jewelry we wear to the accessories we keep within reach, even the smallest possessions become expressions of personal style. Yet as technology plays an increasingly central role in our lives, the devices we interact with most remain largely defined by their utility. Bringing more personality to these everyday essentials is the idea behind Pocket Full of Joy—a new collaboration between ESR, a consumer tech accessories brand, and creative duo Craig & Karl—which transforms phone cases and wallets into colorful, functional accessories.

Known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets. The collaboration draws upon the duo’s affinity for bold colors and familiar imagery, translating their graphic sensibilities into objects designed to accompany their owners throughout the day. The result is a collection that explores how artistic expression can become part of everyday life.

Across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces. A collage of playful symbols evokes the spontaneity of a personal scrapbook, while the graphic “OK” design introduces a lighthearted note of optimism. Elsewhere, the cheerful “HI” motif transforms a magnetic wallet into a small, portable greeting. Each composition reflects Craig & Karl’s recognizable aesthetic while giving everyday accessories a more personal character.

Behind the playful graphics are the practical features that define ESR’s accessories. The Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Flex Stand incorporates a built-in adjustable stand, MagSafe compatibility, and protective construction, allowing it to move between different activities without sacrificing its colorful design. Coordinating magnetic wallets hold cards and cash in compact silhouettes, while the Magnetic Wallet Stand with Grip adds an adjustable viewing stand and finger loop for greater versatility. Together, these features bring Craig & Karl’s expressive graphics to everyday accessories.

The collection’s appeal also comes from the way it brings art into objects that have become nearly inseparable from modern life. Where traditional artworks invite observation, these designs encourage interaction, becoming more personal through repeated use. A phone placed on a café table, a wallet retrieved during a morning commute, or a device propped against a desk becomes a small, unexpected moment of visual interest.

With Pocket Full of Joy, ESR and Craig & Karl make a case for bringing more creativity into the everyday. Sometimes, the most memorable design details are found in the things we carry without a second thought.

The ESR × Craig & Karl Pocket Full of Joy collection will be available Nov. 14, 2026, at esr.com and amazon.com, with iPhone cases starting at $49.99 and magnetic wallets starting at $25.99.

item.title: The Role of UX in Agentic Software Factories
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: analysis of UX in AI software development

In August 2026, Anthropic published its vision of an AI-native software development lifecycle (SDLC) following similar, though less prescriptive, publications by Google (May 2026) and OpenAI (November 2025). The three visions differ in details, but all sideline UX, reducing it to behind-the-scenes context that guides AI generation. But this is only part of the value UX offers. UX also discovers what users need, strengthens the team’s shared judgment about what to build, and evaluates what gets built. Organizations that adopt this model as described risk losing the very user insight their AI context depends on. This article examines Anthropic’s playbook to show where it leaves UX out and what UX teams can do about it.

What Is the SDLC?

The software development lifecycle (SDLC) is the sequence of stages software goes through as it’s built. The stages typically include:

- Plan: deciding what to build and why

- Design: working out how it should look, work, and behave

- Build: writing the code

- Test: checking that the code works as intended

- Deploy: releasing the product to users

- Maintain: monitoring, fixing, and updating the product after release

Early versions of the SDLC emerged in the 1960s, often referred to as "waterfall," before the Agile movement of the early 2000s reworked them into short, repeated cycles.

Anyone working on software is likely familiar with elements of the SDLC, whether they call it that or not. But it’s important to recognize that the SDLC framework primarily describes an engineering perspective. UX has long fought to defend its place in the traditional SDLC.

The AI-Native SDLC

Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI’s publications all make a simple argument: AI agents make writing code (the Build stage) fast and cheap, so the other stages must also adapt to maximize productivity gains. Deliverable creation, human approvals, and governing policies must be redesigned to keep pace with AI agents without lowering quality standards. Google summarizes the main argument of all three well:

"The most profound shift in software engineering isn't a new language, framework, or cloud service. It's the transition from writing code to expressing intent, and trusting intelligent systems to translate that intent into working software.”

What Anthropic’s AI-Native SDLC Playbook Looks Like

Anthropic’s playbook retains the six traditional SDLC stages, but AI becomes the primary executor, and humans monitor quality along the way. The stages revolve around a chain of version-controlled artifacts generated by AI agents in Markdown and reviewed by the individuals who control each approval gate, serving as an audit trail of what was decided and by whom.

What guides the AI’s work is context: curated instructions that tell the AI how the organization does things and that constrain its work. Context can include coding conventions, brand guidelines, security rules, and UX standards. In theory, the better the context, the more likely the AI’s output will meet the organization’s standards without human correction — the ultimate goal. This is a significant departure from the traditional SDLC, in which a person both creates and evaluates all the work.

Versions of this new SDLC are already happening — perhaps you’re right in the middle of it. But it’s too early to tell how well this SDLC suits companies of all kinds, since it’s so heavily oriented to software production. It’s also important to recognize the conflict of interest: AI labs want companies to make this shift because it drives greater use of their products.

UX Context Is Necessary, but Not Sufficient

UX does not own a stage or approval gate in Anthropic’s playbook. It assumes that UX knowledge, codified as context and skills, will help the AI create high-quality, user-centric products. However, it does not define space for UX professionals to get directly involved. Let’s unpack some of these assumptions.

Plan-Stage Assumptions

The lifecycle starts with the creation of an intent.md in the Plan stage. It assumes the author will independently honor user needs rather than just fixating on favorite solutions. What’s to stop the submission of an intent.md that’s not linked to any clear user need? Even a well-intentioned author working with detailed UX context is limited by what they or their organization already knows, and the playbook does not create space to discover new user needs.

The individual creation of intent.mds also encourages silos over collaboration. It becomes easy for individuals (or the system itself) to create these artifacts in isolation without the perspectives of other team members, relying solely on the product owner’s judgment to approve, edit, or reject the proposals. This is a recipe for low buy-in across the team, unchallenged biases, and a flood of intent.md files from every direction.

Product owners, engineering, and UX have long represented three balancing perspectives: business viability, technical feasibility, and user desirability, respectively. But if AI-coding agents dissolve many technical constraints and UX is reduced to context in Markdown files, then all the cards are in the product owner’s hands, and the approval gate is guarded primarily by business needs.

Design-Stage Assumptions

The Design stage assumes that AI will adequately incorporate the organization’s design standards into the spec.md and mockup it creates. It’s true that machine-readable design systems can constrain these outputs to many of the organization’s standards, but someone must curate, manage, and maintain this context just as design-system managers have always done. Is this done by UX? The Playbook is unclear. And what happens when a design need extends beyond the documented context? This is where UX’s judgment has always been crucial for deciding what to build.…

Source: Nielsen Norman Group | Published: 2026-10-30 17:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Original link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-agentic-software-factories/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=rss-syndication

item.title: Experience Design: Dropping the “User” from “User Experience”
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: thought-provoking discussion on UX evolution

I am not one for new terms. When NN/G changed its job titles from “user-experience specialist” to “experience specialist”, I was skeptical. The article we published to explain the change did not convince me either: yet another name for the same thing. I now think the new title was right, but for a reason we did not think of at the time. Our field is no longer only about people directly using products and services. It also includes agents that act on their behalf. UX is not disappearing. But AI is expanding the field in several directions at once.

UX Has Always Been More than UI

Don Norman helped popularize the term "user experience" in the 1990s because "usability" and "user interface" were too narrow. He wanted a name for everything a person experiences with a product, from the packaging to the support call. The term widened the object of design beyond just the digital product, to physical products and services. Yet, the idea of a broader object of design did not really hit home until the 2010s, when modern smartphones rose to ubiquity, and people started using multiple channels to accomplish a goal. As a response, UX and design professionals began creating customer-journey maps and service blueprints to help them understand and track all the possible ways in which a user could interact with the organization while trying to achieve a goal. At that time, we began to understand that a good experience meant that all the touchpoints worked together coherently.

But throughout all these iterations of the work, one assumption stayed constant: that the human was the user — the one who interacts with the company directly, through one of many possible channels.

AI changes that assumption. And not because users can use an AI-chatbot feature to interact with a business. (That is just another channel in the journey-level experience.) But because humans may no longer interact with the company at all. Instead, their personal agents may do so. And these agents may act completely outside the ecosystem of channels and touchpoints that the company has devised.

A person may ask an AI assistant to shop for groceries, file a complaint, cluster photographs, book a flight, or cancel a subscription. The agent becomes the immediate user of the product or service while acting on the human’s behalf.

The journey now spans not only multiple channels but also multiple actors. This is why I believe “experience design” is a fitting name for the broader field.

From User Experience to Experience Design

Experience design is the discipline concerned with designing and evaluating how people accomplish goals through products, services, and systems, whether they interact with those systems directly or through agents acting on their behalf.

The field includes traditional UX but extends beyond it. Like UX, it studies the products people use themselves and the AI systems they interact with, but it goes beyond UX to encompass the systems that agents use on humans’ behalf. It also expands the methods used to design and evaluate experiences.

Experience Design Is Still Rooted in Human-Centered Design

Expanding the field beyond human users does not mean abandoning the principles of human-centered design. The ultimate criterion of success for an experience is whether the human achieved their goals. Designing for agents is not the same as optimizing blindly for agent success; the goals, interests, and welfare of the humans behind them still hold priority. For example, an agent-facing system that facilitates bank transactions would still need to consider the financial safety and interests of the people on whose behalf the agents act.

The Scope of Experience Design

We said above that experience design expands the scope of UX. Experience design deals with designing for:

- Humans interacting with products

- Agents using systems on behalf of people

- People and agents interacting with systems

1. Humans Interacting with Products

AI does not obliterate the traditional scope of UX. All the topics that UX has traditionally studied (such as usability, information architecture, interaction design, content, and accessibility) are still within the scope of experience design.

People will still use products and services directly and they still need to be able to complete the tasks they want, should they choose to do it the regular way. They need to be able to purchase an item, navigate a healthcare website, or complete a tax form. Traditional UX remains the foundation of the field.

However, beyond traditional products, a special type of system is one that uses generative AI: AI features embedded on a website or within an application, AI personal assistants, AI agents, generative UIs, or other AI-enabled products. Many traditional UX methods still apply to these systems, but some of their characteristics (nondeterminism, autonomy, and the ability to make inferences) raise new research questions that those methods were not designed to address. Some of these questions include: When should an agent act without asking the human? When should it ask the human for clarification? What should the agent remember? What should an agent consider as part of its context and what types of information should it have access to? When should control return to the person? How should someone inspect or reverse an action taken by an agent?

Because many of these questions depend heavily on people’s needs, goals, and contexts, qualitative research will remain as important as ever. However, new methods or adapted protocols may need to emerge as well — for example, repeated runs for systems, analysis of a system’s variability, inspection of log traces, observation of how control moves between people and agents.

2. Agents Using Products and Services on Behalf of People…

Source: Nielsen Norman Group | Published: 2026-10-30 17:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: UX Disciplines: Glossary
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: glossary of UX-related terms

People often use terms such as UX, UI, CX, and visual design interchangeably, even though they refer to different fields of practice. This glossary focuses primarily on what each kind of work involves. Some of these terms (such as user experience and customer experience) also have other common meanings. For example, user experience can refer to the field of user experience or to the experience of users interacting with a particular product, while information architecture can refer to the field of information architecture or the content organization on a specific site. Where useful, we note these additional meanings.

Job titles in our field are not standardized. In our UX-careers survey, respondents reported 134 unique job titles related to UX. As a result, the boundaries described here are the typical ones; in any given organization, one person may do the work of several of these areas, and the same title may mean different things.

Some fields in this glossary (e.g., market research) are not traditionally part of UX but are adjacent to it and often confused with it; others (e.g., UX research) are subfields of UX.

Agent Experience (AX)

Agent experience (AX) is the practice of designing digital products and services so that they can be effectively understood and operated by AI agents when acting on behalf of people. Agent experience can include structuring information so that agents can interpret it reliably, tool descriptions and permissions that enable agents to operate, and APIs that allow agents to directly access an offering, without relying on a human-facing user interface.

- See also: user experience (UX)

Content Design

Content design is the practice of determining what information users need, when they need it, and how to best provide it. It involves selecting, structuring, formatting, and presenting content based on user needs and context. Content designers usually have skills in both writing and design and may be responsible for information architecture, wireframing, and prototyping. Content design is broader than UX writing, which focuses on the words in the interface.

- See also: UX writing, content strategy, information architecture

- Related article: Content Strategy vs. UX Writing

Content Strategy

Content strategy is the ongoing practice of planning for the creation, delivery, and governance of useful, usable, and effective content. A content strategy specifies the purpose of the content, who owns and maintains it, its format and distribution, how it is organized, and how it fits into the overall user experience. In other words, content strategy is concerned with the processes around content, whereas UX writing and content design produce the content.

- See also: content design, UX writing

- Related article: Content Strategy 101

Conversation Design

Conversation design is the discipline of designing the exchanges between users and systems that communicate in natural language, such as chatbots, voice assistants, and AI assistants built on large language models. It covers what the system says, how it asks for and confirms information, and what happens when it misunderstands the user. Conversation design combines interaction design and UX writing for interfaces in which the conversation is the main (or only) UI.

- See also: interaction design, UX writing, agent experience

- Related article: The User Experience of Chatbots

Customer Experience (CX)

Customer experience (CX) has two meanings. As a discipline, CX is the practice of studying and improving the relationship between customers and an organization over the lifetime of that relationship.

As an experience, CX is the totality of a customer's interactions with an organization over time, across every touchpoint: advertising, purchase, customer support, post-purchase followup, and so on. UX and CX overlap considerably. Today, some people use “UX” to refer to the experience of a single type of interaction with a product (e.g., registering on a mobile app) and “CX” to refer to all interactions throughout the customer relationship.

- See also: user experience, service design, employee experience

- Related article: User Experience vs. Customer Experience: What's the Difference?

Design Operations (DesignOps)

Design operations (DesignOps) is the orchestration and optimization of people, processes, and craft to amplify design's value and impact at scale. In other words, DesignOps creates the team structures, workflows, and measures that allow a design team to do good work as it grows, so that designers can focus on designing. Common DesignOps roles include design program manager and design producer.

- See also: research operations, UX design

- Related article: DesignOps 101

Employee Experience (EX)

Employee experience (EX) has two meanings. As a discipline, EX involves studying and improving employees' experience of working for an organization, including the internal tools, processes, policies, and physical spaces they deal with.

As an experience, EX refers to employees' perceptions of their interactions with the organization. EX applies to employees the same approach that CX applies to customers. It is often owned by human resources; UX teams usually contribute through service design and through the design of internal software and intranets.

- See also: customer experience, service design

Experience Design (XD)

Experience design (XD) is an approach to creating high-quality, optimized experiences that encompasses all levels of the user's experience: individual interactions with specific products, the user's journey over time, and the customer's lifetime relationship with the organization. The term is used as an umbrella for UX, CX, service design, and product design, which share a focus on people, structured problem solving, iteration, and methods such as user research and journey mapping. In practice, experience designer is often an alternative job title for UX designer.…

Source: Nielsen Norman Group | Published: 2026-10-23 17:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Original link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-disciplines-glossary/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=rss-syndication

item.title: Route 66 is an American icon. That's why international tourists love it
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

Route 66 is an American icon. That's why international tourists love it

There isn't much to see in Amboy, Calif. But if you're traveling on Route 66, the dusty stop in the Mojave desert is a must for its famous 50-foot-tall neon Roy's Motel and Cafe sign. Photographing the sign can wait: Alan Jacob gets out of his rented GMC truck and heads straight for the gift shop.

Others in Jacob's tour group driving the length of Route 66 have bought T-shirts, hats and socks along the way. One even got a Route 66 tattoo. For the sinewy, retired plumber from a small town about an hour North of New Zealand's capital, Wellington, it's all about the fridge magnets along the nearly month-long journey.

"I've been buying magnets everywhere I go," Jacob said. "When I get home, I'm going to get an 8-by-4 sheet, powder-coat it white, put the road on it and put all the magnets where I got them from."

Celebrating the road's centennial

100 years after its founding, the nearly 2,500-mile highway from Chicago to Santa Monica, Calif., continues to capture imaginations far beyond U.S. borders.

According to a 2024 study conducted by the tourism research firm SMARInsights shared with NPR by the New Mexico Tourism Department, international travelers are more likely to travel the entire length of Route 66 than those from within the United States.

"60 to 70% of the people who come here are international travelers," said Samir Patel, the manager of The Wigwam Motel, a popular stop on the highway in San Bernardino, Calif. "And a good chunk of them are Australians and New Zealanders." The highway has been popular for decades with Europeans, he added, and, in more recent years, with South American and Asian tourists.

Driven by a passion for cars

Sam Murray, the New Zealand-based owner of Gilligans Tours — loosely named after the 1960s American TV show Gilligan's Island – has been leading Route 66 trips in the spring and fall for more than a decade. His clientele are mostly tourists from New Zealand and Australia.

Murray said he was drawn to Route 66 through his passion for car racing. The 48-year-old first came to the U.S. as an adult in 2005 for an auto race in Laughlin, Nev. When the event was done, Murray drove down a nearby part of Route 66 for the first time. It made him want to do the whole thing.

"So in 2011, I bought an old motor home in Pennsylvania, drove down to St. Louis, followed Route 66 back to LA," he said. "And then I realized when I got home, people that I talked to had an interest as well in doing Route 66."

Of course, "doing Route 66" these days isn't what it once was. The construction of the modern interstate highway system made older sections of the road obsolete. It was officially removed from the system in 1985. Route 66 now exists as an incomplete patchwork of roads, some of them unpaved.

"We've done quite a bit of gravel driving, which is something I didn't expect to do over here," said retired apple grower Pete Volkers. He opted to ride with Murray rather than drive himself in a rented car.

Volkers was looking to venture out on his own for the first time since losing his wife last year to breast cancer, and Route 66 had long been on his bucket list.

He was steeped in mid-20th century American pop culture growing up in New Zealand — "The American diner thing and TV shows like Happy Days," he recalled.

"On this trip, we've been to so many little towns which have all this stuff that we've seen on TV, and all of these iconic neon signs," said Volkers. "And you just don't get a chance to see that anywhere else in the world."

Volkers said he enjoys wide open roads sprinkled with opportunities to revel in American kitsch and nostalgia. ("At least I can go home and say I slept in a teepee," he said after spending a night in a concrete, teepee-shaped guestroom at the Wigwam Motel.) But Volkers also acknowledges there's a certain bleakness to traveling Route 66 in 2026.

"These little towns that not a lot of people come through. No one stops there," Volkers said. "They're just zooming on to the next big place."

Thriving pitstops along the way

Even if Route 66 isn't what it once was, many stops along the way look like they are thriving — at least for tourists. Oatman, Ariz., is among them.

The windswept former gold mining town is packed with people on a Monday afternoon. To Australian insurance broker Peter Johnson, the rickety clapboard storefronts and local population of roaming donkeys bring classic Westerns to mind. "You should be walking along here with a six gun," Johnson said.

Inside the Oatman Hotel on Main Street, Carrie Eagan is packing bottles of ketchup and mayo instead of a Colt revolver. The restaurant manager at the bustling Route 66 landmark, built in 1902, said she's noticed one main difference between foreign visitors and American ones: "The Americans, they know a lot about the history. But the foreigners are very excited," Eagan said. "They come dressed to impress; ready to go."

This is certainly true of tour participants Kieron and Wendy Guinness. He's sporting a handlebar mustache and white cowboy hat; she's petite and put together in a scarlet sweater. The New Zealand couple are wowed by the thick wads of greenbacks plastering every inch of ceiling and wall space in the Oatman Hotel. "This hotel would be worth a fortune!" Wendy said.

She's been a fan of the United States ever since she spent a year in California as a high school student. "I put on 20 pounds that year because especially when you're young, you come and you're like, 'Oh my God, there's so much good food,'" said Guinness, who managed a women's clothing store before retiring. "We ate out all the time."

Kieron Guinness is nuts about American cars, like many in the group. "I've been around hot rodding all my life, mucking around with old V8s, Chevrolets and Fords and Dodges," he said.…
