item.title: How the Steadicam sprinted up the stairs along with Rocky
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence

How the Steadicam sprinted up the stairs along with Rocky

Sylvester Stallone's underdog story Rocky was crowned the Best Picture at the 1977 Academy Awards. The film's most famous sequence shows the character Rocky Balboa training for his big heavyweight boxing championship.

He runs through trainyards, a crowded outdoor market, and a jogging path. He punches a speedbag, does push-ups and sit-ups, gets repeatedly jabbed in the stomach, and slugs frozen sides of beef with his bare knuckles. Finally, Rocky sprints up the steps of the Philadelphia Art Museum, all the way to the top, where he jumps up and down and raises his arms in triumph.

Now the new movie I Play Rocky tells the story about how Stallone wrote and starred in his movie. It also celebrates the original cinematographer, Garrett Brown. He invented the Steadicam — which is still in use today.

For Rocky, Brown used his invention to shoot from inside the boxing ring; he also wove through the frozen meat locker and ran up those steps with Rocky.

"He's not just holding a camera, he's telling a story," says I Play Rocky director Peter Farrelly. Garrett's smooth camera movements captured Rocky's iconic moment at the top of the stairs that still — a half-century later — has fans cheering wildly.

"Garrett Brown was smart enough and savvy enough and artistic enough," says Farrelly, "[that] he didn't just shoot him going up the stairs, he followed him around and we got to be part of it as an audience."

All the while, Brown was filming with his invention strapped to his chest.

"It has a harness instead of being in your hands," Brown tells NPR about his Steadicam. "And at the business end of that arm is a so-called gimbal, so that any angular thing that I did not get through to the camera."

Brown's contraption included a fiber optic viewfinder strapped to his head. "I can only imagine what that looked like," he chuckles. "You have to be immune to embarrassment to try out inventions like that."

Brown's Steadicam earned him an Oscar in 1978. He went on to invent the Skycam, a flying camera for capturing live sports. He also invented the Mobycam and the Divecam for filming sports underwater, along with other camera innovations that have revolutionized cinematography.

But Brown actually started out in music, imitating the Kingston Trio in high school. In college, he met Alfred Dana Arioli, and they became the folk-singing duo Brown and Dana. They even sang and recorded the song "It Was a Very Good Year" two years before Frank Sinatra's version won a Grammy.

"We were pretty good. We recorded for MGM and did college concerts all around and so on," Brown reminisces. "For me, that ended with a car crash on the way from a gig in Winnipeg. Then the Beatles came out. We looked at each other and thought: 'we are toast.'"

Brown got out of folk music, and for a time was selling cars while teaching himself to become a filmmaker.

He started his own production company and began creating live-action videos for Sesame Street in the 1960s.

Brown also came up with new ways to shoot commercials.

"I did invent a weird, wonderful dog's eye view dolly," he says. "My little device made a very realistic point of view of a beagle. That intrigued the hell out of me."

Brown says he was fed up with the bigger, cumbersome dollies used to pull cameras. And he found handheld cameras too jerky.

"If you taped a camera to your head, which the French New Wave guys did, it looks horrible, very unlike what humans see," he says, "You know, we don't see it bouncing like that. We see it smooth."

Brown says he locked himself in a hotel room for a week in 1974 until he came up with a sketch for the Steadicam.

Then with his invention, he went all around Philadelphia taking what he called "30 impossible shots."

Those test shots caught the attention of filmmakers.

In 1976, Brown and his Steadicam wandered through a labor camp following the Woody Guthrie characters for the movie Bound for Glory.

Brown's "30 impossible shots" included him following his then-girlfriend — now wife Ellen, as she ran up those steps of the Philadelphia Art Museum. The same steps used in Rocky. You can see that original footage in the new film about Rocky.

For the 1983 Star Wars film Return of the Jedi, Brown walked through a redwood forest shooting slower than one frame a second with his Steadicam. Speeded up, it created the 100 mph chase scene.

Later, Stanley Kubrick used Brown and his Steadicam for his 1980 horror film The Shining. The inventor has since shot many other films, including Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom.

Brown says the Steadicam replicates the native human look, which is stable.

"It turns out that our eyes are internally stabilized by our inner ear," he says. "In fact, your human eye looks very much like a Steadicam, because when you walk, you don't even see yourself go up and down. You see a very smooth shot."

Brown says his invention takes a very skilled human to operate — something that could never be done realistically by AI.

Correction Nov. 19, 2026

A previous version of this story incorrectly said The Shining was released in 1990. It came out in 1980.

item.title: The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence

The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife

The ‘Magic Six’: How to strengthen your marriage in midlife

Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.

She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."

It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)

As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?

David and Nina's Four L's

When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:

Love. "You gotta love each other."

Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me, and she still has her."

Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.

Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.

The Magic Six

I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn. She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection, where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.

Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?

The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six.

Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.

Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.

Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.

Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.

Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.

Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.

State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.

Listen. Don't Fix.

Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.

"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.

Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."

It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.

Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.

Find Your Rhythm

Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?

Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order. Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.

As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."

So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."…

item.title: She Was a Victim of Jeffrey Epstein. She Also Helped Him Find Other Girls.
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence

During the four years that Marina Lacerda was abused, she introduced Jeffrey Epstein to many of her friends. And they, in turn, did the same with their friends. How do these women live with the anger, guilt, and shame Epstein forced upon them? How do they live with each other? Jen Percy grapples with one of the most painful aspects of Epstein’s legacy:

He tried to pit the girls against one another by comparing them, inciting jealousy. He made comments about their bodies. He would call one on the phone, ignoring the others. He didn’t like the girls getting too close—he had more control when they were fighting for his attention. Sometimes the girls they brought weren’t good enough. He said they looked too tired, too old, too dark or too heavy. Sometimes he’d say they wore too much makeup.

Lisa treated finding girls like a job. She was always thinking, I need to go talk to this girl. Sometimes Lisa brought two or three girls a day. She’s pretty sure she brought the most girls of anyone in Queens, maybe in all of New York and Florida. She felt like it was all day, every day, constantly for at least seven years. She met them everywhere: the nail salon, shopping centers, clubs like Marquee. She knew how to find girls like herself: No parents, no job, drug addiction? Perfect. She figured that was the kind of girl she could help. Lisa would say: “Oh, my god, I love your shoes. Where are you from? What do you do?” And once she heard their story, she would tell them she knew Epstein. She felt like a savior. She was giving young immigrants the chance at the American dream.

item.title: Dollywood After Dolly: My Pilgrimage to a Grieving Tennessee
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence

Soon after Dolly Parton’s passing, Marisa Meltzer heads to Dollywood, in the heart of Dolly country. Expecting a shared experience of mourning, she finds people reluctant to talk to her. Perhaps it’s simply too soon after Dolly’s death—or perhaps, as Meltzer suggests, it’s because she is “unlike about 50% of the people there,” not wearing “a T-shirt emblazoned with a Bible verse, a military slogan, or a celebration of America’s 250 years.” Instead, she finds Dollywood carrying on as usual, even without its “dreamer-in-chief.”

But more than a museum, Dollywood is an amusement park, and a much bigger one than I had realized. It’s a place where you can stand in line for 45 minutes to buy a corn dog while listening to a four-person singing-and-dancing group in the vein of the Mickey Mouse Club does peppy but half-assed covers of Fleetwood Mac and Van Halen. Looping rollercoasters and water tube rides leave families soaking wet in matching T-shirts commemorating their vacations. Dondre, my colleague and our photographer for this journey, waits probably a full hour to squeeze into a vintage muscle car with me so I can simulate steering around a track. It wasn’t until deep into our wait time that we realize this is a children’s ride. At this point, the two of us notice that, in the sea of people, we are the only ones who are childless, wearing dark colors, and audibly bemoaning that Dollywood is dry. (Parton was not a strict teetotaler, but the park bills itself as assertively family-friendly. “Weapons and alcoholic beverages are not permitted on Dollywood Property” is the only explanation given on its website.) No one else seems to care. The ride is quick, but we are ecstatic, high on refillable Diet Cokes, kettle corn, and driving a car, which neither one of us knows how to do in real life.

More picks on the late, great Dolly Parton

item.title: The Lost World of Aquaterra
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence

“We can’t grasp the depth of the ocean,” writes Elisa Gabbert, “until we throw a skyscraper down there.” How about the edges of early human civilization? For The Atlantic, Toby Lester offers a fascinating, mildly haunting overview of the underneath—specifically, the “submerged prehistory” buried beneath the oceans, and the researchers salvaging it, bit by bit. Reading, I felt awestruck, not merely for the scale of history that lurks beneath our rising waters but the implications for the future of humanity. “What if archaeologists of the future could study only what remained above sea level, in places that today sit well inland from the coast?” an archaeologist suggests to Lester. It’s a wonder to watch Lester play with the hypothetical, to help us better grasp the depths and imagine their future reach.

The chance to name a giant new Earth feature doesn’t arrive often (Antarctica, one of the most recent additions, began to appear on maps in the 1880s, although the word had been around for centuries), and if that feature happens to be largely invisible, you’re likely to run into difficulties persuading others to go along with your name. Call the feature what you will, but it exists: During the past 20,000 years, huge stretches of formerly inhabited land along the world’s coastal shelves have disappeared underwater, taking with them tens of thousands of years of human history.

Until recently, that is. During the past few decades, artifacts and sites dating back millennia have been found off the coasts of every inhabited continent. A growing number of researchers—geographers, archaeologists, anthropologists, amateur enthusiasts—are turning their attention to what lies offshore. “Everywhere we’ve systematically looked, we’ve found some areas where the former landscape has survived,” Jessi Halligan, an anthropologist at Texas A&M, told me. “And in a lot of those places, those former landscapes have had sites on them.”

Mapping complicated terrain

Have We Been Measuring Mountains All Wrong?

“A new method for quantifying grandeur is reshuffling the pecking order of the planet’s most impressive peaks. Turns out Everest has steep competition.”

How to Map Nothing

“What if we took each sourdough selfie, each Zoom class, each Peloton ride, each Netflix binge and mapped the ecology of resources and services that have made it possible for some of us? And at the same time impossible for others?” On pandemic maps and the Great Pause.

Here Be Dragons: Finding the Blank Spaces in a Well-Mapped World

Maps are how we orient ourselves, and how we donate a place’s value — and by extension, the value of that place’s inhabitance. What does that means for the place still left un-mapped?

item.title: How Do We Keep Our Daughters Alive?: Motherhood, Survival, and Visibility in Margaret Elysia Garcia’s “the daughterland”
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence

In her debut full-length collection of poetry, the daughterland, Margaret Elysia Garcia dissects and grounds the experiences of Chicanx girls and women. She interweaves the landscape of Southern California with her own Chicanx identity and experience as a brown woman in America. Her poetry asks: How can women of color protect their daughters from danger if love is not enough to stop racial attacks, sexual predators, and self-harm?

Garcia’s poems are set in the socio-political atmosphere inflated by the 2016 election and the incoming president’s racist and anti-immigrant rhetoric, heightened by the escalation of a global pandemic revealing systemic disparities impacting communities of color in America. Garcia sets up her poem, “History Lesson,” with the context in parentheses and italicized: “(The president said Lat-tee-nex aren’t getting vaccinated because we fear documentation and deportation. Demoralization. Department chair: don’t they realize they’re all from farm workers?)” This poetry collection is even more relevant today with the corrupt surge of ICE agents across the country, state violence against communities of color, and undisclosed rape and abuse against young Latinx women in detention centers, than when it was published in 2023. Her rich imagery of isolation and grief, vibrancy and hope, tolls truer today with a presence both haunting and embracing. Body, mind, family, femininity, and landscape unite in the speaker’s deep willingness to learn and understand survival: in persisting as a person of color through enforced assimilation; as a young girl in a world of predators who invade even the space of home; and living through psychological ghosts and demons manifesting as depression and self-harm.

Garcia uses the imagery of whiteness to illustrate the suppression of feeling and identity. In her poem, “Your Parents’ Intentions,” the speaker explains:

If we fell

apart

we’d do so quietly, whitely,

suffocating tears into stained pillows

and overworked livers.

In this line, the adverb “whitely” parallels the adverb “quietly,” highlighting Garcia’s portrayal of whiteness and order as suppressive. The speaker describes how she and her husband would quell their breakdowns and arguments, which she experienced firsthand from her own parents, to shield her daughter from their marital strife. However, this repression leads to “suffocating tears” and “overworked livers,” which can be interpreted as self-harm, and the internal pain shapes into discreet yet destructive behavior. By depicting the harm in suppressing internal emotion and sentimentality, Garcia highlights the importance of expressing intimacy, starting within the home. When parents conceal and repress their emotions, whether love or anger, they teach their children to isolate themselves and suffer alone. The resulting loneliness deepens depression in younger generations as a consequence of the tradition to appear stoic, familiar to immigrant parents and grandparents.

The concealment of intergenerational trauma and sexual violence simultaneously suppresses women while enabling men to take advantage of this forced silence and prey on young girls. Garcia writes in “White Cousin Rapist,” “The curiosity of power, / with that gun in his pants. / An army of one.” We see the weapon of manhood hidden, and his threat underestimated with an “army of one,” while his “curiosity of power” suggests that he is dangerous. By the end of her collection, Garcia writes:

[…] Me barricading

in front of her with my armor and

my shield, while the world crept up

behind us, taking her prisoner

and me by stupid surprise.

Garcia illustrates an external and concrete ambush on girlhood and identity aided by concealment, depicting the violence against women and young girls in militaristic terms. In “Rural Mountain Town,” Garcia describes, “The boys’ anger bubbles out of their babybird mouths, / angry with a world they’ve already won,” highlighting the privilege and inheritance engrained in manhood and an early harboring of anger transformed into violence directed toward girls and women. Despite the innocence evoked by the image of “babybird mouths,” such masculine hostility and violence is made tangible by Garcia, challenging how harmful behavior directed toward young girls and women is disguised and normalized by our culture.

Garcia’s portrayal of whiteness often mirrors the harm of silence, marking direct and physical self-harm. The repression of both positive and negative emotions leaves evident damage on both parents and their children, meaning no one is being protected by avoiding their feelings. The speaker addresses her daughter directly: “You grew up in this peaceful house: / with a quiet air so thick / You began to cut yourself with it.” The peace of the house is sustained by suppressing and silencing one’s own self. This practice normalizes the withholding of pain and concealing it from others and mirrors how the parents cope by crying secretly and consuming alcohol. From the surface, the house and family both appear peaceful, but left unsaid, and avoided due to fear of confrontation, is the visibility of self-harm. Subsequently, in “Rural Mountain Town,” the speaker notes, “The girls who leave town mark time in knife lines / The scar of this tranquility on their skin.” The word “tranquility” echoes the adjective “peaceful” in Garcia’s previous description of the speaker’s home life. The silence and non-confrontation painted as “peace” pervades these young children’s lives, resulting in the unresolved tension manifesting as bodily self-harm.…

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

The U.S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice. According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing lead azide, an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “unacceptable risk of accidental detonation.” Intentionally detonating the barrels is considered the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined.

However, the explosions are expected to release a large plume of lead particles, and lead is a neurotoxin. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, a town of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa. People and farms would be in the path of the plume as it blows for miles.

The detonations were briefly delayed by the backlash and rescheduled for Nov. 23, 2026. A federal appeals court paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit for the detonations on Nov. 20 after two groups sued, but the Justice Department argued that the permit wasn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat.

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan. We asked him about the risks and what happens to the lead in an explosion.

What risks do the Army’s planned explosions pose for people?

If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets.

Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The big concern there is for young children. If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.

Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies, including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to hide out in bones and teeth, where it can leach out and cause harm.

Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body. That’s a pretty strong statement.

What’s known about where the plume is likely to travel?

Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.

We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.

In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.

If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.

If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan on Nov. 23, the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southeast. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead as it slowly floats by.

That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.

What can people do to stay safe in those areas?

Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a list of precautions that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.

The Army is advising people near the plant to vacate their homes during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.

Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.

After the plumed dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.

Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some dairy farmers are concerned about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.

Our results from sampling during and after the plume should help people better understand the risks.

What is your team planning for testing?

My colleagues and I will be looking at two aspects of potential exposure to lead: the airborne dust, which we’ll collect with instruments during the plume to get the lead concentration, and then dust that settles on surfaces and the ground, which we’ll collect with gauzelike pads and send to a lab for analysis.…

item.title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections.

And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK.

These gestures may be ridiculed as “passports to Pimlico”, but they reflect a deadly and earnest predicament. An emergency Commons debate last month heard the immigration minister, Anna Turley, proclaim Piddington’s fate as “in the national interest”. It would help stop the need for asylum hotels in the middle of towns and cities at a cost rising to billions.

But shouldn’t these villagers have a say? In the planning policy framework introduced by David Cameron’s government in 2012, communities were invited to prepare “neighbourhood development plans”. But from day one, central government treated these as mere wishlists. Delivery targets were progressively introduced that overruled local planning control, none more radical than Labour’s “growth targets” in 2024.

Prime ministers of both parties have drawn up housebuilding targets for every English locality. Councils, it was suggested, should disregard labels such as green belts or areas of outstanding natural beauty when planning where to build. This was despite independent surveys constantly protesting that the national target of 1.5m new homes could already be met within existing built-up areas, with two thirds of sites already with planning permissions. The reality is that private developers make more money building in the country – and the government is in thrall to them. The name of the game is profit.

Hence the imposition from government now witnessed in small towns and villages across England’s south and midlands. Last year, Moreton-in-Marsh in Gloucestershire was ordered to double in size. In a poll, 96% of local people protested, but to no avail. The town is now a gallery of housing horror, encased on all sides by bland private estates. No attempt has been made to build in a village style, let alone fuse estates with the rural landscape. All that matters is the number of houses. Southern England is seeing a repeat of the suburban sprawl over London’s home counties between the wars.

What is stark is the total impotence of local people to play any part in combating this assault. Soon after taking office, Keir Starmer was insulting villagers as “blockers and Nimbys”, as if defending one’s environment was a crime. Andy Burnham then upped the ante by removing powers to block rural development from local planning committees.

This disempowerment is inconceivable in other European countries. In France, Germany, Switzerland or Scandinavia, local communities enjoy sovereignty over their future. They call it democracy. France’s 35,000 communes build plenty of houses, but they grow organically, not by an invasion of “volume builders” whipped on by central government.

The status of small communities is not a quaint archaism. The English village is a valued social construct. Its institutions are the school, the church, the pub and the youth club. Its lifeblood is the high street. Such an informal cohesion of the neighbourhood came to life during the Covid-19 pandemic. It supplied mutual help in time of trouble. It was a salve to loneliness.

Rural parish councils need to be granted powers over their future like those enjoyed by similar communities abroad, notably in planning. But such councils are needed in cities, too. In 2007, Tony Blair’s government boldly attempted to extend parishes from rural to urban areas. Apart from one council created in London’s Queen’s Park, the attempt was snuffed out by Whitehall.

Everywhere should be a parish. The case is overwhelming for the liberation of the village and its inhabitants. Piddington has shown the way.

- Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist, author and BBC broadcaster. His book The Village in Britain: And Why Place Matters is published this month

item.title: While the headlines rave about Milburn’s Neets review, the young people I know are angry and frustrated | Felicity Halstead
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

I was at my desk last Thursday morning as a steady stream of young people filed into GoodWork’s central London community hub for a day of employability workshops. Despite the accusations of disengagement among young people, they didn’t need me to tell them that proposals to cut some benefits for under-25s were all over the news. I could hear them talking about it as soon as the lift pinged open – and the mood was low.

Alan Milburn has made a concerted effort to say that he doesn’t believe young people are to blame for dire levels of youth unemployment. He says the system has let them down and only a decade-long transformation will fix a problem that is complex and deeply entrenched. Simply recognising the scale of the problem and being willing to invest in a solution is a positive start.

But what I’ve heard from young people is frustration that their struggles in the job market are framed primarily through a need to reform the welfare system. They hear a lot about their responsibilities and benefit entitlements, but less about what is being done to make the job market fairer.

Our employability programme focuses heavily on the art of getting work – helping young people from low-income backgrounds to navigate a system that is often stacked against them. Increasingly, finding a good job feels like a game in which they are repeatedly set up to lose.

In April, we worked with the Inside the Mind of a Young Neet report, commissioned by the Milburn review, to host a round table, bringing young people and employers together to discuss some of these issues. The picture was complicated. Young people wanted to know why employers aren’t offering more opportunities, and why they’re being “ghosted” and not given feedback on their applications. Employers talked about the rising cost of hiring, budget pressures, hundreds of AI-generated job applications, and organisational instructions to avoid giving any feedback out of fear that it may lead to litigation. This has all created a job market where entry level jobs are almost impossible to access without experience, traditional hiring practices have broken down and young talent is increasingly lost and confused.

So how does the Milburn review address this? My biggest hope was that it would set out how the government could create a labour market that offers opportunities at scale for young people. It goes some of the way, notably by proposing “opportunity” and “support” guarantees, which ensure every young person can get a college place, training, apprenticeship, high-quality work experience or a job. It could make a real difference – but it’s understandable that a lot of young people, who have been made to feel like a low political priority, have limited confidence in whether the government could deliver this for them.

Take Lucy, 22, who tells me that she “can’t afford to be Neet”. She wants to work in the creative industries but is stuck taking any work she can get because her family needs her to be earning. For young people like Lucy, there’s not much in the review to get excited about. The report opens by saying that “a young person’s future should depend on their aptitudes and aspirations not their background or their birth”. It does very little to make the possibility of a career – not just a job – a reality.

My fear is that the recommendations don’t go far enough or fast enough to create decent opportunities. Proposed cuts to employer national insurance contributions would be slow, and targeted initially at retail and hospitality, creating new vacancies but limiting choice. More apprenticeships are welcome but they won’t do much for the 15% of Neets who have a degree. The opportunity guarantee is promising at first glance. But I am sceptical of its “personalised participation plan”, as young people have told us that their experience of state-sponsored support into work doesn’t usually pay much attention to the sort of work they want to do.

For small- and medium-sized enterprises there needs to be clearer support for hiring young people. While hiring costs might be offset by the youth jobs grant, young people who have been Neet for more than six months are likely to need strong wraparound support, on-the-job training and pastoral care to make work placements a success. There are tentative measures that the report wants to “explore”, but I suspect it’ll be some time before we see an increase in hiring at scale.

Milburn’s report makes a lot of the “duty to engage” for young people. What’s missing is the same duty for employers. The “first chance” commitment outlined in the report makes sensible recommendations – creating more jobs, apprenticeships and work experience, and committing to giving feedback on applications. But it stops short of mandating employer action, meaning there is no clear framework for accountability if recruitment processes remain opaque, or young people are not offered meaningful work or opportunities for development.

There’s a disconnect between how the review positions itself as responsive to young people’s needs and how it’s actually being received by many young people. As I write this, our 23-year-old communications assistant, Manal, is scrolling through TikTok to gauge how young people are feeling about the headlines, which are overwhelmingly focused on welfare. “They’re angry,” she says. I’m not sure I blame them.

- Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity

item.title: Why I take this posh salt scandal with a pinch of you know what | Thea Everett
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

This week, a report by the Observer found that the king of flaky salt, Maldon, was using imported German rock salt in its Essex production plant. It has since followed that Cornish Sea Salt (another industry leader) is also importing European salt in its production, this time sea salt. There has been a food media outcry, with a tone that has felt very “I’m not angry, I’m just disappointed”. According to the Observer report, “tonnes of mined rock salt are being poured into the production line” at Maldon. The scandal is that Maldon calls itself sea salt (made by evaporating seawater), but rock salt is mined from dried-up underground seabeds (that were once also seas). Salt companies combine one type of salt with another to ultimately produce … salt. As food manufacturing goes, I don’t find it the most shocking transgression.

“Posh salt”, once marketed only to the upper classes in Harrods and Fortnums, has been gaining popularity over the last half century. In the early 00s, the major supermarkets started selling Maldon sea salt, and over the last 20 years, with the chef-ification of home cookery, flaky salt has reached never-before-seen heights.

The growth of salt personalities, as I will call them, has only furthered the cause. Nigella Lawson famously said she “always [has] a pinch pot of Maldon in [her] purse”. Molly Baz regularly pours flaky salt from the packet like it’s water from the tap on her popular YouTube channel. Then of course, there was Salt Bae, the restaurateur who went viral after delicately sprinkling flaky salt on top of a steak. Today you’ll find home cooks sprinkling flaky salt on porridge, chocolate mousse and even ice-cream.

So what is so special about flaky salt? In cooking, the important thing with salt is the size of the flake or grain. This is what dictates how it behaves in your food. It’s the reason people say table salt tastes saltier: the reduced surface area means you get more grains per teaspoon than you do with flakes. It’s not materially saltier, there is just more of it. Fancy salt flakes are favoured for their texture and the way they can be crumbled with pressure from your fingers, à la Salt Bae, allowing for precise seasoning.

But ultimately, salt is salt: the chemical compound sodium chloride (NaCl). Whether from Essex estuaries, German mines or the flats of Mexico, it is essentially the same stuff. Neither rock salt nor sea salt is more refined than the other. With the exception of sulphurous black salt from the Himalayas, even the most impressive taste tester in the world would have no clue what country a salt was from in a blind tasting. If they say they do, they’re lying.

In other artisanal food production, provenance affects flavour. Think cheese (made with milk flavoured by the grass the animals graze on), or olive oil and coffee (where geography and climate have a huge effect on fruit and bean). Salt’s not like this. Artisanal salt’s USP is crystallisation, and how the shape of the flake behaves in our food. It is the production method that dictates whether you end up with chunky rocks, thin flakes, pyramids or tiny grains. Once processed, a salt’s characteristics won’t tell you anything about its origins. Even when posh salt actually is what it says it is, it’s still just salt.

There is a place for all salts. Table salt, the most refined salt product, is 99% sodium chloride, with the other 1% being anti-caking agents and iodine. But it’s cheap. In my cupboard sits Aldi’s own-brand table salt, and Maldon. The table salt is what I use in bread, stocks, stews and anything that needs a large quantity of salt that is going to dissolve away to nothing – fine grains are more easily dispersed in foods. Like most people, I can’t afford to pour Maldon by the cup each day. I reserve it for finishing dishes, vegetables, salads and desserts.

Maldon isn’t cheap, but neither is it the price of gold. I buy 1.4kg tubs of it for £15 from an Italian wholesaler in Croydon. At that price, I am not surprised that the source ingredient is imported. The Welsh salt company Halen Môn’s offering retails at £32.50 a kilo. The end product tastes pretty similar. Maybe Maldon is fancy salt for the masses. Maybe that’s fine. A family business making the big time and not being able to maintain its original protocols is a well-trodden path.

To me, the Maldon “scandal” is akin to going off your favourite band when you’re a teenager because they released a more mainstream third album that they recorded in LA. Mass production and popularity come at a cost. The demand for Maldon has simply become too great and it has had to dip into other sources to meet it. For some, that’s a great sin. It’s true that Maldon should declare the provenance of its product. But I won’t be getting salty about it: as the cheapest flake available to me, I’ll still be buying it by the bucketload.

- Thea Everett is a London-based food writer who runs a recipe Substack called What’s That You’re Cooking, Thea?

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-20 06:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The Average Cost of Thanksgiving Dinner in the U.S. in 2026, Mapped
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Thanksgiving is fast approaching, and if youâre in the midst of preparations, you know costs can add up quickly. From the all-important turkey to stuffing, mashed potatoes, and pumpkin pie, Thanksgiving meals can take a lot of time and a lot of cashâthough exactly how much cash depends on what you purchase and where you live.

The American Farm Bureau released its 41st annual Thanksgiving dinner price report on November 18, 2026, using data from its yearly survey of Americans in all 50 states and Puerto Rico. It found the average Thanksgiving meal for 10 people will cost $58.63, a 6% increase from 2025. This is the first time that Thanksgiving dinner prices have increased year-to-year since 2022.

The priciest and most inexpensive Thanksgiving meals across the U.S.

The region serving up the most expensive Thanksgiving in the United States is the Northeast, where the meal will cost around 5% more than anywhere else in the U.S, at $61.57 for 10 people. The South saw the lowest cost for Thanksgiving for 10, at $54.33 on average.

The Midwest and West, meanwhile, saw prices closer to the national average, with the West spending an average of $58.74 and the Midwest spending $56.89.

Changing food prices across America

Turkeys cost an average of $23.68 in 2026, an increase of 10% from 2025, according to the American Farm Bureau. Boneless ham, dinner rolls, sweet and russet potatoes, cranberries, frozen peas, and frozen green beans all grew more expensive in the past year as well. About a third of the items tracked in the survey decreased in price, including frozen pie crusts and whipping cream.Â

That rise in prices is connected to rising energy costs in part due to the Iran war, which has led to increased diesel prices for farmers who rely on it to power their equipment. Something to celebrate is that prices are still lower than they were in 2022, when the average Thanksgiving cost an average of $64.05 in the U.S. partly due to the Ukraine war.Â

âHigher prices for these items arenât a complete surprise, as the effects of significant spikes in prices for critical inputs throughout the food chain, like fuel for processing and transportation, have made their way to consumers,â Farm Bureau economists Faith Parum and Cameron Castillo wrote. Still, all this doesnât mean that farmers are raking it in. âEven if the farmer does capture some additional revenue, those earnings are needed to cover increased fertilizer, fuel, and other production expenses,â they continued.Â

item.title: The Real Philosopher Who Inspired ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

In June 2024, when Scholastic announced a fifth Hunger Games novel set on the morning of Haymitch Abernathyâs reaping, the statement from Suzanne Collins started with philosophy: âWith âSunrise on the Reaping,â I was inspired by David Humeâs idea of implicit submission and, in his words, âthe easiness with which the many are governed by the few.ââ Hume, who lived from 1711 to 1776, was a leading figure of the Scottish Enlightenment. Collinsâs earlier books leaned on Greek myth and Roman gladiators, but this time she opened the novel with two passages by him, and his influence runs through the story.

Sunrises and Billiard Balls

Collins didnât find Hume in grad school: her father was a historian and a doctor of political science, a career Air Force officer who taught at West Point before he left for Vietnam, and he treated his kids as never too young to learn. âMy dad introduced me to David Hume when I was a child, along with many other philosophers,â she told her editor, David Levithan, in Scholasticâs interview for the book. âHe talked about them while using more kid-friendly examples. Like, in Humeâs case, sunrises and billiard balls.â

Those are Humeâs own examples: in his 1748 Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, he used billiard balls to argue that you canât know one thing will move the other until youâve watched it happen. He used the sunrise to make the bigger point: âThat the sun will not rise to-morrow is no less intelligible a proposition, and implies no more contradiction than the affirmation, that it will rise.â Nothing guarantees the future will behave like the past, no matter how many mornings in a row it has.

Thatâs the argument Haymitch loses to Lenore Dove in the first chapter. Heâs certain the reaping will always fall on his birthday because it always has, and she points out that itâs only been around for 50 years. âShe makes Haymitch promise that he will fight to make sure there is never another sunrise on the reaping,â Collins said, and thatâs where the title came from.

Force Is on the Side of the Governed

The second passage is the one Collins most wanted readers to sit with. It comes from Humeâs essay âOf the First Principles of Government,â and it asks why a handful of rulers can control a population that vastly outnumbers them: âWhen we enquire by what means this wonder is effected, we shall find, that, as Force is always on the side of the governed, the governors have nothing to support them but opinion.â

âIf all people do is read this Hume quote and discuss it, this book has been a win for me,â Collins said. She went around asking people whether Hume was right that the few end up governing the many, even in a democracy (âevery single person I asked about this said yes. No one seemed happy about itâ), and she built the book so that implicit submission plays out on three levels: âindividual, Hunger Games, and national.â Haymitch has to decide whether heâll keep submitting to the Capitol as an alliance of tributes in the arena tries to upend the Careersâ usual run, and meanwhile, the whole country has handed its power to Snow. The opinions that prop it all up are manufactured by propaganda, which the Capitol wields in various ways, from Plutarchâs altered District 12 reaping to âthat endlessly waving flag.â

Hume wasnât the first philosopher sheâd borrowed from. For the previous prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, she handed out aspects of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau to her characters, with Coriolanus inheriting Hobbesâs view of human nature from Volumnia Gaul.

The Philosopher Who Couldnât Get Hired

Hume never sold anything nearly as successful as The Hunger Games in his own day. His first book, A Treatise of Human Nature, fell âdeadborn from the press,â as he later put it, and the reputation it earned him as a skeptic and an atheist led to public opposition to his 1745 application for a philosophy chair at the University of Edinburgh. He never held an academic job. His essays did much better with ordinary readers, which is part of where the line about the many and the few comes from.

Meanwhile, Sunrise on the Reaping sold more than 1.5 million copies in English in its first week, and Lionsgateâs film adaptation hits theaters on November 20, 2026, putting an 18th-century argument about whether the sun has to come up into multiplexes.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-19 22:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The Greek Myths and Heroes That Inspired All 5 'Percy Jackson and the Olympians' Books
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

The latest season of Percy Jackson and the Olympians debuts on Disney+ on November 20, 2026, bringing The Titanâs Curse to life in live action for the first time. The season will focus on Percy Jackson teaming up with unlikely allies to rescue Annabeth Chase from the forces of Kronos, a quest that will determine his role in the Great Prophecy that guides the series.

In an interview with D23, author Rick Riordan explained that his goal with the Percy Jackson franchise was to create stories that were âfun and enjoyable and also kind of a stealth education in mythology.â Simply reading the books or watching the series will introduce audiences to the gods and monsters that populate Greek mythology, with a few direct references to the myths they come from. But Riordanâs way of infusing Greek mythology into his stories actually goes much deeper.

While the series as a whole functions as a modern remix of Greek mythology, throwing lesser-known characters like Procrustes into the same narrative as mythological icons like Medusa and the Minotaur, each book also follows the broad strokes of one or more Greek heroâs quests. Below, we break down the seven heroes and myths that serve as key inspirations for each book in the Percy Jackson and the Olympians series.

The Titanomachy

The series-long conflict in the Percy Jackson and the Olympians series is based on the return of the Titans, so itâs vital to understand the myths surrounding them and their conflict with the gods. Ancient Greek cosmology claimed that the universe was once controlled by the primordial deities Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky), but Gaia asked her son Kronos to overthrow his father. He agreed, establishing himself and his siblings as the supreme deities on Earth. However, after defeating his father, Kronos was warned that he would one day be overthrown by his own son.

Fearing this, Kronos ate his children as soon as his wife bore them, including five of the Olympian gods. His wife hid their youngest son, Zeus, who was raised in secret before returning to force his father to vomit up his siblings. With the gods free, Zeus launched a war against the Titans that would last ten years. The gods finally gained the advantage after freeing the Cyclopes and Hecatonchires from Tartarus. The Cyclopes created symbols of power for each of the male gods, crafting Zeusâs lightning bolts, Poseidonâs trident, and Hadesâs helm of darkness. Using these weapons, the Olympians finally conquered the Titans, casting them into Tartarus and taking their place.

The series takes all of this as a starting point, with Kronos attempting to reclaim power by manipulating demigods. Each of the first four books takes a step toward his resurrection, culminating in the second great Titanomachy in The Last Olympian. Kronos and the other Titans play an active role in the story, remembering their first defeat and actively trying to change the outcome. But while they overtly serve as the seriesâs primary antagonists, the Titans also contribute to the story's thematic arc by asking whether the cycle of son betraying father is inevitable.

Perseus, the Gorgon Slayer

Turning to the more specific inspirations in the Percy Jackson franchise, the first figure that you need to understand is Perseus, a demigod who was chosen as Percy's namesake because he received a happier ending than most Greek heroes. Perseus was the son of Zeus and a princess named Danae, who had been imprisoned by her father thanks to a prophecy that claimed that her son would one day overthrow and kill his grandfather. Like so many mythic figures, Perseus had to grow up in hiding to avoid being killed.

Despite that, Perseus had a relatively happy childhood until he was tasked with killing Medusa, a snake-haired monster capable of turning men to stone with a single glance. King Polydectes threatened to capture Danae if Perseus did not succeed at killing the Gorgon. So Perseus sought advice from the Grey Sisters, who, in certain stories, helped him find Medusa, the Helm of Hades, and a set of winged sandals. These tools gave Perseus the mobility and stealth he needed to behead the monster.

He then met Princess Andromeda, who was chained to a rock as a sacrifice to a sea monster. Perseus spoke to her father, who agreed to let Perseus marry her if he could defeat the monster. Perseus produced Medusaâs head, which promptly turned the creature to stone. When he returned home to find that King Polydectes had been abusing his mother, Perseus also used the head to get revenge on the king. With his enemies thwarted, Perseus settled down with Andromeda, eventually becoming the great-grandfather of Heracles.

Perseusâs story has a lot of influence on The Lightning Thief, from the broad strokes of Percy needing to kill Medusa and rescue his mother to the more specific details, such as the use of an invisibility cap and flying shoes. The idea that Percy is fated to kill some portion of his family also appears throughout the franchise, forcing him to confront his rocky relationship with the gods whenever a new prophecy puts the fate of the world in his hands.

The Odyssey

The Odyssey is one of the most well-known pieces of Greek mythology in the modern day, but it tends to be boiled down to a handful of plot points that appear in Books 9 through 12. After fighting in the Trojan War for 10 years, Odysseus attempts to take his men home to Ithaca. After trying and failing to conquer the Cicones, Odysseus and his crew escape from the Lotus-Eaters, whose food makes the travelers forget about returning home, and confront the cyclops Polyphemus. Although Odysseus is able to save many of his men by outwitting and blinding Polyphemus, he eventually tells the cyclops his name, which launches a conflict with Poseidon.…

item.title: Eurovision took its song contest to Asia – bringing its political drama and cultural tropes along for the ride
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

ABBA and Céline Dion came to the world’s attention thanks to the Eurovision Song Contest, an annual showcase of pop music, camp and spectacle.

Filipino singer Carmelle is hoping that the Eurovision Song Contest Asia will serve as a similar springboard to international fame. On Nov. 14, 2026, Carmelle bested entries from 11 Asian countries to be crowned the Asian edition’s first-ever winner. The competition marked Eurovision’s boldest expansion of its format in its 70-year history.

As a scholar of contemporary European popular music and politics, I study the ways in which Eurovision shapes notions of what it looks like and sounds like to be European. Knowing that the Asian edition would be organized by European broadcasting executives, I wanted to see how closely Eurovision Asia would resemble the flagship Eurovision, or whether it would carve out an identity of its own.

Stops and starts

Eurovision’s proposed expansion into Asia dates back to 2008, when the European Broadcasting Union – the transnational coalition of public service media organizations that has organized the Eurovision Song Contest since 1956 – announced plans for “Our Sound – The Asia-Pacific Song Contest.” Originally slated to debut in 2010, the project never materialized.

On March 31, 2026, however, Voxovation, a European-led production company that oversees the development of Eurovision’s spinoffs, announced that Bangkok would host the inaugural Asian competition in partnership with Thailand’s Channel 3 and S2O Productions.

Eurovision Asia is now the second European Broadcasting Union-licensed global spinoff to make the airwaves.

In 2022, Voxovation organized the American Song Contest, which included original songs by artists from all 50 U.S. states, five territories and Washington.

Despite being promoted to the American public in a Super Bowl commercial featuring hosts Kelly Clarkson and Snoop Dogg, the competition failed to attract a large viewership and the spinoff wasn’t renewed.

‘You will be blown away!’

Given two decades of uncertainty, as well as the failure of Voxovation’s U.S. spinoff, some critics doubted whether the Asian version would succeed. And for a moment, it looked like everything might fall apart: In late October 2026, the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet reported that Eurovision Asia’s original budget of approximately US$4.5 million had been reduced by US$1 million.

The European Broadcasting Union, however, confirmed that the show would go on as planned, and at 8:30 p.m. Bangkok time on Nov. 14, the show’s two hosts, Thai media personalities Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop, welcomed viewers from around the world tuning in via television broadcast and the YouTube livestream.

“Maybe you’ve never heard of Eurovision before, or maybe you’re one of the hardcore Eurofans,” said Bishop. “It doesn’t matter, because you will be blown away by the talent here tonight!”

For the next two-and-a-half hours, each country’s representative performed an original song, with Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên opening the show with her song “Em Tiên” (“Fairy Maiden”).

Vietnam’s entry had many of the spectacular ingredients of an ideal Eurovision entry: bilingual lyrics, large props, flashy outfits and a dance break. The song’s instrumentation included a flute accompanying Tiên’s melody and a bamboo xylophone. It concluded with a second, high-energy dance break reminiscent of electronic dance music genres.

The song’s use of traditional Asian musical signifiers followed the approach of the European entrants that have incorporated folk traditions to promote their national cultures to an international audience.

For example, Ukraine’s 2004 winning entry, Ruslana’s “Wild Dances,” opened with the trembita, a long alpine horn associated with the Hutsul people of the Carpathian Mountains. Armenia’s 2008 entry, Sirusho’s “Qele, Qele,” similarly combined a traditional Armenian duduk flute, zurna trumpet and dhol drums with an upbeat dance track and contemporary pop vocals. While some scholars claim that these musical gestures strategically romanticize and exoticize regional cultures, it’s a way to fuse national identity with modern music.

Other Eurovision Asia entrants also pulled from this playbook. Mongolia’s singer, Beck, wore a deel, the country’s traditional robe, while performing. He also incorporated a traditional Mongolian string instrument into his performance.

Voting, which was open to the general public via an online form, began just before the first performance. Viewers were allotted eight free votes, on the condition that they had to vote for at least three different countries. They could purchase 10 additional votes. The public accounted for half the votes, while a jury made up of representatives from each nation accounted for the other half.

Carmelle’s winning song – a Filipina women’s empowerment anthem titled “Sobra-Sobra” (“Too Much”) – featured a repeated musical line played by a kulintang, a Filipino percussion instrument, and a frenetic dance break. The song’s bridge was rapped in Tagalog, the country’s national language.

As part of her reward, Carmelle will perform “Sobra-Sobra” at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Burgas, Bulgaria.

Europe, Asia … the world?

No Eurovision competition would be complete without a measure of political controversy.

From broadcaster boycotts over Israel’s participation amid the war in Gaza to suspicions that Franco’s Spain rigged the 1968 Eurovision vote in its favor, political disputes have long been part of the competition.

Normally, political statements are not permitted in Eurovision, though exceptions have been made for humanitarian causes. Ukraine’s victory in Eurovision 2022 took place just a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the former Soviet republic. Oleh Psiuk, the frontman of Ukraine’s entrant, Kalush Orchestra, pleaded for support for Ukraine at the end of the performance, which the European Broadcasting Union ended up allowing.…

Source: The Conversation | Published: 2026-11-19 13:42 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: When Animals Were Put on Trial in Medieval Europe
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Most of us twenty-first-century urbanites have a fairly sentimental view of farm animals, precisely because so many generations have gone by since they’ve been part of our daily lives. Perhaps that’s why so many restaurants in Seoul advertise their meat with pictures of the animals it comes from, sometimes dressed in chef’s garb and cheerfully serving up the very dishes they’re about to become.) Things were different in medieval Europe, where animals were both a necessity and a potential danger. History records many instances of serious harm done to humans by horses, bulls, and especially pigs, who seem to have had a particular tendency to turn on children.

Today we would describe the killing of a child as an inhuman act, a term that, in these cases, applies more than figuratively. As for the fate of the violently offending animal, we might imagine that it would be summarily slaughtered, but between the tenth and eighteenth centuries — and especially in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries — it might well have been brought into a courtroom first. Though other creatures had already been subject to legal proceedings for quite some time, “the earliest recorded pig trial took place in Fontenay-aux-Roses, just outside Paris, in 1266,” writes Alexander Lee at History Today. “By the early fifteenth century, however, they had become established practice throughout Normandy and the Île-de-France,” eventually spreading beyond the border to Italy, Germany, and the Low Countries.

“As contemporary students of the Corpus iuris civilis knew, it was a basic principle of Roman law that animals could not be culpable,” Lee adds. “Lacking reason, they were incapable of harboring criminal intent and hence could not be guilty of a crime.” But in un-Roman northern France, “the administration of secular justice was still largely the concern of local seigneurs and was governed predominantly by custom rather than statute.” Thus sustained, animal trials served purposes beyond simple punishment. “For medieval people, the world was created by God in a very logical way, with animals created first, in order to serve and help human beings who were created in the image of God,” says University of Liverpool medieval European monster expert Damian Kempf, quoted in Popular Science by Anne Ewbank. In that worldview, trying and executing a pig could “restore what was broken.”

Unlike domestic animals, according to Sonya Vatomsky at JSTOR Daily, destructive mice, beetles, snails, weevils, and other vermin would be sent to ecclesiastical tribunals. “Despite being unlikely candidates for Catholicism, such creatures were punished with excommunication, not execution,” she writes, since casting them out of God’s domain would allow humans to exterminate them with peace of mind. Vatomsky also quotes economist Peter T. Leeson’s theory that the Catholic Church tried more animals when people got lax about tithing, with the aim of “bolstering citizens’ belief in the validity of Church punishments for tithe evasion.” Putting animals on trial may now strike us as grotesque, but like any alien-seeming episode of history, it also reveals the beliefs on which a past society operated — a mode of analysis that gets one wondering how far the modern United States is from giving them the right to sue.

item.title: 2,800-Year-Old Bone Flute Unearthed in Troy May Have Been Played During Homer’s Time
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Image by Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, via Twitter

The prolific Hans Zimmer scored Christopher Nolan’s films over the dozen years from Batman Begins through Dunkirk. From 2020’s Tenet onward, Nolan has employed the younger Swedish composer Ludwig Göransson. Just what difference this has made in the resulting pictures is a matter best left to the scrutiny of the most obsessive fans, but any viewer can hear how much Zimmer and Göransson differ stylistically. This past summer, the siren song included on the soundtrack of The Odyssey featured one of the latter’s particularly notable choices: the use of an aulos, a double-reeded wind instrument much played back in ancient Greece.

Though Göransson didn’t have a genuinely ancient aulos on hand, of course, the sound produced by the replica proved evocative enough. But just this year, as it happens, a bone flute actually dating from the period in which Homer wrote The Odyssey was unearthed from the archaeological site of ancient Troy in modern-day northwestern Turkey.

As Smithsonian.com’s Meilan Solly writes, the past 160 years of digging there have produced “a pair of gold diadems, more than 100 two-handled wine goblets, and arrowheads and weapons dated to the Late Bronze Age, among other artifacts.” This 2,800-year-old flute isn’t just the first musical instrument discovered at the site, but also further evidence that Troy wasn’t the ghost town it was once assumed to be in the eighth century BC.

As always when dealing with ancient artifacts — and especially ones, as these pictures reveal, in a less-than-whole state — we should be careful with our terms. “Calling the object a flute is the excavators’ choice of word, and the type remains open,” says Ancient Origins. While this new discovery could potentially be a real Greek aulos, “without hole counts or a published drawing, matching the Troy find to that design is premature.” Archaeologists have unearthed similar instruments elsewhere, dating from different periods, but never before has one emerged from the buried remains of a city so rich in legendary associations. To those in search of a deeper understanding of antiquity, the site continues to sound a siren song of its own.

item.title: Watch Seoul’s 6,500-Year Evolution in a Mesmerizing 3D Animated Time Lapse
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

In this century, few countries have been as visibly successful as South Korea. China’s vertiginous economic rise once absorbed vast amounts of news-media attention, but its soft power has comparatively little reach across the wider world, at least in English-speaking countries. By this point, many if not most Westerners haven’t just eaten Korean food, but also driven a Korean car, heard Korean pop music, or watched a Korean film or TV show. The resulting sense of familiarity can prove deceptive to those who eventually make the trip there, but it does, at least, mark an improvement on the scant knowledge of the place they had before. Not so long ago, they could say little with certainty except this: South Korea’s got Seoul.

I first saw that pun on a T‑shirt in high school, long before I knew much of anything about Korea myself. Now, having lived there for more than a decade, I’ve been able to watch from the inside as the country’s capital has become an unlikely object of general interest. As evidence, take the 1.2 million views already racked up by the new video from Latos Charts above, a 3D animated time lapse showing the evolution of Seoul over six and a half often tumultuous millennia.

It reveals, among other things, that the city didn’t exist for most of the history of Korean civilization — but then, neither did the country. The postwar division of the peninsula into North and South has a kind of precedent in the warring kingdoms that occupied it before its unification by a series of states culminating in the 500-year rule of the Joseon Dynasty.

If you’ve watched one of the many popular historical “K‑dramas,” Joseon was most likely its period setting. Now generally regarded as the predecessor of modern-day Korea, it passes in two minutes of the time lapse, during which Seoul, then known as Hanyang, takes amid its geomantically protective mountains more or less the shape it has today, at least north of the Han River. In fact, up until the seventies, there was no city to speak of south of the Han: the development of the more recently musically satirized Gangnam, literally “south of the river,” was part of the top-down push for economic development — in effect, hitting the fast-forward button on history — that followed the devastation of the Korean War. That chapter of history comes around eight minutes into the video, after which lookalike high-rise complexes start popping up like mushrooms after a monsoon.

However comfortable a lifestyle they’ve offered to middle-class Seoulites, the sight of those apateu danji unsettles some Western observers, who encounter them in photographs meant to depict the city as a kind of futuristic dystopia. They exaggerate, of course, but even someone who appreciates Seoul as much as I do has to admit that, alongside its impressive qualities — the magnificent subway system, for example, extolled in the Not Just Bikes video above — the city has its problems, as does the nation for which it stands. Understanding it in all its complexity requires first (even before learning the Korean language) grasping its sheer centrality, greater than Tokyo’s to Japan or even Paris’ to France. To a great extent, South Korea hasn’t just got Seoul, it is Seoul. And maybe, if its prominence in the wider world continues to grow, the punning will eventually stop. In Korean history, stranger things have certainly happened.
