item.title: Why Do We Say We “Barked” Our Shins?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, clear explanation

After Diana from Williamsburg, Virginia, scraped the front of her leg on a chair, she fretted to her grown daughters she had barked her shin. Neither daughter had ever heard the expression. This kind of bark refers not to what a dog does, but to removing, peeling back, or scraping, just like stripping bark from a tree. Ouch! The phrase goes back at least to the early 1810s. This is part of a complete episode.

Transcript of “Why Do We Say We “Barked” Our Shin?”

Hello.

You have A Way with Words.

My name is Diana Stafford, and I’m in Williamsburg, Virginia.

Oh, well, it’s nice to talk with you.

What’s what’s on your mind today?

Several weeks ago, I scraped my leg against a chair, and just the very front part of my leg.

And when my daughters asked me what had happened, I said, I barked my shin.

And these are two daughters who are well educated and well read, They both said, I’ve never heard that expression before.

So I thought maybe you people would help me figure out where that came from.

Oh, and how old are they that they didn’t know the expression?

They’re in…

They’re both in their fifties.

Fifties.

Wow.

I’m just kinda surprised.

Martha, is this an expression that you know if you’re walking around in the dark and you you bang an ankle on the Bark table.

Shin.

Yeah.

You know, I never used it growing up.

I only learned it when I started working with language much much later.

Yeah.

It’s got a…

It’s not quite archaic, I wouldn’t say, but it’s certainly a little fossilized.

‘ Cause what’s happening here is we don’t really use barked that way very often.

And this is the verb bark, meaning to remove or peel back or to scrape something like you might do with the actual bark of a tree, which is what it’s referring to.

So, barking something may mean taking the bark off of it and that’s kind of what you’re doing if you injure yourself enough to peel back the skin.

And then shin, of course, is just another name for a particular body part down there at the lower leg.

And together, they’re just…

It’s kind of a set expression, colloquialized and lexicalized and set.

It goes back at least to the early eighteen teens.

And one of my favorite early uses of it that I could find is from a story called…

A newspaper article called The Miseries of Brooklyn from 1825, and it…

It’s got all these things that are terrible about living in Brooklyn, New York.

And one of them is treading on the hoops and poles in front of a Cooper’s shop and thereby barking your shins.

Ouch.

And I just love the the hoops and poles for a Cooper shop.

It’s such a picture of another era.

Right?

Like, two hundred years ago, we just…

There aren’t many Cooper shops left Yeah.

To go barking your shins by.

Yeah.

I was confused the first time I ran across this expression because I thought of, you know, barking aloud in pain, but it’s a different kind of bark.

Yeah.

And it…

They’re not etymological connected.

The barking of a dog and the bark of a tree just…

It’s like so many other, you know, homonyms or homographs in English.

It’s just a coincidence that they’re the same.

So, yeah, it’s nothing to do with dogs.

So, Diana, a teachable moment with your dog.

Although, know we’re gonna get calls from people in emails going like, but what about…

What…

My dogs are hurting me.

Yeah.

That’s different, and it’s not related, but ok.

Right.

I know it’s feet, but it’s not related to this bark.

Well, Diana, thank you so much for calling with this question.

Alright.

Thank you.

Bye.

Enjoy your show.

Thank you.

Thanks.

item.title: Inspiration from Charles Bukowski: You Might Be Old, Your Life May Be “Crappy,” But You Can Still Make Good Art
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, cultural context

Now more than ever, there’s tremendous pressure to make it big while you’re young.

Pity the 31-year-old who fails to make it onto a 30-under-30 list…

The soon-to-graduate high schooler passed over for YouTube stardom…

The great hordes who creep into middle age without so much as a TED Talk to their names…

Social media definitely magnifies the sensation that an unacceptable number of our peers have been granted first-class cabins aboard a ship that’s sailed without us. If we weren’t so demoralized, we’d sue Instagram for creating the impression that everyone else’s perfectly filtered life is leading to book deals and profiles in The New Yorker.

Don’t despair, dear reader. Charles Bukowski is about to make your day from beyond the grave.

In 1993, at the age of 73, the late writer and self-described “spoiled old toad,” took a break from recording the audiobook of Run With the Hunted to reflect upon his “crappy” life.

Some of these thoughts made it into Drew Christie’s animation, above, a reminder that the smoothest road isn’t always necessarily the richest one.

In service of his ill-paying muse, Bukowski logged decades in unglamorous jobs—dishwasher, truck driver and loader, gas station attendant, stock boy, warehouseman, shipping clerk, parking lot attendant, Red Cross orderly, elevator operator, and most notoriously, postal carrier and clerk. These gigs gave him plenty of material, the sort of real world experience that eludes those upon whom literary fame and fortune smiles early.

(His alcoholic misadventures provided yet more material, earning him such honorifics as the “poet laureate of L.A. lowlife” and “enfant terrible of the Meat School poets.”)

One might also take comfort in hearing a writer as prodigious as Bukowski revealing that he didn’t hold himself to the sort of daily writing regimen that can be difficult to achieve when one is juggling day jobs, student loans, and/or a family. Also appreciated is the far-from-cursory nod he accords the therapeutic benefits that are available to all those who write, regardless of any public or financial recognition:

Three or four nights out of seven. If I don’t get those in, I don’t act right. I feel sick. I get very depressed. It’s a release. It’s my psychiatrist, letting this shit out. I’m lucky I get paid for it. I’d do it for nothing. In fact, I’d pay to do it. Here, I’ll give you ten thousand a year if you’ll let me write.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

item.title: “Just Deserts” or “Just Desserts”?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, clear explanation

Is it just desserts or just deserts? This particular desert isn’t an arid place, however. This desert is an old noun coming from French, which means “something deserved.” The after-dinner dessert, on the other hand, is from an entirely different French word meaning “to clear the table,” which is what happens before those last sweet treats are set out. This is part of a complete episode.

Transcript of ““Just Deserts” or “Just Desserts”?”

Gina Bradshaw from Harvest Alabama emailed us with a question.

I’ve heard the phrase just dessert many times, and in my mind, I thought it was spelled d e s s e r t, as in someone getting the dessert or treat they deserved good or bad.

But I recently read the phrase and noticed it was spelled d e s e r t, like an arid place with little precipitation.

Have I been mentally spelling this wrong my whole life?

Well, Gina can relax and not worry about it because that is an incredibly common confusion.

A lot of people aren’t quite sure what that dessert is in there in the middle.

Is it the food?

Is it a dry place?

Is it something else?

It is what you deserve.

item.title: “Pony” as a Study Aid, From 19th-Century British Translations to Maritime Academy Tests
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, historical context

Joe from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, asks about pony, the term he and his fellow maritime academy students used to mean “a practice test” or “a copy of a previous test” to help them crib for an exam. Among 19th-century British students, the slang term pony meant “a translation or summary used as a study shortcut,” also known as a horse or trot. Linguist Connie Eble notes that the same concept has been modernized in North Carolina college slang as automobile and bicycle—something that, in other words, allows a student to coast through an exam. A listener who graduated from a merchant marine engineering school in the early 1980s emailed to say he remembers that when he was a student, a pony was “a copy of a test from previous classes,” and savvy instructors sometimes changed tiny details from year to year to thwart cheaters. This is part of a complete episode.

Transcript of ““Pony” as a Study Aid: From 19th-Century British Translations to Maritime Academy Old Tests”

Hello.

You have A Way with Words.

Hi.

I’m Joe, and I’m calling from Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

Hi, Joe.

Welcome to the program.

What’s up?

Hey.

I had a question for you guys about a word that we used in college, And this is something that I’ve found…

I went to maritime college, so studying to to work on ships when you graduate.

It’s a word that I think is only used at maritime colleges.

I’m not sure about that.

But the word is pony.

And we use pony to describe a practice test or if you had, like, an old copy of a test from a year prior, you’d say, oh, did you study the pony?

Did you get a copy of the pony?

And I’ve never heard of anyone from, like, a normal college using this word, but everyone from from the maritime colleges knows and uses this word.

That’s so interesting.

So we’re talking about p o n y, like the horse.

Yeah.

I don’t even know how it’s spelled, honestly.

I don’t know if it’s n I e or n y.

I don’t know.

And so It was a…

It’s a verbal word.

You know?

Is that…

So the Maritime Academy, is that the only place that you encountered it in your schooling?

Yes.

So I went to the US Merchant Marine Academy, but there’s actually seven maritime academies in America where you go and you graduate with a coast guard license and a and a bachelor’s degree after four years.

But everyone in the in the industry kinda knows and uses the word.

Mhmm.

I’ve never heard it used anywhere else.

And when I reference it to, like, anyone who’s not, you know, a maritime person, they look at you like you’re crazy.

Well, rest easy, Joe, because I know we can answer this one.

Yeah.

This is so interesting because, Joe, this is a real old student slang sense of the word pony, p o n y, but it’s much older and broader than the US maritime academies.

It turns out that it’s as old as the nineteenth century in British school slang.

A pony was a literal translation or a summary of a text that was used as a shortcut or or a study aid, you know, something that you could use to to crib.

And sometimes these were called ponies.

Sometimes they were called a horse or a trot.

And the idea in all of those cases appears to be essentially that instead of doing the intellectual walking yourself, you’re riding on this thing that’s taking you there and and making it easy.

So instead of plotting, you’re racing around the track at high speed.

With exactly the same concept.

It’s like this crib sheet.

Sometimes it’s pure out cheating where you’ve got a paper up your sleeve and sometimes it’s just you have the answers or the exam in advance.

Yeah.

Exactly.

An automobile or a bicycle.

Bicycle.

Yeah.

That’s the other one.

So two hundred years back to the eighteen twenties at least.

I’ve got one more very cool thing for you that you’re gonna appreciate, Joe.

About five years ago…

I’m looking through our email here.

About five years ago, we got an email from a guy named Rob Kright, and he says he graduated from a merchant marine engineering school in the early nineteen eighties.

And he says, to us, a pony was a copy of the test given to previous classes.

And so they use the word pony where he went to school.

He doesn’t say which school, but he also adds that on many Yeah.

On many occasions, the instructor knew there was a pony out there.

So he would throw in little gremlins in the test to trick unwary students.

Changing one number.

Yeah.

Yeah.

Did you did you find that as well?

Yes.

They would.

They would they would have very similar questions, but they would change little details.

So you…

But if, you know, if you had the pony, you knew what the test was gonna look like, and that was the important thing.

But, Joe, that’s what we know about pony.

A long…

Two hundred years of history, eighteen twenties at least.

Used to be broader now, more specific, but it’s still obviously got a legacy in the merchant the merchant maritime schooling.

Yeah.

I wonder if they still use it over in The UK or not.

Good question.

Well, our British listeners our British listeners will let us know.

Thank you so much for sharing with us.

We really appreciate it.

It’s really interesting.

But when you really look into it, so often, it’s got a deeper history that connects to other parts of of history and culture and other societies.

And we love talking about that kind of language here on the show.

item.title: 'Best in world' Price set for Cardiff stadium fight
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

'Best in world' Price set for Cardiff stadium fight

She is already one of the most decorated fighters in British boxing history, and now Wales' Lauren Price is set to headline a summer stadium show at Cardiff City Stadium or Cardiff Arms Park.

Price dominated Michaela Kotaskova in Cardiff on Friday night, winning every minute of every round as she became Wales' first unified boxing champion by locking up the welterweight division.

With her stack of titles added to an Olympic gold medal, Price is now set to get to the next level, with negotiations already progressing for a stadium contest in the summer, with Chantelle Cameron or Mikaela Mayer â who fight on Christmas Eve â among the list of possible opponents.

The 32-year old Welsh fighter was so dominant in unifying the division on Friday it prompted her usually reserved trainer, Rob McCracken, to name her as the world's best female fighter, and now Price is set for a bumper 2027.

"If we can bring the big names and the big fights to a stadium, it's going to make a massive difference to Wales and Cardiff and everyone involved, and Lauren is very passionate about that," Price's promoter Ben Shalom told BBC Sport Wales.

"She is unique in the attention that she can generate and therefore I think she can demand to make sure that the fights happen in Wales.

"A lot of eyes will be on [Chantelle] Cameron and [Mikaela] Mayer's fight, and that is a fight [the winner versus Price] that we'd love to make.

"That fight in May or June at Cardiff Rugby Club or Cardiff City Football Club, you know, you're doing 15-20,000 ticket sales with Lauren Price there, so fingers crossed."

BBC boxing expert Steve Bunce says a deal for a stadium fight in the summer has been agreed, with a mandatory defence likely to come first in February. France's Emilie Sonvico has been touted as a possible opponent.

"She has a sneaky fight in February and then an outdoor fight in May or June, at Cardiff City Stadium, that's done and dusted, that's going to happen," he told BBC Sport.

"It won't be Claressa Shields in the opposite corner, but it will be a big opponent in May or June outdoors in the Welsh sunshine."

Price feels she needs to move to bigger capacity venues to secure her legacy, despite already being one of the most decorated fighters in British boxing history.

"It's about now moving on to what's next, and there is talks that it could potentially be a stadium fight in the summer, and that's what it's about now, the legacy and the fan base growing," she explained.

"My team know I will fight anyone."

'Best in the world'

Price's trainer McCracken, who runs the Team GB boxing programme, says the Ystrad Mynach southpaw is now the best female fighter on the planet and only likely to improve.

"Lauren's been an incredible female boxer for Great Britain; she's won the Olympics, she's won the World Championships, European Games, everything, every belt in boxing at welterweight," he told BBC Sport Wales.

"She is only going to do more and improve and gain from this experience; there's a massive journey still to come. She's only had 11 professional fights.

"She's done her bit, learned, developed and gained the experienceâ¦ and I feel she's the best female in the world.

"I have done for about 18 months, and I think she'll only improve and she'll only get better.

"In my lifetime, Joe Calzaghe is probably the best British professional I've ever seen, and I feel Lauren Price is the best female that I've ever seen. She's a super talent.

"There are bigger nights in Wales for Lauren and for everybody, and it will be a fantastic journey to be a part of."

The top two in the market were both successful last time out. Matty’s Getaway took a 10-runner race at Chepstow on 11 October, coming nearly 10 lengths clear at the finish on soft ground, while Seaniecon led home a 19-runner field at Cheltenham’s October meeting.

It looks as though Matty’s Getaway has lost a shoe on the way to post. He’ll need to get that fixed before they can, er, get away.

There’s a bit more for the punters to get stuck into in the next race at Haydock, a handicap hurdle over three miles, with nine runners going to post following the scratching of Yellow Car.

Matty’s Getaway is the 100-30 market leader, with my fancy Seaniecon next in on 7-2 and Hartington on 4-1.

2.10 PUNCHESTOWN RESULT: LOSSIEMOUTH IN A CANTER

1. LOSSIEMOUTH (Paul Townend) 1-6 fav, 2. Blake. 4 ran.

Three to jump in the Morgiana Hurdle, Lossiemouth one-and-a-half up on William Munny, still the same order with two to jump …

Two out, Lossiemouth leads and starting to extend, she’s four up with William Munny being ridden …

Down to the last, Lossiemouth all on her own, going well clear in the closing stages … and it’s a flawless return for the champion!

Lossiemouth goes straight into the lead, William Munny tracks her in second …

Down past the stands and onto the second, Lossiemouth skips over …

Another slick jump at the third, and then the next ..

Off and running in the Morgiana Hurdle …

William Munny, the runner-up in the Supreme Novice Hurdle in 2025, is the only other runner in the four-strong field at a single-figure price. Barry Connell’s gelding is 7-1, and it’s 20-1 bar the two.

To no-one’s surprise, Lossiemouth can be backed at no better odds than around 1-7, if that’s your thing.

Most of us will, hopefully, just be watching on in admiration as one of the most popular horses in training returns for another campaign.

All eyes on the stunning setting of Punchestown in County Kildare now, as Lossiemouth, the champion over hurdles, makes her first start of the 2026-27 season in the Grade One Morgiana Hurdle.

She arrives with a career record of 15 wins from 19 starts including no fewer than 11 Grade One successes, and has finished second in three of her four defeats.

Freddie Gordon is talking to ITV Racing on the way back to unsaddle and suggests that Kocktail Bleu may now head over fences for a novice chasing campaign.

1.50 HAYDOCK RESULT: KOCKTAIL BLEU CHEER FOR BACKERS

1. KOCKTAIL BLEU (Freddie Gordon) 6-5 fav, 2. My Chiquita. 6 ran.

Down the back again, Kocktail Bleu takes over in front again, Miss Maverick makes a mistake six out …

Kocktail Bleu has built a useful lead over Smokeringinthedark …

Three to jump now, turning out of the back …

Into the straight, Kocktail Bleu leads over the third-last, My Chiquita has made rapid strides to join him …

The three of them are still together over the second-last, Kocktail Bleu back into the lead going to the last, he just needs to jump it …

And he does! Kocktail Bleu is going clear and it’s going to be a comfortable win.

Off and running in the 1.50 at Haydock …

Kocktail Bleu straight into the lead but it’s nothing like the fierce pace in the last race here ….

Miss Maverick is settled second, then there’s a gap back to Smokeringinthedark …

All runners travelling well and hurdling fluently …

Down the straight, Miss Maverick now goes on by a length from Kocktail Bleu …

Kocktail Bleu is going to go off at around 5-4 for this handicap at Haydock, Smokeringinthedark is the only other runner attracting any cash, at 9-4.

News arriving from Punchestown that the five-year-old Mighty Park was at the head of a 1-2-3 for Willie Mullins in the Beginners Chase.

He was ninth of 11 in last season’s Supreme Novice Hurdle but looks made for chasing and will head to a sterner target at one of the big Christmas meetings in Ireland according to his trainer.

He has a super jump in him. I’d imagine Mighty Park will stay at around two miles. I don’t think we’ll be going up in trip yet, we don’t need to.”

The well-fancied Manganese – priced up at around 11-2 – has come out of the handicap hurdle that is next up at Haydock, and Kocktail Bleu is a very warm favourite at around 6-4.

Smokeringinthedark is next in on 5-2, it’s 11-2 for Give It To Me Oj, and 10-1 bar the three.

1.30 ASCOT RESULT: KATEIRA FROM THE FRONT

1. KATEIRA (Tristan Durrell) 11-8, 2. Lucky Place. 3 ran.

Only two to jump, Kateira the narrow leader around the home turn, Lucky Place winding up to challenge …

Three in the air together over the second-last …

Down to the last, still Kateira in front, Lucky Place second, looks like that’s how they’ll finish …

A little surprisingly, Kateira leads with Lucky Place just behind, Fiveonefive brings up the rear …

Out onto the far side, no change in the order and all hurdling well until a slight error by Fiveonefive five out …

Kateira still leads four out, pace has been very, very steady throughout …

Off and running in the Grade Two Ascot Hurdle …

Kingofthefrontier was giving weight to his field in the last race, but it will be level-weights in the Grade One Formby Novice Hurdle at Aintree on Boxing Day if, as seems likely, that’s where he heads next. John Dawson is looking ahead in the winner’s enclosure:

We’re just feeling our way through. Our next plan would be the Formby. We just wanted to see if he was fast enough around here. He laid up nicely and as soon as Conor gave him a squeeze, he responded quickly.

The three-runner Ascot Hurdle is imminent at Ascot: the front-running Lucky Place is odds-on at around 4-7, and it’s easy to see Nicky Henderson’s gelding getting a very easy time of it on the lead.…

item.title: Washington Spirit vs. Kansas City Current: NWSL Championship preview
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The 2026 NWSL Championship is hours away from kickoff, with home side Washington Spirit vying for the NWSL Championship trophy for the third time in three seasons, this time with the Kansas City Current to beat.

Washington Spirit vs. Kansas City Current: NWSL Championship preview

Trinity Rodman and Temwa Chawinga headline the NWSL Championship match.

Both teams are star-studded with distinct styles that have brought them a lot of success this season. This matchup is guaranteed to deliver entertaining and high-quality soccer.

Kansas City is making their first finals appearance since 2022 hoping to win the trophy for the first time in club history. After winning the Shield last season with the best regular season record, the team made an unceremonious exit from the playoffs in the quarterfinals. This year, however, in the words of midfielders Croix Bethune and Lo’eau LaBonta, “It’s personal.”

Current head coach Chris Armas enjoyed his first season not only at the club, but in the league. His priority has been steadiness and continuity, trusting players to continue with the high-pressing and aggressively transitional style that has brought them a lot of success over the past three seasons.

In particular, forward Temwa Chawinga has scored two goals every three games this season when available thanks to her pace and technique up front. Her ability to speed past defenders, dribble through anyone in her way and shoot is so immense that even with three years worth of tape in the NWSL, teams struggle to contain her.

The Current also boast the newly crowned Midfielder of the Year, Croix Bethune, who broke a 10-year record for assists in a single regular season with 11. Bethune ranks high in the league in turnovers forced in the attacking and middle thirds of the pitch, making her the engine that kickstarts the transition chances that the team thrives on.

On the right wing, Michelle Cooper has similar pace and technicality to Chawinga on the left, making both sides of the pitch difficult for opponents to defend. Finally, striker Haley Hopkins, who scored the game-winner against Gotham FC in the semifinals, always finds herself in the right spot to clean up any leftovers created by her teammates or by botched clearances. Kansas City ended the regular season with the most goals scored in the league, and that wasn’t by accident.

On the defensive end, center backs Kayla Sharples and Gabby Robinson have led the team in limiting their opponents to only one goal so far in this post-season. Rookie right back Laney Rouse has been a revelation on both sides of the ball and stalwart left back Izzy Rodriguez contributes defensively while also delivering long balls with pinpoint accuracy in both live and dead ball situations.

Unfortunately for the Current, dead ball situations are the only ways they’ve managed to find the back of the net in the playoffs so far. A penalty in extra time won them the game against Angel City FC in the quarterfinals, and two free kicks were the difference between them and Gotham FC in the semifinals. Still, containing the offensive firepower that they do have can never be a guarantee for their opponents.

And perhaps fortunately for Kansas City, their opponents have only conceded set piece goals in their post-season so far.

Washington gave up two goals in their road to the finals, both of which came from corner kicks. The Spirit conceded the second-most set piece expected goals (xG) of all teams this season, beating only last place Chicago Stars. Players and staff alike from the Current have mentioned an emphasis on set pieces, and perhaps this strategy is the right one when they’re facing the second-stingiest defense in the league.

As for the Spirit, the team is benefitting from recently signed Clara Luvanga. The Tanzanian international striker made her debut for the team on Sept, 26 and has recorded seven goal contributions in seven appearances, including the game-winner in the semifinal against the Utah Royals. Luvanga has recently found chemistry with USWNT star Trinity Rodman.

On the defensive end of things, the Spirit have benefitted massively from the return of defensive midfielder Andi Sullivan from maternity leave, who has been key in cleaning things up in front of the defensive line and preventing opposing chances. The last time the Spirit played a final with Andi Sullivan as an active rostered player, they won their first ever championship back in 2021.

Also key are center backs Tara Rudd and Esme Morgan, with the latter leading all defenders in passing accuracy this season. Perhaps even more impressive is the fact that Morgan also leads defenders in passes into the final third. Her passing will play a huge role on Saturday against a high pressing team like Kansas City that is looking to force turnovers in dangerous areas. If Morgan can alleviate that pressure with line-breaking passes, the Spirit will both prevent the Current from attacking the way they like and find themselves in a favorable offensive position with their opponents caught too far forward.

Both teams vying for the trophy this weekend have very distinct styles of play that have brought them a lot of success, particularly at this crucial point in the season. The game will ultimately come down to which team succeeds at forcing the game to be played their way.

The Spirit do have home field advantage which is nothing to scoff at, especially at their ground which has been nicknamed “Rowdy Audi” for a reason.

So, while the Kansas City Current have put on an incredible end to their season, Washington end up having enough to win 2-1 in the final.

Vollering is considering taking on all three Grand Tours in 2027

Earlier this week, retired pro Annemiek van Vleuten suggested that her young compatriot Demi Vollering might like to target all three 'Grand Tours' in 2027 as a way to one-up a 2026 season that has featured 18 wins in 33 race days, including four major Spring Classics, the Giro d'Italia, Tour de France Femmes, and finally, world and European titles.

"It will be very difficult for Demi to match this season," Van Vleuten told Wielerflits. "But perhaps she can try to win the three Grand Tours, because the Vuelta 's schedule is now positioned differently in the season."

Vollering has won the Vuelta twice before, but has never been able to combine all three major events. But in 2027, the Spanish stage race is moving from early May to September, immediately following the men's edition (which is itself starting a week later to make way for the Super Worlds in the Haute-Savoie), meaning that it can now more-comfortably be combined with the Giro (29th May - 6th June) and Tour Femmes (30th July - 7th August).

"It is certainly something I have discussed with the team," Vollering told NOS at a tribute event in her home town of Pijnacker, South Holland. "That move offers an option, so to speak. That if you win the Giro and the Tour, you can say: I can extend the season. If that is not the case, then you can skip the Vuelta.

"Personally, I am certainly really looking forward to racing again. Especially because it will be in that beautiful rainbow jersey; that gives extra motivation to train hard."

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

UCI sees no wrongdoing in Schreiber relegation, but Luxembourg federation considering further action

A little under two weeks after a devastating relegation saw Marie Schreiber lose the European Championship title to Lucinda Brand in Zeddam, Netherlands, the Luxembourg cycling federation (FSCL) has received a response from the UCI.

"They don't see that a bigger mistake has been made," the FSCL told Luxembourg's RTL. "The answer from the UCI was kept quite general and no further explanation was given."

There was widespread uproar following the elite women's race for which an official result took a long time to come through as the jury deliberated over Schreiber's deviation in the final two-rider sprint to the line. The resulting relegation was later questioned by Schreiber, her coach Sanne Cant, and several other big names throughout the sport, with Brand's own coach Sven Nys even expressing sympathy for the Luxembourg camp, which is not happy with the UCI's response.

"We do not want to simply accept this," the statement went on. "In our Board of Directors, we will now decide how we want to proceed. We do not want to close the file like this, and above all, we do not want to let the UCI close it so easily."

The FSCL may still take the case to CAS (the Court of Arbitration for Sport), but the wording of the final line above indicates also that they want a more detailed explanation of a rule that, in the 'cross regulations, invites varied interpretation.

15 mins. A clean lineout win from Itoje is moved quickly to Smith who finds another kick in behind for Joseph to chase. It’s a decent foot race but Bauden Barrett is first to it.

England v New Zealand: Nations Championship rugby union – live

🏉 Nations Championship updates, 2.10pm GMT kick-off

Sat 21 Nov 2026 09.29 EST

HakaWatch!

The teams assume the position for the anthems and sundry formalities. We’ll soon have the haka then a game of rugby will break out.

Tommy Freeman out!

England are having to make a late change after the Northampton wing withdrew before kick-off

Pre-match reading

Send all your thought to me, including your own best and worst compound nouns to me on the email up to and throughout the match.

Teams

England

George Furbank; Cadan Murley, Henry Slade, Seb Atkinson, Will Joseph; Fin Smith, Jack van Poortvliet; Fin Baxter, Jamie George, Joe Heyes; Maro Itoje (capt), Alex Coles; Ollie Chessum, Ben Curry, Ben Earl.

New Zealand

Beauden Barrett; Will Jordan, Anton Lienert-Brown, Jordie Barrett, Josh Moorby; Damian McKenzie, Cam Roigard; Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor (capt), Fletcher Newell; Scott Barrett, Fabian Holland; Tupou Vaa’i, Peter Lakai, Wallace Sititi.

Replacements: Asafo Aumua, George Bower, Pasilio Tosi, Anton Segner, Leicester Fainga’anuku, Cortez Ratima, Richie Mo’unga, Rieko Ioane.

Preamble

Alastair Campbell has a book out called Persevilience, the title apparently a mash-up of perseverance and resilience (see what he did there) to form the worst compound noun since dorkburger. Although, one imagines the creator of the latter wasn’t trying to make it “the word the world needs now” like Big Al is on the cover of his volume.

However hateful the word, a still injury ravaged New Zealand need to show some of it today as they attempt to shrug off their seventy-three years in the making dorkburgering in Cardiff last week.

Since 1996, where the All Blacks have played tests with no more than a 21-day gap they suffered defeat in 52 first-up fixtures, with only 18 of the follow-up matches being a loss. Fourteen of those next-up losses were against either South Africa (10) or Australia (4), and they have only lost two consecutive matches on their November tours on one occasion in 2021 (Ireland, then France). On the 31 occasions they followed a defeat with a win, the week one loss margin average is seven points (sound familiar?) and the week two win margin is 26.

Thus, history tells us that such a situation tends lead to a rage filled bounceback being the order of the day, but matching the historic 26 point next-up winning spread will be a tougher ask than usual. The Dave Rennie led 2026 All Blacks are not the team of yore, and that’s before we consider their medical list, plus they must deliver it at SponsorDome Twickenham versus an England side on a decent run of form and results.

Exactly how good the home side’s run is can be debated;…

item.title: LATAM Airlines unveils new A321XLR cabins with eye on US expansion
item.description:

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of airline expansion with clear details and useful vocabulary.

The next frontier for the Airbus A321XLR is South America.

After opening dozens of new transatlantic routes, the long-range narrow-body will make its debut with LATAM Airlines in March 2027. The airline has yet to say which routes the XLRs will fly, but executives have previously outlined opportunities to connect the U.S. and South America.

LATAM, a close partner of Delta Air Lines, will outfit its fleet of XLRs with 174 seats. Business class will feature 12 lie-flat suites supplied by Thompson Aero Seating in a 1-1 layout with privacy doors.

The suites include 19-inch personal entertainment screens, Bluetooth connectivity and in-seat charging options.

Economy features 13-inch screens at each of the 126 seats, which are supplied by Recaro, plus Bluetooth connectivity and USB-C outlets. The cabin includes 36 extra-legroom seats.

“The Airbus A321XLR allows us to take our value proposition to the next level and elevate the travel experience for our passengers,” said Paulo Miranda, the chief customer officer of LATAM, in a statement. He described the interior, which features red, orange and blue hues, as “inspired by South America.”

LATAM executives have said it could fly the XLR on routes into the U.S. from its hub at Jorge Chavez International Airport (LIM) in Lima. However, those plans were called into question in May over the addition of a "connection fee" at LIM.

The airline and Delta serve six U.S. destinations from LIM: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Orlando International Airport (MCO) and, since January 2026, Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC).

LATAM did not comment on specific route plans for the XLR.

The XLR is the second new airplane type for LATAM in as many years. The airline took delivery of its first Embraer E195-E2 in October. It will use the small jet to expand its feeder network in Brazil and support additional long-haul, intercontinental flying.

item.title: Exploring Rabat, Morocco – this year’s Unesco World Book Capital
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging travel piece with cultural context and personal narrative.

The first book I read willingly was Bridget Jones’s Diary. I was 19. Up to that point, I hadn’t been much of a reader. I’d been more into football, or Baywatch, or Robin Budd in the year above – anything really. Given the choice between reading a book and staring at a wall, I would have plumped for the latter.

After finishing my A-levels, I worked in a barbecue restaurant in Portsmouth – which is where I found Bridget Jones. The book was lying around in the staffroom. I picked it up and read a few pages, and then a few more, and then a few more. It felt exciting. Like I’d met someone. Like I was suddenly in a relationship. Over the next few days, I remember cancelling nights out so I could go to bed and read. My mum thought I was depressed.

It hardly matters what book gets you going. For Jeanette Winterson, it was the Book of Deuteronomy. For David Nicholls, it was Tales from Moominvalley. What matters is that a book gets you going. Throughout my 20s, I worked as a carer, but I was always reading and scribbling on the side. I became a published author seven years ago. It’s not an overstatement to say that Bridget Jones changed my life. That books did.

So when I learned that 2026 was National Year of Reading (a UK-wide campaign intended to promote the importance and joy of reading) and that Rabat was to be this year’s Unesco World Book Capital (a rotating designation intended to promote the importance and joy of reading), I packed a few volumes and set off for Morocco’s capital. I was hoping for a cultural adventure, and perhaps a tagine, in this ancient seaside city perched scenically between Casablanca and Tangier.

Rabat was made the capital of Morocco in 1912, at the beginning of the turbulent 44-year period when the country found itself under the thumb of the French. The first thing I saw of the city was the New Town, or Ville Nouvelle, which was laid out in the 1920s à la française, meaning it looks nothing like the huge medieval medina that’s just up the road.

From the central train station, I proceeded to the solar-powered Mohammed VI Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, where the permanent exhibition – Shifting Horizon(s) – does exactly what it says on the tin. Highlights include the abstract paintings of Mohamed Melehi and a provocative photograph by Lalla Essaydi. Part of a series called Bullet Revisited, the latter shows a woman covered head to toe in gold bullets, and is a powerful indictment of the violence women suffer.

I walked north to the medina, an irregular network of narrow streets lined with small shops flogging mint, slippers, strawberries and sabon beldi, a black soap made from the flesh and oil of olives. The medina was busy but calm. Not once was I asked to consider a carpet or sample a sardine. Indeed, I felt rather invisible. In this respect, the customer service was uncannily French.

I followed my nose to the Kasbah of the Oudayas, an enchanting district of low whitewashed houses. Built on high ground in view of the ocean, this former royal citadel was ideally placed to spot visitors on the horizon, and greet them appropriately.

After checking into a riad on Rue Bazou, I descended a flight of stone steps to the beach, a modest curve of sand where scores of people were playing football and volleyball. I crossed the cooling sand and climbed on to the breakwater to better observe a neon sun sink slowly seaward, as a lone surfer, way out in the offing, sought inch-perfect swell.

I took a pew at the beachside Relais Marin restaurant. I didn’t deliberate over the menu. Like casserole and paella, tagine is a dish in two senses; both the cooking vessel and the meal, on this occasion a confusion of lamb, almonds and prunes in a delicious gravy that, with time, had reduced to a bold, flavourful pesto, which I mopped up with chunks of khobz (Moroccan flatbread). I could have eaten another.

The next morning I went to the Cafe des Oudayas. Situated next to the Andalusian Gardens – a wonderful place full of orange and pomegranate trees – this alfresco cafe offers three things: mint tea, biscuits and an excellent vantage point.

As I eked out the tea, I watched a boy poised on the edge of a towering rock, 30 metres above the Bou Regreg river. Goaded by his friends, he meant to jump, but he hesitated for minutes in the intensifying sun. His dive, when it finally came, was a thing of beauty – a wide and graceful arc, shapely, immaculate, somewhat divine, almost unreal. The gallery held its breath until he re-emerged – to be met with disingenuous disdain. “La poule a attendu une éternité!” (The chicken waited for ever!) Lads, eh?

On a whim, I boarded an electric tuk-tuk, one of 60 in the city. I asked the driver to take me directly to the Chellah, a medieval necropolis that also houses what’s left of the Roman city of Sala Colonia, but, knowing best, the driver instead went out of his way to show off his home town, swinging by St Peter’s cathedral and a nightclub called Amnesia, where Morocco’s king is said to have boogied back when merely a prince.

The Chellah – when I finally got there – did not disappoint. After doing a round of the picturesque ruins, I climbed to a gorgeous onsite cafe and ordered the couscous. Befitting tradition, the dish comprised a pyramid of seven vegetables, a moat of couscous, a jug of broth and some meaty treasure hidden within the veg. It was unmistakably bon.

If one requires beer in Rabat, one heads to Le Dhow, a bar and restaurant on a boat moored in the shadow of the kasbah. Sitting on the upper deck, I savoured an ice-cold pint while chatting with a British undergraduate studying at the Université Internationale de Rabat. I asked if she felt comfortable in the city. “It’s been fine,” she said. “Some men have said hello. One asked for a photo. To be honest, I’ve experienced a lot worse in Worcester.”…

Source: The Guardian Travel | Published: 2026-08-01 06:00 UTC | Difficulty: 50/100

item.title: £600 for cheese? The Brazilian beach scams that cost visitors dear
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Informative article on travel scams with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

When Lisa Selby* used her debit card to pay for two slices of barbecued cheese from a beach vendor in Rio de Janeiro, she expected to pay 40 reais (£5.90) for the snack.

“He showed me the right number on the contactless terminal, but then turned it round to face him and, unbeknownst to me, added two zeros just as I was about to tap with my phone,” she said. “He then gestured that there was no paper for a receipt and walked away.”

Holidaymakers have been warned to beware of the crime in Rio. Last month a beach vendor was arrested after a British man was duped into paying £1,500 for a kebab, while an Argentinian tourist discovered a £3 corn on the cob had cost her £3,000.

What it looks like

Unscrupulous traders take advantage of tourists who are unfamiliar with the local currency and are less likely to notice a doctored sum.

A common ploy is to ask the customer to confirm the correct figure on the card reader, then to alter it surreptitiously before the card is presented.

Some scammers thrust their card reader at the customer’s card or phone to complete the payment before the customer has checked the total.

What to do

The scam exposes a gap in UK consumer protection. Customers who are tricked into sending money to criminals by bank transfer in what’s known as authorised push payment fraud are usually entitled to a refund from their bank. However, victims of face-to-face vending scams are unlikely to get their money back unless they can produce evidence that they were overcharged.

Selby discovered the fraud shortly after the payment and immediately alerted her bank, Monzo. An agent told her that since the transaction was still pending it would be returned to her. Monzo later admitted that she had been wrongly advised and said that authorised payments cannot be reversed.

Her attempts to claim the money via her card issuer’s chargeback scheme, which allows a dispute to be raised with a trader who is in breach of contract, failed because she did not have an invoice or receipt showing the agreed price.

Monzo refunded her as a goodwill gesture after contact from Guardian Money. It said that reports of beach vendor scams are increasing but that Selby’s experience is classed as a buyer/seller dispute rather than fraud because she had authorised the card payment.

A spokesperson said: “We understand this was a very frustrating experience for the customer. While our reasons for rejecting the claim were correct, we recognise that our communication fell short of our usual high standards.”

The Financial Conduct Authority, which regulates UK banks, confirmed that pending transactions cannot usually be reversed, and that chargebacks are a voluntary service offered by card issuers, which are free to decide their own criteria and processes.

It said victims may be able to submit a claim to their bank for an unauthorised transaction since they had not consented to the amount that was debited and that they can complain to the Financial Ombudsman Service if they are unhappy with the response.

To avoid being caught out, holidaymakers are advised to pay mobile vendors in cash, or to insist on holding the card reader to insert or swipe their card themselves to prevent a last-minute alteration to the price.

* Name has been changed

Source: The Guardian Travel | Published: 2026-05-24 06:00 UTC | Difficulty: 40/100

item.title: How I Got My Visa to France
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Personal travel story with some useful vocabulary but lacks depth and detail.

How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

In short, I needed a change.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

- Student visa

- Long-term visitor visa

- Entrepreneur

- Talent visa

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work?…

Source: Nomadic Matt | Published: 2026-02-16 08:25 UTC | Difficulty: 30/100

Original link: https://www.nomadicmatt.com/travel-blogs/france-visa/

item.title: A Deep Dive Into Alabama’s Reading Gains
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

A Deep Dive Into Alabama’s Reading Gains

In 2015, Alabama ranked 45th in NAEP scores. By 2024, they had climbed to 13th. Journalist Liana Loewus describes what shifted and what’s next.

In recent years, four southern states appear to be leading the way in reading growth: Mississippi, Louisiana, Tennessee and Alabama.

Decades of policy and commitment to the science of reading in Mississippi has been reported and analyzed extensively, but a new report from Thomas B. Fordham Institute continues to highlight states part of the “southern surge” — this time placing the spotlight on Alabama.

In 2015, Alabama was ranked 45th among states on the fourth grade National Assessment of Educational Progress, but in the years that followed rose to 18th in 2019 and 13th in 2024.

In a 42-page study, journalist Liana Loewus reports the history of Alabama reading policy, looking back at over three decades of initiatives, including a failed expansion in the 2000s resulting in pulling back efforts and a reinvestment in literacy coaches, curriculum and intervention since 2019.

Alabama “has been one of the few states to show academic improvement over the last two rounds of NAEP,” Loewus wrote in the report. “After falling below the national average for fourth-grade reading between 2013 and 2022, the state is closing the gap again. Its 2024 average scale score was … just two points below the national average.”

In an interview with The 74, Loewus spoke in depth about her findings and the state’s next steps.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Q: I’ll kick off our conversation by asking you to summarize your findings with this report, mainly about Alabama’s early adoption of literacy reforms, what went wrong and where we’re at now.

A: The Alabama story is just so fascinating. You can really see the beginning and trajectory and follow the line very clearly between policy implementation and impact on students.

Alabama is still not at the top, but they were making gains when no one else was, even staying steady when the pandemic hit and it was important to look at why.

The story really starts 30 years ago when Catherine Mitchell, after working in the Alabama State Department of Ed for nearly 20 years, took over literacy in 1998. She raised $1.5 million with two unlikely allies, A+ Education Partnership, a progressive advocacy group and the Eagle Forum, a very conservative group, who all agreed they wanted to teach kids how to read, launching a program that became the Alabama Reading Initiative.

It started with 16 schools. Mitchell said ‘Give me your non-readers, and we’re going to teach them how to read,’ and she will say no one in Alabama knew anything about phonics at that time. She had to write training modules for the teachers about phonics and phonemic awareness. She hired teachers who knew about comprehension, teaching kids how to understand what they were reading and language comprehension. At the end of the year, the data was really good, there were fewer referrals to special education and reading scores went up.

She went back and got the state legislature to fund $6 million. By the mid 2000s, a literacy coach who was trained by the Alabama Reading Initiative, an arm of the Department of Education, was put in every single K-3 school. Between 2005 to 2007, fourth grade reading scores jumped more than any other state. They were basically on par with the national average by 2011, which was pretty important for them because they had been far below for a long time.

In 2012, the state superintendent at the time decided to expand on the coaching initiative; they’d decided to bring coaches to all schools, K-12, and other subjects but there was less training. The whole initiative was watered down, ARI funding went from $58 million in 2013 to $40.7 million by 2018 — funding went down but the initiative had expanded.

In 2018, Mississippi started to get attention, and there’s a little bit of next door rivalry, so leaders in Alabama, including Rep. Terry Collins went to Mississippi to find out what’s happening. Collins became convinced that Alabama needed a law like Mississippi’s 2013 Literacy Based Promotion Act, pushing really hard for comprehensive literacy law.

The law passed in 2019 with flying colors. This year, ARI is funded at $152 million.

At The 74, we launched the Bright Spots series, highlighting schools that are beating the odds in literacy. In Connecticut, a district talked about three things: accountability, coaching and curriculum, which aligned with your report and three main things you’ve taken out of Alabama. Which of those three would you say has had the greatest impact?

Coaching is a huge piece of it.

It’s extremely prescriptive, Alabama ensures that all coaches are trained in the same way and they all have the same base knowledge. The state also gives every single school $85,000 for a literacy coach, where in a lot of places, they’ll say you need coaches and it’s unfunded.

I think the most important thing that Alabama does is they wrote into the law that these coaches have to focus on coaching. They wrote a list of things these coaches cannot do. They can work with teachers and sometimes with students, but they cannot do extra recess and administrative duties. They cannot fill in as subs, they can’t be pulled for other things.

Another thing I learned that has a large impact is having steady leadership that is committed to research-based practices and hires people who really understand it. We had Terry Collins, Dr. Mackey and Gov. Kate Ivey. Dr. Mackey has been in office for nearly nine years at this point. Terry Collins was in the legislature for 15 years. They’ve stuck with the policy, they’ve stayed the course and that’s a big deal.…

item.title: LAUSD Spent Over $6 Million on a Phone Ban. Survey Data Show Mixed Results
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

LAUSD Spent Over $6 Million on a Phone Ban. Survey Data Show Mixed Results

In the first district-wide survey since the policy began, students and staff did agree that engagement has improved.

A majority of students are complying with Los Angeles Unified’s cellphone ban and paying more attention in class, at least according to school staff.

That’s one finding from the first survey of students and staff to include questions about bell-to-bell restrictions implemented in February 2025.

“It’s a big difference in terms of [students’] ability and willingness to focus on whatever we’re doing in class,” said Elizabeth Ruff, an English teacher at Garfield High School. “Obviously there are always some kids who are distracted … even if it’s not their phone. But that has decreased a lot really, really markedly.”

But there are still unanswered questions about what effect, if any, LAUSD’s student phone-use restrictions have on student learning and behavior, including recent gains on state tests.

Compliance varies, too: Middle school staff estimated that two-thirds of students “mostly” abided by the restrictions. Among high school staff, that number dropped to just over half.

More than 160,000 students answered the survey, as did more than 21,000 staff members.

The results of the spring 2026 School Experience Survey, which queries staff, students and parents on a number of topics, are the first public, quantitative measure of how LAUSD’s updated cellphone policy has changed student behavior on campus. While some survey answers are available online, results of the questions specific to the cellphone policy were released to LAist only upon request.

LAUSD’s policy predated the state of California’s requirements for all schools to restrict student cellphones by July 2026. At least 40 states and the District of Columbia have similar restrictions, according to Education Week, largely based on the premise that phones and social media distract students from learning and amplify conflicts, among other concerns.

How middle and high school students differ

LAUSD middle and high school students are split nearly evenly on whether the policy improved their focus in class.

Myson Thomas, 17, is a senior at King/Drew Magnet High School. He said he doesn’t use his school’s magnetically sealed Yondr pouches, but he also isn’t on his phone in class.

“I’m at school to learn, so I’m gonna turn my phone off,” Thomas said. “I already take rigorous courses, so it’s no point of me using my phone at school.”

Fewer than half of high school students reported they focused better in class all or most of the time without their phone compared to nearly 58% of their peers in middle school.

“In implementing a phone-free policy across the district, we recognized that changing long-standing habits would take time,” a district spokesperson said in a statement to LAist. “We recognize there is still work to do and will continue listening to students, families and staff as we refine our approach to support focused learning and meaningful in-person connections.”

Board Member Nick Melvoin, who co-sponsored the cellphone policy, said he was “really encouraged” that most middle and high school student respondents said they were interacting with each other more without their phones.

“This isn’t just about trying to be punitive adults,” Melvoin said. “This is about [students] having a much more engaging day, a more fulfilling day when you’re not just scrolling or texting.”

How we got here

LAUSD joined a growing number of districts and states clamping down on student cellphone use in June 2024 when the school board voted to extend the existing class-time ban to include lunch and passing periods.

Board members cited concerns about the effect of phones and social media on youth mental health, bullying and distraction from classroom instruction.

Educators who spoke in support of stricter rules said their schools had few resources or administrative support to enforce the existing rules and said that policing phone use ate up time and created conflicts with students.

“It definitely felt a little bit like playing Whac-A-Mole in terms of trying to do everything else I’m supposed to be doing in the classroom and also be looking out for who secretly has a cellphone behind their book,” said Ruff, the Garfield High School teacher.

How LAUSD enforced phone restrictions

The board’s vote allocated $7 million to implement the policy. Schools could choose whether they wanted to purchase pouches or lockers to store students’ phones or rely on the “honor system,” and ask students to keep their devices powered off and in their backpacks.

About half of schools purchased devices to enforce the ban, according to a district spokesperson at the time the policy went into effect.

Documents provided to LAist through a public records request show LAUSD spent about $6.35 million on products related to cellphone policy implementation during the 2024-25 school year. Of that, the district spent $5.42 million on Yondr products (including phone pouches) and nearly $930,000 on products from Amazon, including phone lockers.

What we know about the effectiveness of phone restrictions

LAist first spoke to Miles, a student at the Sherman Oaks Center for Enriched Studies, when the restrictions began in 2025. At the time, he called the phone-free policy “really, really annoying.”

“I think it’s still a pretty useless policy,” Miles, now a junior, said. ”It doesn’t change anything other than how we hide our phones.”

LAist agreed not to publish Miles’ last name to protect his privacy.

He, like Thomas, said he doesn’t use his school’s phone storage pouches and doesn’t use his phone in class.

Students have also reportedly circumvented the pouches by storing a dummy phone or breaking open the locks.…

Source: The 74 | Published: 2026-11-21 11:30 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.

On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.

The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.

But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.

Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.

“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.

Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.

The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.

More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.

The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea, stoking concern about the security of the suneung.

In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”

His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.

The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.

Choi has ruled out postponing the exam, which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017, after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.

Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.

The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.

Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.

To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.

Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.

In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.

“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-11-18 02:03 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: NYC Public School Enrollment Drops, Raising Questions Over Budgets and Closures
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

NYC Public School Enrollment Drops, Raising Questions Over Budgets and Closures

Public schools have lost about 23,000 students, or nearly 3%, from the year before, according to preliminary numbers from the Education Department.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

New York City’s public schools lost about 23,000 students, or nearly 3%, from the year before, according to preliminary numbers the Education Department released Monday.

That leaves the nation’s largest school system with about 766,900 students, from kindergarten through senior year, as of Oct. 31, with several contributing factors leading to the drop: falling birth rates, families leaving the city, and a slowdown of immigration into the five boroughs under President Donald Trump.

Over the past decade, the city has lost about 200,000 students, or nearly 20%.

Enrollment in city-funded preschool programs was up slightly, thanks to the rollout of a new program for 2,000 2-year-olds this year as well as an uptick in 4-year-olds signed up for prekindergarten programs.

What the dip means for school budgets remains murky. Historically, when schools have fewer students than projected on their roster, the Education Department claws back money in the middle of the school year. But since the pandemic, the city has largely kept school budgets steady despite enrollment declines. Officials declined to say whether they planned to continue that policy, known as being “held harmless.” Since 2020, New York City has spent nearly $2 billion to prop up budgets at schools with declining enrollment.

Any changes to wind down that policy could be politically explosive, as schools could have to cut back on after-school and other enrichment programs this school year and eventually let go of teachers. When former Mayor Eric Adams proposed phasing it out, the blowback was so intense that City Council members apologized for giving him the green light. (The decision was later rolled back.)

In his first budget deal, Mayor Zohran Mamdani kept school budgets whole, though some experts warn that approach is inequitable because it allows schools with declining enrollment to spend significantly more per student than other campuses.

Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels has repeatedly raised concerns about declining enrollment, saying that the city will need to look closer at closures or mergers for schools too small to offer a full array of courses. Already, the city is floating proposals to close two small schools in Harlem and one in Brooklyn, as well as merge two sets of schools in the Bronx and Brooklyn, according to public documents. Those plans are expected to be voted on by the Panel for Educational Policy over the next two months.

“We’ve started to have conversations in communities,” Samuels told the Chancellor’s Parent Advisory Committee last week. “It doesn’t mean it’s not going to be tough sometimes, but they have been going pretty well.”

Enrollment is projected to continue declining. By the 2034-35 school year, the city is predicting that the student population will fall by another 130,000, according to demographic projections from the School Construction Authority.

The declines in New York City mirror national trends. Thirty states have seen public school enrollment declines since 2014. Many large school systems — including in Los Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia, and Houston — are also grappling with sharp drops.

Mamdani’s administration pointed to some efforts to help bolster city schools, including reducing class sizes, which is required by state law and has likely been aided by declining student headcounts. Aside from continuing some of his predecessor’s initiatives, Mamdani has yet to articulate a vision for the public school system. He has focused more on his affordability agenda and expanding his free 2-K program, which expects to add 10,000 more seats next year.

When the city’s free preschool programs for 2-, 3-, and 4-year-olds are included in the enrollment tally, the total is 863,100, according to the Education Department’s preliminary data. That was down about 2.6% from the previous year.

Chalkbeat New York Reporter Michael Elsen-Rooney contributed.

Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools. This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters
