item.title: Macron banned smartphones in schools. A month later, France was ablaze. Could they be connected? | Joseph de Weck
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

Remember the 1999 blockbuster The Matrix? It may be more than a quarter of a century old, but it has become a byword and a meme for a frighteningly plausible kind of 21st-century tech dystopia.

A quick recap: the computer hacker Neo discovers that machines rule over humanity. They keep people trapped in pods, their minds immersed in a virtual reality designed to keep them docile (the “Matrix” of the title). Once he becomes aware of the world he actually inhabits, Neo decides to take up arms.

Is that the kind of awakening France’s youth is experiencing today? Could a government-mandated digital detox have had the unintended consequence of protests and riots on such a scale that the army was brought out on to the streets?

This October, hundreds of thousands of French youngsters walked out of school and joined mass protests. Their demands include fixing France’s moribund school infrastructure and restoring every graduate’s right to choose their university and degree programme. Above all, they want to revive the école de la République, France’s public school system, as the engine of social mobility. Today only sport stars, crypto bros and influencers seem to be getting ahead in life.

These problems are nothing new. But what has triggered a reaction on this scale now?

Mara Goyet, a teacher in Paris, argues that the phone ban in lycées, introduced in September, helped spark the uprising. Suddenly disconnected from their own matrix, the pupils raised their eyes from their phone screens and could no longer tune out the grim reality of the world they inhabit, Goyet writes.

Emmanuel Macron decided to make the war on les écrans – screens – a legacy of his botched second term.

In 2024, the Élysée Palace asked a panel of experts, including neurologists and psychiatrists, to analyse the effects of digital technology on youth. It found that young French people aged 16 to 19 spent more than five hours a day staring at their phones. Shortened attention spans, a sedentary lifestyle and mental health issues were the consequence, the panel found.

Following the report, on 21 July the national assembly passed a law restricting social media access for under-15s and banning phones in lycées, coming into effect for the new school year. Perhaps paradoxically, the leftwing France Insoumise (LFI) had voted against the law, denouncing it as “a form of digital paternalism”. The far-right Rassemblement National abstained.

The constitutional court quickly overturned the social media ban. But when teenagers returned from their summer holidays, teachers were asking them to leave their phone in lockers or put them in sealed pouches.

A teacher working in a Parisian suburb, writing anonymously in Le Grand Continent, describes a classroom transformed: “As soon as the class, with its necessary tyranny, came to an end, the brains switched off. The 30 or so brains were drained by the image drug. My class became a group of zombies … This year, without their phones, my students are more lively, more engaging, more engaging, more disorganised, more excitable, more childlike. They’re also more of a pain.”

Another teacher told me much the same story: with the arrival of smartphones, breaktimes had grown quieter, with many pupils absorbed by their TikTok feed or playing games. Now, the hallways are loud again, buzzing with life.

For a shared political consciousness to form, people need to break out of isolation, talk to one another and build trust. That seems to have happened. And for pupils pushed back into the analogue world, political action goes beyond online posting and out into the streets.

Appropriately, the trigger for the French student movement that erupted into the era-defining protests of May 1968 was another interdiction: a ban on female and male students spending the night together in dormitories at the Nanterre campus, University of Paris.

By protesting as their forebears did in 68, today’s students also briefly disrupted what Guy Debord described as the “society of the spectacle”: a world in which reality is shaped by a flood of images, performative acts and mediated information. Here, by contrast, was the direct experience of reality. Standing together in the clouds of teargas that engulfed Paris and other cities on 17 October, a new generation of French citizens forged a collective lived experience that showed them they could be actors, not just spectators of political life.

Sociologists will have to study whether the enforced digital detox has really helped trigger this movement. After all, pupils have also organised their actions via social media, and the protests are extensively live-streamed on the same smartphones and platforms they have been detached from at school. This is a hybrid uprising.

But one thing is already clear. Students are not taking to the streets because they want to overturn the phone ban.

Louis Letoublon, vice-president of Les Lycéens!, an organisation of high school students, says: “The phone ban is unbearable, as it infantilises the students.” Some protest posters read: “Adult and vaccinated, but I am still getting my phone taken away at school.” Or: “You can take away my phone, but not my voice.”

But the government has set up a platform where pupils can register their demands. According to preliminary results based on more than 60,000 contributions, 70% said school days were too long, and 48.2% cited poor infrastructure, particularly the cold in winter and heat in summer. Only 9% of students demanded that the phone ban be overturned.

France’s young people took to the streets because they want better schools, not because they see Macron as an overbearing father, confiscating phones as punishment.

Two years ago, Macron declared that it was urgent to “retake control of our screens, that too often enclose us, where they should liberate us”. The irony is that, by unplugging teenagers from the matrix, he may have unleashed a storm that has sealed his decline and fall.…

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-11-18 05:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/18/macron-banned-smartphones-in-schools-a-month-later-france-was-ablaze-could-they-be-connected

item.title: With free-tuition promises, some colleges try to untangle confusion over what they cost
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

MIDDLEBURY, Vt.

There’s a golf course on this campus. The student-faculty ratio is an exclusive 9-to-1. And an undergraduate tour guide is telling visiting prospective applicants about a classmate who spent a semester learning how to forage in Malaysia.

Middlebury College looks and sounds … expensive. But like other universities and colleges, it’s working hard to persuade people that it’s not.

Middlebury has announced that, starting next year, students from families with annual household incomes up to $175,000 can enroll tuition-free. It becomes the latest of a growing number of schools to make this kind of promise, including Princeton (for most families earning up to $250,000, with typical assets), the University of Chicago ($250,000), MIT ($200,000), Harvard ($200,000), Swarthmore ($200,000) and Davidson ($175,000).

These may seem like generous expansions of financial aid; after all, $175,000 is more than double the nation’s median household income. But while it’s true that few additional families will benefit — 35 to 50 in the incoming class at Middlebury, which typically enrolls about 630 new students per year, the college says — most people in those earnings categories already attend without having to pay tuition.

When families see these pronouncements, they think, “ ‘Oh, wow, the college is cutting the price.’ And that’s almost a perfect example of the misperceptions of the pricing system,” said Phillip Levine, an economist at Wellesley College who studies higher education finance and is the author of the book “Hidden Tuition: An Insider’s Guide to College Pricing and Financial Aid.”

In fact, said Levine, whose research bears this out, at most of the institutions making these tuition-free guarantees, “the college was already free for almost all those kids.”

The real purpose of what Middlebury and other schools are doing, he and other experts say, is to solve a problem that has soured many Americans on higher education: how frustratingly hard it is to figure out what college will cost.

“Let’s make it as non-complicated as possible,” said Ian Baucom, president at Middlebury: “If your family income is $175,000 or less, at Middlebury, you don’t pay tuition.” What the school is doing, he said, is trying to “just [be] really clear and get that out of the way, and then let the students decide.”

Most of the growing number of income-based tuition plans take effect next year, as at Middlebury, or began for students who enrolled this fall.

That’s not coincidental. Many of these schools have reached or surpassed a listed price of attendance of $100,000 a year; at Middlebury, it’s $97,386. And public confusion about how much they actually cost after discounts and financial aid is helping drive a near-record-low confidence in higher education that threatens to exacerbate enrollment and revenue challenges.

Nearly 70 percent of students and parents think the financial aid process is partly or completely confusing, according to a separate survey by the Strada Education Foundation.

Most Americans also think that colleges are overpriced, with nearly two-thirds saying four-year institutions are unaffordable, a Gallup survey found; among parents who don’t want their children to go to a four-year college, it found, the biggest reason was the cost.

Related: Some colleges aim financial aid at a declining market: Students in the middle class

A culprit for this is colleges’ own increasingly self-destructive policy of advertising a high list price that almost no one pays, then giving discounts. It’s a strategy that has evolved from a time when the price was intended to signal value and the discounts — which the colleges call “scholarships” — to entice the most desirable prospective students to enroll.

Guarantees do not include room, board and other expenses, though separate financial aid is often available for those.

Source: The Hechinger Report | Published: 2026-11-13 14:33 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://hechingerreport.org/with-free-tuition-promises-some-colleges-try-to-untangle-confusion-over-what-they-cost/

item.title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories

Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.

An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.

Many parents do not.

"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."

When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom.

But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified, Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.

In a post on X, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.

A baffling move

Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.

She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C.

Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search.

"The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."

When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement, where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.

NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.

The "AI or nothing" approach

In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an "unacceptable risk" rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.

The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.

Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois.

"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.

Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.

He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging.

"Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."

The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.

Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen

Google is a financial supporter of NPR.

item.title: Foley Catheters and First-Year Composition: Implementing High-Impact Practices through Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

According to the Association of American Colleges and Universities, active learning is an essential part of a modern college education. High Impact Practices (HIPs) use collaborative and active learning strategies to improve student engagements and outcomes. White (2018) explained that while HIPs can positively impact student success, budgetary restraints can present challenges to implementation. Therefore, faculty are finding ways to create active learning experiences without a high cost to institutions.

Cross-disciplinary collaboration presents an opportunity to use HIPs to engage students in the core curriculum. In my case, the First-Year Writing (FYW) classroom offers a unique setting to use HIPs to build on how writing creates common spaces not only in FYW, but also expands those spaces into discipline-specific areas, such as nursing. Cross-disciplinary collaboration through FYW not only provides students with an early look at their majors but also teaches them how to decompartmentalize the writing skills they learn in FYW and apply them to a broader experience.

This article will focus on one such collaboration between English (English 1101) and Nursing and the impact of cross-disciplinary activities and HIPs on students in a discipline-specific FYW course.

Importance of Collaboration

Collaborative projects can provide students with deeper learning experiences and opportunities for increasing communication (written and oral) skills both inside the classroom and within the community (White, 2018; Bresciani, 2015). The FYW classroom provides a unique setting to build on momentum in cases where students are unable to have an early introduction to their major. FYW challenges students to understand the connection of strong writing to their majors, especially if the material in the course correlates to relevant subject matter in the major. The goal in creating this cost-effective nursing-specific English 1101 was to ask students to think specifically about how writing relates to a more universal experience (medical professions) in order to express the importance of humanities beyond the composition classroom.

Collaboration, particularly in course design and implementation, can often seem like a heavy lift. In some cases, faculty can be protective of course material and design, and in others, challenges exist in finding partnerships outside of specific disciplinary departments. In the following, I hope to show how this type of critical work can happen organically and effectively while bringing satisfaction and appreciation not only to students but to the faculty involved.

Process of Implementation

Over the course of a semester and over the summer, I worked with a nursing faculty member to refine the necessary concepts for bringing the course into the classroom. I started with the basic course learning outcomes for our institution’s English 1101.

From there, I and my nursing faculty partner, explored what concepts would be important for students interested in the nursing program to learn early in their academic careers. I began with highlighting the connection between the humanities and health care through learning about and constructing a medical narrative where students had to articulate their interest in pursuing a nursing career. Then, I focused on the importance of communication in relaying critical information through instructions by creating a process project, which included a demonstration (by my nursing partner) of a Foley catheter insertion using a medical mannequin, followed by a hands-on opportunity for students to practice this foundational healthcare procedure. Finally, I had students hone their research skills by exploring relevant and current healthcare-related issues and presenting them in a multimedia assignment. Instead of MLA, as is common in most humanities courses, students used APA formatting and citations throughout the course to better prepare them for the nursing program.

Please scan the QR code below for copies of the assignments.

Lessons Learned and Advice

Engagement

Students were more motivated to engage with assignments. They appreciated exposure to nursing concepts early in their academic careers and enjoyed forming an early relationship with a nursing faculty member. The course sparked their intellectual curiosity and got them thinking about the deeper issues within their major and future profession. When learning is decompartmentalized, students can see connection between academic and life experiences. Potential nursing students expressed excitement for discipline-specific core classes and, sometimes, students realized that the hands-on activities showed them that nursing was not their best fit, well before they spent years working towards acceptance into the nursing program.

Collaboration

Collaboration opportunities don’t have to be complicated, expensive, or overly time-consuming. Simple conversations and activities can be cost-effective while academically sound and engaging. Partnerships can happen in surprising situations. The nursing English 1101 collaboration started as a kernel of an idea while riding in the back of a college-issued Ford Taurus on the way home from a teaching and learning conference. It’s important to note that collaborative course work should involve immediate supervisors (chairs and deans), advisors, and the Registrar. In my situation, we needed to make sure the course was populated with future nursing students, which would be information the Registrar provided and advisors actively used for registration.

Final Thoughts…

Scouts say they face Â£1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips

Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of Â£1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England.

The overnight levy would allow councils and regional authorities to charge visitors an additional fee for their accommodation, including campsites, raising money to be spent on local services.

The increased cost from the Visitors Levy could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.

Dwayne Fields, the UK's Chief Scout, has called for youth groups to be exempted and said the charity - which sees more than 1.4m overnight stays a year - would be "firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations".

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government told the BBC that local leaders who introduce the levy "will have the option to exempt certain types of accommodation in their areas, including accommodation which is often used for trips by youth groups like Scouts and Girl Guides - such as camping pitches".

They added money raised from the levy will "stay local and be invested in the visitor experience and local growth including in high streets, parks and events".

Labour mayors have indicated they would cap the levy at 5% but the legislation contains no maximum limit.

In a statement, the Scout Association said the tax, if set at 5% across the country, could cost the charity Â£1.04m a year and force volunteers to deal with onerous paperwork.

They worked this out by assuming the levy would be set at 5% for all the 1,423,344 annual overnight stays across Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and volunteers.

Girlguiding would also be subject to the levy.

In a statement, Fields said: "We strongly support investment being made available to strengthen local communities. Well-crafted legislation can unlock that opportunity.

"But we are firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations for camping trips that equip young people with skills for life, while burdening volunteers with the role of unpaid government tax collectors."

Chris Taylor, lead volunteer for Greater Manchester East Scout County, called the levy a "tent tax" and branded it "madness".

Referring to the levy being applied to the Linnet Clough campsite run by his group in Stockport, he said: "Our members spent nearly 25,000 nights away from home last year, and a 5% levy would add over Â£11,000 a year to the cost of their camps and sleepovers."

He added: "On top of that, and as a charity, we'd have to employ someone just to collect the tax and send returns to the Mayor's office. That's another Â£7,000 a year, and that's just one campsite - there are plenty more across Manchester."

Labour MP Gareth Snell, who challenged ministers when the levy was debated in the House of Commons , said Scouts "provide some of the most memorable experiences for young people up and down the country."

The Stoke-on-Trent Central MP called on the government to take the decision out of mayors' hands and ensure Scout camps are exempted from the bill.

The Welsh Government has announced young people staying in hostels, campsites or outdoor centres would be exempt from its tourism tax, due to come into effect next year.

item.title: ‘National scandal’: residents in England rally against surge in mega-warehouse developments
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging article on a contemporary issue affecting residents, with concrete examples and useful vocabulary.

When a planning application for a lot next to his new home landed in his letterbox, Jon Davis was crestfallen.

He had just moved into the property in Bingham, Nottinghamshire, with his wife and toddler in June.

Now, he said he was being told: “‘By the way, there’s going to be 21.5-metre-high warehouses right next to you, and there’s going to be eight of them, and you’re going to have 400 HGVs and it’s going to be a 24-hour operation’.”

He added: “I’ll be honest with you, I cried. I was so upset.”

That planning application would add to the more than 8,500 warehouses or large distribution units that have been approved across England in the past decade, fuelled by the growth of online shopping.

Analysis of official figures by the Guardian showed that almost all (95%) of the 9,009 planning applications for “megasheds” were given the go-ahead in the 10 years up to June 2026.

Of the 4,300 approved in the last five years, nearly half (1,922) were in the east, south-east and north-west of England, and 17 were in national parks, despite them having stricter rules on major developments. Six industrial developments were approved in the South Downs national park since 2021, alongside five in the North York Moors and one in the Lake District.

England’s “golden logistics triangle” – historically the Midlands area, which is within a four-hour drive of 90% of industrial developments – has expanded significantly, with the data showing that many planned developments are in newly-held Reform councils or constituencies.

Robert Jenrick, Reform MP for Newark, which Bingham falls under, met with the developer and the local council to discuss residents’ fears about the developments.

Davis closely followed events in Astley, a village in Wigan, where a public inquiry was held over towering mega-warehouses licensed to operate 24/7 being built metres from people’s homes. The powerful fightback of Astley villagers against what they described as “torture” from increased noise, light, and traffic made them figureheads in a nationwide battle against superstructures.

Davis considers them “the canary in the coal mine”.

“They’ve been so inspirational,” he added. “Seeing their videos, I was like, ‘Well, if they can do it, I think we can and I think we should.’”

Astley’s villagers had help from the Community Planning Alliance, an umbrella organisation for around 700 community groups nationwide.

Other local groups have highlighted instances where planning proposals were subtly changed or where councils cited un-evidenced demand for warehouse space. There were also suggestions that the government was not helping, after the National Planning Policy Framework, which was published in August, made it more difficult for the public to challenge planning decisions.

“The planning system is 100% biased against communities,” said Marj Powner, who runs the CPA. “We have so little power, it’s unbelievable.”

She said developers had six months to appeal a planning rejection, whereas communities had “zero, no right of appeal, none whatsoever” if an application was approved, leaving a judicial review as their only option.

“The community have six weeks to find and instruct a legal team and put together the grounds that they may have for their judicial review, and it will cost them around £60,000, which that community has to raise from donations,” she added.

Ten minutes away from Astley, residents near a 70 hectare (173 acre) site in Gibfield began their own campaign against a development that they said would tower over their homes and take away their only green space.

The development was initially backed by the Reform-led Wigan council and is managed by the Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners, which is privately run by the billionaire John Whittaker. Although the developer outlined warehouses 12.5m tall, the elevated ground level put the true height closer to 15.5m, relative to their homes, residents said.

“I think there’s just this view that we’re all kind of middle-class nimbies. We’re not. We’re normal working-class people,” said Amanda Coleman, who lives in a house immediately adjacent to the site. “It’s heartbreaking.” The site is one of a number of green belt areas controversially designated as “grey belt”. While intended for previously developed land when it was introduced in 2024, a CPRE report found that 88% of grey belt approvals upon appeal were on land that had never been built on.

Protecting nature was at the heart of many of the battles different groups were embroiled in across the UK.

In Northamptonshire, campaigners spent six years fighting two mega-warehouses on a 60 hectare (150 acre) site that is adjacent to the Upper Nene Valley Gravel Pits, a legally-protected nature reserve for golden plover and lapwing birds.

Sharon Cole, who is part of a local group, Save Titchmarsh and Upper Nene Countryside and Habitats (Staunch), appealed against the planning decision on the grounds it was in breach of international law.

She said vital habitats across the UK were being destroyed through “greed” and that developers were “ looking for all the loopholes that they can find, so they can develop [land]”.

Staunch has also campaigned for the creation of an all-party parliamentary group to scrutinise the planning process.

“When I started, I truly believed that the legal system and the planning system would come good, because we knew our facts were right, and it hasn’t happened,” Cole said.

She added: “The truth’s got to come out, because this is a national scandal across the country, what is happening within the planning system. It’s going to be the ruin of our country if something doesn’t change soon.”

A North Northamptonshire council spokesperson said the council recognised “that there are a range of strongly held views” on the warehouse proposals, but could not comment on potential legal proceedings.…

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-21 10:00 UTC | Difficulty: 65/100

Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair.

Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan, which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost.

In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger.

Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters.

Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”.

JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk.

Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported.

Bank share prices rallied after Healey’s October announcement because the increase was less than many people in the industry had expected. The chancellor said at the time that he was “looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families”.

JP Morgan declined to comment.

item.title: COP31: Why India’s Stress on Country-led Just Transition Pathways Is Justified
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Insightful piece on climate change policy, with a focus on a developing country's perspective.

The transition away from fossil fuels must adopt a country-driven approach that suits the socio-economic realities of each nation, India said at the 31st United Nations Conference of the Parties on climate change, commonly referred to as COP31. The conference is being held in Antalya, Turkiye, during November 9-20.

“India supports the operationalization of a two-tier, Party-guided Mechanism, responsive to developing-country needs and respectful of national sovereignty and diverse national circumstances,” India’s Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav said at COP31 on November 16.

This means India wants a mechanism in which global goals are set without imposing blanket, industry-wise mandates or creating new obligations. A one-size-fits-all approach won’t work, Yadav argued.

He called for just transition initiatives through a whole-of-economy and whole-of-society approach. Employment, social protection, adaptation, poverty eradication, energy access, and sustainable development are among the aspects that need to be addressed. For this, countries need to be supported with adequate finance, technology transfer, and capacity-building. These are essential to enable developing countries to implement their national priorities, he said.

Yadav’s stress on country-driven approaches is rooted in India’s reality. India’s energy transition is already advancing considerably faster than its social-protection and economic-rehabilitation arrangements.

According to an estimate by the Niti Ayog, the government’s top policy advisory body, coal mines and thermal power plants support about 1.5 million formal and informal workers, but the economic dependence goes beyond them and involves informal livelihoods across supply chains, transportation, and services concentrated in fossil-fuel dependent regions. The body said in a February 2026 report titled “Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero: Social Implications of Transition” that livelihood diversification strategies have become essential for fossil-fuel-dependent regions.

In short, India cannot afford to phase out coal too fast because that can adversely impact the socio-economic conditions of communities dependent on or around coal mines and thermal power plants.

In 2015-16, the share of thermal power, including oil and gas, stood at 210.67GW, or 69 percent of India’s 305GW installed capacity. Of this, coal accounted for 185.17 gigawatts (GW), or 61.5 percent of India’s 305GW installed capacity.

Following a decade of exponential growth in renewable energy, solar in particular, the share of fossil fuels in India’s installed capacity has slipped to 44.5 percent of its total installed capacity of 563GW. Coal’s share stood at 40 percent as of October 31, 2026.

India, the world’s second-largest coal producer, has not announced an immediate nationwide coal phase-out. Coal remains central to electricity generation. Mine closures have started accelerating nonetheless. The government has set an ambitious target of scientifically closing 147 more mines by 2028-29.

About a dozen research papers in the past five years have highlighted the negative impact of mine closures, especially on informal laborers and people living around coal mines and power plants. And the country has not yet established a comprehensive, adequately financed system in place.

An October 2026 report showed that fossil-fuel revenues from coal and petroleum resources made up 13.1 percent of own tax and non-tax revenues and 7.7 percent of total revenue receipts of Odisha. This eastern state is considered one of India’s fastest-industrializing ones.

The report, published by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, an international non-profit research and think tank organization, argued that the state’s fiscal structure’s close links to fossil fuels and extractive industries have created growing exposure to transition, market, and environmental risks.

“Given the importance of mineral royalties and coal-related revenues to the state’s non-tax income, a sustained slowdown in fossil-fuel activity could affect fiscal stability, employment, and long-term economic growth,” warned the report, titled “Sustainable Finance for a Just Transition in Odisha.” It called for a sustainable finance framework, including a dedicated transition fund.

The Council on Energy, Environment and Water, a not-for-profit policy institution and think tank based in New Delhi, published a study in March 2026. It found that 79 percent of the 700-odd respondents believed they would earn less outside coal. The survey was conducted among departmental and contractual workers in underground and opencast mines in Jharsuguda, also in Odisha.

The report, titled “Assessing India’s Coal Mine Workers: Skills, Preferences, and Future Opportunities,” showed that nearly half the workers did not want to relocate for alternative employment. About 61 percent of the respondents perceived very limited employment opportunities outside coal.

The reason is understandable. As many as 73 percent learned on the job, acquiring expertise through observation and practical experience. Only 25 percent had formal training before entering coal work.

The NITI Aayog’s report mentioned above said that over 150 districts across India are significantly dependent on fossil-fuel supply chains, directly or indirectly sustaining livelihoods for nearly one-third of India’s population.

According to their estimate, about 345,000 workers are employed in coal mines, while the informal workforce in this industry is at least twice as large, which means that over a million people are directly dependent on coal mining. The report says that approximately 178,000 formal mining jobs could be affected by 2030. At least twice as many informal jobs could be potentially affected.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-20 02:53 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Update on the situation in Ukraine, with a focus on European leaders' stance.

Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders â Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron â were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.

He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity."

"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying: "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."

Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.

The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.…

item.title: Finding Steadiness When the Ground Feels Shaky
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear, well-structured English with useful vocabulary and concrete detail

Finding Steadiness When the Ground Feels Shaky

By Leo Babauta

These days, the world (and our lives) can feel out of control — alarming news, a wild political situation, global warming and economic markets all in turmoil.

When things feel this shaky and out of control, our emotions can spiral and it throws our lives into chaos. What can we do?

The practice I’m going to share with you today is how to find internal steadiness, when everything around you is unsteady.

The practice is to focus on attending to our internal state. To find calm and peace no matter what’s happening externally.

Let’s dive into it!

Focusing on What We Can Control

We can’t control the markets, what’s happening politically, how other people are acting, the ongoing climate change crisis, or the AI revolution. When things feel out of control, it can send us spinning.

So our practice will focus on what we can control: putting our attention on our internal state. We can’t necessarily control our inner state — if it’s in turmoil, we can’t always stop that — but just by resting our attention gently on the inner state, things can start to calm.

So let’s talk about how to practice.

How to Practice

First, just notice that you’re feeling shaky. Maybe you’re feeling a lot of uncertainty and overwhelm, maybe frustration or anger, maybe you’re feeling shaken up and in turmoil. Just notice it, and name it: what are you feeling?

Don’t get caught up in thoughts about what you’re feeling, or judgments. Just notice that it’s there, and name it. Don’t add a whole narrative, or catastrophize about it. It’s not a big deal to feel something.

Next, just rest your attention gently on the sensations of the feeling. That means notice how the feeling feels in your body, as physical sensations. Does it feel tight, does it move around? Just bring awareness to the physical sensation, and keep your awareness there — stay with it.

Breathe deeply and slowly, soothing your nervous system.

Let yourself settle down in the moment with whatever you’re feeling. It’s OK to feel turmoil — can you sit calmly in the center of the storm of what you’re feeling? This takes practice, so don’t expect to be any good at it at first. But you’ll start to get the hang of it, if you practice a few times a day for just a minute or two.

Slowly, you’ll develop the ability to sit calmly and openly in the middle of any storm.

And that’s when you’ll feel powerful: because you don’t need the world to change to find your inner calm. It’s always there, always accessible, and always beautiful.

item.title: The Human Habits That Still Matter
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

The Human Habits That Still Matter

By Leo Babauta

These days, you can’t avoid hearing and thinking about AI — it’s all around us, and it’s taking over the world. So much of our lives are being automated … which in some ways is breathtaking.

In other ways, I think we can all feel that we’re losing something.

This is a moment to stop and reflect: what is important to remain human? What human skills do we want to protect?

Let’s explore some of those very human habits that we can’t let fall to the bots.

The Habits That Matter

While AI can generate a lot of amazing things, and help us in incredible ways … there are some things that are ours, as humans:

- Being present: The AI bots can’t actually be present with us. That’s for humans to do with each other. There’s something in our nervous system that gets soothed when we’re in the loving presence of someone we care about. There’s something that opens in us when we’re present with someone we’re learning about.

- Caring: One thing we notice from AI generated stuff is that it’s very intelligent … but there’s no feeling that it cares. Of course not — because AI doesn’t care. That’s for us humans to do, and it’s incredibly important in our lives. We can’t lose connection to what we care deeply about.

- Sitting with discomfort: I think technology is slowly seeping away our ability to be OK with discomfort. Our phones, computers, social media, AI, and the abundance of entertainment means that we can be comfortable all the time. But it’s a very human capacity to allow ourselves to sit in the middle of discomfort. And it matters: it’s how we expand, connect with each other, have difficult conversations where we disagree, and meet our resistance to doing hard things.

- Choosing what matters: Sometimes, we want things to be chosen for us, because we have so much decision fatigue. But AI can’t choose what matters, because nothing matters to it. That’s for us — we have to think deeply about what matters to us, and choose to step in that direction.

The Habit of Being Human

All of this is a choice: we can choose to care, to sit with discomfort, to be present with the world and each other, and decide for ourselves what matters.

And it’s a choice we can make a habit — something we do regularly, because we care about these human things. Because they matter to us.

I encourage us to make it a habit to do our focused work — the work that matters to us — in the presence of another human being. And have conversations with them, even if it’s uncomfortable. Go deeper, and discover something new together, without reaching for AI.

Notice when you reach for technology when you’re uncomfortable, bored, feeling resistance or uncertainty. And then turn towards that, as a human habit. Feel it. Only we can feel boredom, and sit with that discomfort. In this place, the deepest discoveries of humanity have been made. What would Aristotle, the Buddha, Epictetus, Shakespeare, Tolstoy, Jane Austen, Newton have created, if they had technology to keep them from being bored?

Choose to care about what you work on, what you put your attention on, who you spend your time with. Find a deeper appreciation for each of these, in each moment. Let yourself be filled with wonder, that great human experience that’s always available to us.

Slow down, and let yourself savor human connection and weirdness and huge loving hearts.

These are the human habits I urge you to care about. Automation will eat the tasks. But we are so much wilder than our tasks.

Source: Zen Habits | Published: 2026-09-25 00:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: How to Stop Trying to Optimize Your Life
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

How to Stop Trying to Optimize Your Life

By Leo Babauta

These days, so many people are trying to optimize their lives in every way — and I’m as guilty as anyone. Life optimization seems to be the theme for many of us.

But the thing is … it never ends. You can spend months trying to optimize every facet of your life … and you will still feel like more needs to be done. That’s because underneath the optimization mindset is the hidden message: My life as is at the moment isn’t good enough.

We want to optimize our health because our fear is that we’re not going to be able to handle the future without it. We want to optimize our productivity because we judge ourselves for not being more productive. We want to optimize our morning routines, sleep routines, finances, and more … because we fear that we’re not doing good enough at life.

This mindset stems from a fundamental dissatisfaction with our lives and ourselves.

We’re always looking toward a better future, instead of just living with gratitude in the life we already have in front of us.

This comes at a cost: we put pressure on ourselves, it stresses us out, we are comparing our lives to everyone else on social media, we’re rushing (because going slow isn’t optimal), we always feel behind, never done. Does any of that sound familiar?

So what can we do instead?

Let’s lay out some credos of the Unoptimized Life.

- Let some things be sub-optimal. It’s worth asking yourself why you want everything to be optimal — is there a fear that if it’s not the most optimal, you’ll be doing things wrong or failing? Entire industries have been formed on people wanting to optimize everything, and being afraid of missing out on what’s the absolute best. It’s OK to be inefficient or suboptimal, if it means hours of less stress. Have fun with a task, enjoy the activity, don’t worry about perfection. Wander and explore.

- Let yourself do things without an outcome in mind. What if you could start something and not need to get to a certain place. I’m learning the game of Go right now, and it’s fun to just learn for the sake of learning, without needing to “get good” or achieve a certain rank.

- Practice getting to “good enough.” Not everything needs to be absolutely perfect — in fact, most things don’t. You might explore getting to good enough … and then stopping there, and being satisfied with that.

- Don’t focus much on metrics. Sure, some things need to be tracked, but not everything does. Lots of meaningful things are better without being tracked or measured for progress.

- The big one: from improvement to appreciation. Instead of asking, “How can I make this even better?” … you might ask, “What’s already beautiful about this?” The practice of appreciation is deep and powerful.

Let yourself be human. You’re not an improvement project. You don’t have to always upgrade.

Growth is fun, but having a death grip on progress and perfection takes all the fun out of it. Let it be joyful! Let it come from curiosity and enjoyment, rather than all the ways we feel inadequate.

And practice just being here, without having to get anywhere.

Source: Zen Habits | Published: 2026-09-18 00:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The Phone Addiction Loop, & How to Break It
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

The Phone Addiction Loop, & How to Break It

By Leo Babauta

I’ve talked to close to a dozen people recently who have been struggling with phone addiction — it seems to be widespread, across all generations these days.

It’s not just a trivial problem … it can cause sleep problems, have us fall behind on the things that are important to us, miss deadlines, get overwhelmed by how behind we are.

And maybe just as important: it’s not how many of us want to live our lives. We don’t want to be trapped in a phone addiction loop. We want to be doing things that feel meaningful and joyful.

Let’s talk about the phone addiction loop, and then how to apply the habit ideas I’ve learned over the years to break the loop.

How the Loop Works

It’s a fairly basic habit mechanism:

- You have a trigger (let’s say stress, overwhelm, boredom, feeling behind on things).

- You reach for the phone

- You get a quick reward.

And repeat. That’s the cycle, and it works that way for most addictive habits (food, alcohol, games, Youtube, social media, smoking, drugs).

So how do we change this?

First, Ask Why

Before you start to change something like this, ask yourself why you want to make the change. Is it just because you think you should, and you’re judging yourself?

If you’re coming from a place of “should,” you’ll just give up as soon as it gets hard.

If you’re doing it because you think there’s something wrong with you, and you’re hard on yourself … you’re only going to get discouraged and give up.

So instead, find a positive reason that’s meaningful to you. For example:

- I want to get good sleep and feel good during the day

- I have some creative work I want to get done

- I want to be more present with my loved ones

- I want to read more books

- I want to get more active and take good care of my body

What would be your meaningful reason? Write it down.

Then Create a Commitment & a Moat

Now make a commitment … not just to yourself but to others. Promise a close friend, your partner, an accountability group. Tell them your plan. Commit to accountability.

Then create a moat — something that makes it hard to get to the phone when the trigger happens. This will allow you to have awareness that your addiction loop has been triggered, and then allow you to do the next phase (below).

Some examples of moats:

- Put the phone in a different room, so you have to walk all the way across the house/office to get it. Leave it there, and only give yourself 2 minutes in the room with it.

- Give it to your spouse/friend/coworker and say, “Don’t give it back to me until (5pm, tomorrow morning, etc.).”

- Use a blocker app (or device like the Brick) but let someone else set the password so you don’t know it. Have it set to block you on a schedule.

- Lock it in a drawer/safe with a key, give it to someone else.

You might also make the phone less attractive: put it in greyscale mode, turn off notifications, and delete the most tempting apps.

The idea isn’t that you can never use your phone — it’s that the friction to use it is greatly increased, so that you are more intentional, and you know when the trigger is happening.

Deal with the Trigger

The secret sauce is not just to stop yourself from using it, but to find new ways of dealing with the trigger — usually boredom, anxiety/stress, overwhelm, or feeling bad about yourself.

If you’re feeling that, instead of using your phone to cope … what if you could find a healthier coping mechanism?

It’s important to bring awareness to when the trigger happens … when it does:

- Notice what you’re feeling when you want to reach for your phone. Bored? Feeling stressed, overwhelmed, anxious? Feeling bad about yourself or your life?

- Take a few breaths. Let your nervous system be soothed. If the feeling is intense, get up and move around, distract yourself with something else. You’re creating a tiny pause, where you have choice.

- Now try to choose an alternative to cope with the feeling, other than your phone.

What alternatives? You might experiment to see what works for you — throw a bunch of things at the wall and see what sticks!

Here are a few ideas:

- Deep breathing

- Go for a walk

- Do some exercise — pushups, yoga, etc.

- Talk to someone

- Make a gratitude journal — or just journal about your feelings

You might find your own ideas as well. You’re practicing being OK with a bit of discomfort, and finding a way to deal with it that feels healthy.

The Importance of Grace & Compassion

This isn’t going to be simple — like food, a phone isn’t something most of us can just quit. We have to find a balance in our lives, between being able to function, and overdoing it.

We’re interrupting the loop, instead of relying on willpower. We might even set some phone-free periods that will start to feel refreshing.

But we might slip up, and that’s OK. It’s a process, not a switch we just flip. We’re trying to break the loop rather than let it be a repeated cycle. Sometimes, we might not do so well, and in those cases, it’s important to give ourselves some grace. Be compassionate, not harsh.

You can do this!

Source: Zen Habits | Published: 2026-09-12 00:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: When the Work Feels Hard
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

When the Work Feels Hard

By Leo Babauta

Sometimes, it just feels like the work you’ve got in front of you is hard: you aren’t feeling up to it, you want to turn to distractions.

That’s completely normal — most of have these days. Or weeks, or even months, when things just feel hard. It’s important not to be too tough on ourselves, and give ourselves grace for not being super fired up and productive all the time. We’re human.

That said, how do we deal with this feeling that the work is hard? There isn’t a simple answer, so I’m going to share a handful of ideas with you today.

1: Take a temperature check

As humans, we have so many things that might affect whether we feel motivated or not. It’s good to do a bit of a reflection, and see what might be contributing. That’ll help you sort it out.

Some things to check on:

- How’s your sleep been lately?

- Are you feeling high stress from your life, or high anxiety in general? Is your life outside of work super busy or chaotic?

- Have you been moving your body, in ways that make you feel generally healthy? Do you have health issues affecting you?

- Has something happened that got you feeling low? Is it possible you’re suffering from mild (or worse) depression?

- Is there something about the work you’re doing that’s scary, or that gives you a lot of resistance or overwhelm, that you’re trying to avoid? Are there unknowns that are making it feel tough?

- Anything distracting you that you’re obsessed with? Anything weighing on you heavily? Any grief or anger?

You might have more than one of these be true, or maybe it’s something else. The key idea is to take a brief assessment — be honest with yourself.

Once you have an idea of what might be making things hard, it can help to start to address them. If you have depression, get some mental health support. If you are having some emotional issues, talk to somebody, or do some journaling, to process the emotions. If there’s fear or overwhelm, can you make it smaller so it’s less scary and overwhelming?

There might not be easy answers, but at least taking a look at the issues and starting to address them is the way to go. Small steps. The idea of “work is too hard” is the symptom, not the problem.

2: Let yourself play

If work is feeling too hard … then let yourself play. Take a break from the hard things and then go have some fun doing something else! It might be work, or it might be getting outside and exploring, without a phone. Or reading something fun.

Then, after a bit of a break (for an hour, or a day, or more if needed and possible) … come back to the work but bring a lighter sense of play.

There isn’t a right way to bring play to your work … play with it! Be lighthearted, and have fun.

3: Stay in relationship with the work

Just because the work is hard, doesn’t mean you have to just walk away from it. You might not be able to completely go full in with it … but you can stay connected to the work.

Stay in relationship with the work — meaning don’t just drop off.

That might mean just doing a little work for the next few days, whatever you can manage. It might mean letting people know you can’t get things done when they’re expecting it, and renegotiating deadlines or other dates.

It could also mean taking a part of your work that feels meaningful — just a chunk of it — and going somewhere else to work on it. Go to a coffee shop, or a park, or a library. Play some relaxing music (in your earbuds, if you’re in public!).

Or let yourself go for a long walk, and just reflect on things. It’s a way to go deeper without doing the part that feels too hard.

4: Work your way back

If you do fall away from the work a bit, it can be hard to come back to it. That’s OK, it’s just a bit like going uphill instead of walking on normal ground. Sometimes we have to go uphill, right?

The idea is to find a way to ease yourself back into it. It’s harder coming back, so take small steps. Don’t expect yourself to be running right away.

When I come back after falling off, I give myself gentle days, and just do some of the easy stuff. Small batches, with breaks. Make it lighthearted.

What would be an easy way to bring yourself back?

Source: Zen Habits | Published: 2026-09-04 00:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The Mental Habits We Practice the Most
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

The Mental Habits We Practice the Most

By Leo Babauta

There’s an old idea, often misattributed to Aristotle, that “we are what we repeatedly do.” That idea is true of our physical acts, but also of our mental habits.

What we’re practicing the most is what we think every day, and that becomes who we are.

For example, if we’re constantly complaining (even just in our own minds), that’s what we’re practicing all the time … and that shapes our experience of life, and how we impact other people.

The mental habits we’re practicing all day long are incredibly important in our lives — and yet we’re often not even aware we’re doing them.

Some of the most common mental habits that can have negative impacts on our lives:

- Complaint

- Blaming others

- Telling ourselves it’s OK to put something important off for one more day

- Deciding we need to check email, messages, social media one more time before focusing on the things that matter

- Self-criticism

- Judging other people

- Worrying about what everyone else thinks

- Ruminating on past mistakes or past hurts

- Limiting ourselves by how we see ourselves (I’m not smart enough to do that)

- Worrying about the future or possible failure

- Stressing ourselves out with all the things we think we need to do

- Getting stuck in indecision because it’s overwhelming or hard to choose the “right” decision

Do any of these feel familiar? They all have a big impact on our lives if we’re practicing them over and over, every day.

Let’s talk about how to shift these patterns by practicing new ones.

Practicing Different Mental Habits

The idea is to come up with replacement habits, and to practice them every day, as often as you can.

Start by noticing which negative mental patterns you practice regularly — do you notice any of the ones above?

Try to spot them as they happen: if you’re complaining, can you notice when you’re in the act of complaining?

Then practice the replacement mental habit. If you do this, you’ll start to replace the old habit with the new one, and it will start to become your default over time. It takes concerted effort, but the payoff is huge.

Some ideas for replacement mental habits:

- Gratitude and appreciation instead of complaint

- Taking responsibility for your part, instead of blaming others

- Putting important things as a priority that you’re committed to, instead of putting it off for one more day

- Focusing on the things that matter first, before allowing yourself to check email, messages, social media

- Self-appreciation, instead of self-criticism

- Appreciating the great quality of other people, instead of judging them

- Caring about what you think, instead of worrying about what everyone else thinks

- Acceptance, instead of ruminating on past mistakes or past hurts

- Expanding our view of ourselves, instead of limiting ourselves by how we see ourselves

- Focusing on what we can control, instead of worrying about the future or possible failure

- Focusing on one thing right now, instead of stressing ourselves out with all the things we think we need to do

- Making a choice from the gut, instead of getting stuck in indecision because it’s overwhelming or hard to choose the “right” decision

You might have other ideas for replacements — that’s OK, these are just ideas. Decide for yourself what would be most helpful.

In the end, it’s about deciding what we want to practice every day — the things that will lead to the lives we want, or that will keep us stuck.

Source: Zen Habits | Published: 2026-08-28 00:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://zenhabits.net/mental-habits/

item.title: The September Health & Fitness Challenge
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

The September Health & Fitness Challenge

One of the hardest things to do as we create a better life is to show up for yourself regularly.

But we can train that. And one of my favorite ways to do that is with a health & fitness challenge — where you commit to showing up for your body and yourself every day. And prove to yourself that you (and your health) matter.

In September, I’m launching a 6-week Health & Fitness Challenge for my Fearless Living Academy members … and I’d love for you to join us!

Here’s how the challenge works:

- Sign up for Fearless Living Academy and then join the challenge in our Circle space (our community forum).

- Commit yourself to something every day for 6 weeks. You choose: some fitness challenge (yoga every day, running and weightlifting alternately every day, eating 5 vegetables a day, etc.).

- You get a video each week from me, meant to help you practice showing up for your commitment.

- Hold yourself accountable each week, and share how it’s going with the challenge group.

- Learn, grow, get stronger, and build the muscle of showing up!

It’ll be fun!

What You’ll Walk Away With

Here’s what we’re aiming for you to get out of this:

- You’ll learn about what it’s like to show up for your body, and learn what gets in the way (and how to handle that).

- You’ll create a non-negotiable habit that you chose and tested over the course of 6 weeks.

- You’ll start to recognize your patterns, and your own sabotage triggers (travel, stress, low motivation days), because you’ll have hit them during the challenge and practiced navigating them.

- You’ll learn a repeatable framework for creating any kind of practice for yourself going forward.

This challenge, then, becomes proof-of-concept for how you build solid habits in general.

This isn’t a fitness challenge that focuses on streaks or perfection, nor one that is focused on a specific outcome (lose weight, etc.).

This is processed-focused, and it’s a practice of fearlessness — show up for yourself even when it’s challenging.

Six Weekly Themes

Our structure is to have a new theme for each of the 6 weeks:

- Commit & Start: Pick your daily action, and make it small and doable. Declare it publicly, and get started!

- Show Up with Curiosity: Start to explore the habit, and bring curiosity — see what you can discover and appreciate about the habit process.

- Find Your Resistance: Identify exactly when/why you want to skip it (mornings? travel? mood?) — get curious, not critical.

- Build Your System: Design your environment. Remove friction, set up new reminders, find workarounds for your obstacles.

- Push Through the Middle: The motivation dip often happens by week 5 … this week is about identity (“I’m someone who does this”) over motivation.

- Reflect: Reflect on the 6 weeks, decide what stays post-challenge, celebrate the proof of what you care about.

It’ll take 6 weeks to build this deeper self-trust that you’ll show up for yourself Not perfectly. And it won’t be easy. But you’ll practice curiosity, courage, and a willingness to learn in the midst of the challenge.

Are you ready to join us? Join Fearless Living Academy for the September Health & Fitness Challenge, and let’s start.

item.title: One Tab, One Task, One Breath
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

One Tab, One Task, One Breath

By Leo Babauta

Let’s do a quick test: how many tabs do you have open right now? How many apps on your phone or computer? How many tasks are competing for your attention right now?

Let’s also be honest about something: most of us are working in a constant state of fragmentation — so much so that it feels completely normal, and don’t even notice the effects it has on us.

I blame the environment rather than the individual person — but that said, I think there are things we can do to change our environment and reclaim our focus and our sanity.

The Fragmentation Problem

Our work environments have us constantly surrounded by things trying to claim our attention. This creates busyness and fragmented attention, and sacrifices depth and focus.

Every email, every message, every open tab is another claim on our attention. It drains our cognitive bandwidth.

As a result, we’re always half-present. Half in, no matter what we’re doing.

And again, it’s not a failure of you as a person — it’s just the environment that has been created all around you.

The Three-Part Practice

We can reclaim that bandwidth and focus with a three-part practice …

One Tab: Close every tab and app that isn’t the work you have to do right now. You might have a million tabs open — save them or close them. You don’t need them all right now. Close any open apps that you don’t need. Put your phone in silent mode and put it somewhere else as well. Clear everything so you can reclaim your attention.

One Task: Before you sit down to do something, name the one thing you’re going to actually focus on. You might need to open your task list and take a look, but choose something. Commit to focusing on it. It can also help to set a timer, for 10 or 20 or 30 minutes, to remind you that you’re focusing on one task right now.

One Breath: Before you begin on your one task, take a slow, deep, conscious breath. Be fully present with the breath, and let it release any tension you have. Let it be a prayer to start your task with focus and intention.

This breath signals that you’re present for this one task. Everything else is put on hold — in fact, there’s nothing else in the universe but this one thing.

This is a simple, powerful ritual to signal your conscious intention and to practice the focus that you’d like to have in your life.

The Practice Needs to Be Simple

With everything demanding our attention, we need to simplify in order to reshape our focus.

That’s why this practice is so simple. We narrow everything down to one tab, one task, one breath. And in doing so, we are retraining our brains to simplify.

This is radical simplicity — not necessarily doing less, but being fully present with what we choose to do.

Source: Zen Habits | Published: 2026-08-21 00:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://zenhabits.net/one/
